title: How Wicket localizes
text: Where the locale of a page comes from, why texts live in properties files next to the components that use them, and why the page can override its panels.
keywords: i18n internationalization l10n translation locale language resource bundle properties file style variation skin browser language Accept-Language
body: Wicket localizes an application with the same building blocks as Java: a java.util.Locale that names a language and country, and properties files with keys and translated texts. What Wicket adds is where it looks for those files. Instead of one bundle for the whole application, every page, panel and component can have its own, and Wicket searches them along the component tree. The exact search order is listed in Where Wicket looks for texts; this page explains the ideas behind it.

title: Markup or properties
text: You can localize in two places. Properties files hold texts, and the markup refers to them with <wicket:message> or receives them through models. A localized ma
body: You can localize in two places. Properties files hold texts, and the markup refers to them with <wicket:message> or receives them through models. A localized markup file, HomePage_de.html next to HomePage.html, replaces the whole layout for that language. Properties files keep one layout for all languages, so a change to the page has to be made only once. Localized markup files suit pages where the languages differ in more than words: a legal text that is structured differently per country, or a layout for a right-to-left script. Most applications use properties files and add a localized markup file for the few pages that need one.

title: One mechanism for every text
text: The lookup is the same for every text Wicket shows. Component#getString, ResourceModel, StringResourceModel, <wicket:message>, the error messages of validators
apis: Component ResourceModel StringResourceModel Localizer Application ResourceBundle
body: The lookup is the same for every text Wicket shows. Component#getString, ResourceModel, StringResourceModel, <wicket:message>, the error messages of validators and converters, and the placeholder text of a drop-down all go through the Localizer, which asks a chain of string resource loaders. A validator you write can ship its messages in a properties file next to its class. Wicket’s own messages, such as '${label}' is required. and the messages of its validators, live in the bundle of the Application class, near the end of the search, so that your bundles can replace them. Because the loaders form a chain, you can add your own, for example to read texts from a database or from an existing Java ResourceBundle: see Load texts from your own source. For the everyday work of translating a page, see Translate component texts.

title: Style and variation
text: Besides the locale, two strings take part in the lookup: the style and the variation. The style belongs to the session (Session#setStyle) and stands for a skin
body: Besides the locale, two strings take part in the lookup: the style and the variation. The style belongs to the session (Session#setStyle) and stands for a skin or brand, such as a white-label version of the application for one customer. The variation belongs to a component (Component#getVariation, inherited from the parent) and stands for a version of that component, such as a compact layout of a panel. Both become part of the file name, ProductPanel_compact_acme_de.properties, and Wicket tries the names with style and variation before the plain name. The same names apply to markup files and package resources, so a style can change texts, markup and CSS together, while every file that has no styled version falls back to the plain one.

title: Texts belong to components
text: A Java ResourceBundle has one base name and is looked up once. Wicket reuses the naming scheme of bundles, Name_de_CH.properties, but runs its own lookup over m
body: A Java ResourceBundle has one base name and is looked up once. Wicket reuses the naming scheme of bundles, Name_de_CH.properties, but runs its own lookup over many files: the bundle of the page, of each component on the path to the component that needs the text, of their superclasses, of their packages and of the application. The reason is reuse. A panel that is shipped in a library brings its own texts in a properties file next to its class, just as it brings its markup file. Whoever uses the panel does not have to copy its keys into an application-wide bundle, and translating the panel means adding DatePanel_nl.properties beside it. The same holds for class hierarchies. A BasePage.properties provides texts for every page that extends BasePage, and a subclass can override single keys in its own file, the way markup inheritance lets a subclass fill in parts of the base markup.

title: Where the locale comes from
text: When Wicket creates a session, it takes the locale from the request, which the servlet container derives from the Accept-Language header that the browser sends.
body: When Wicket creates a session, it takes the locale from the request, which the servlet container derives from the Accept-Language header that the browser sends. A visitor whose browser prefers German gets a session with a German locale, without any code in your application. Components do not store a locale. Component#getLocale() asks the parent, which asks its parent, up to the page, which asks the session. So Session#setLocale switches the whole user interface at once, from the next render on. Override getLocale() on a panel to render that part of a page in another language, for example a preview of an email in the language of its recipient. Everything that depends on the language reads the locale this way: the lookup of texts, the choice of markup files, and the converters that format and parse numbers and dates in form fields and labels. A Dutch user types 3,5 and a British user 3.5, and both end up with the same Double.

title: Why the page wins over its panels
text: When a label inside a panel inside a page asks for a text, Wicket looks in the bundle of the page first, then the panel, then the label. That order surprises pe
body: When a label inside a panel inside a page asks for a text, Wicket looks in the bundle of the page first, then the panel, then the label. That order surprises people who expect the most specific file to win, but it follows from reuse. Picture three teams. Team A writes a reusable panel with its own texts. Team B builds a larger component that contains A’s panel, and wants one of the texts to read differently. Team C puts B’s component on a page, and later the customer asks for yet another wording on that page. If the innermost bundle won, B and C would have to change code they do not own. Because the outer bundle wins, B overrides A in B’s bundle and C overrides both in the page bundle, and nobody touches the component they use. Keys can also be aimed at one component. In the bundle of a page, form.name.Required applies only to the component at path form:name, while Required applies to every component that asks for that key. This lets one page bundle hold different texts for different instances of the same panel.

title: Models and component data
text: Why a component reads its data through a model, what happens to that data between requests, and why wrapping an entity in Model goes wrong.
keywords: data binding getObject setObject detach serialization NotSerializableException LazyInitializationException stale data entity raw object
apis: IModel IDetachable Model LoadableDetachableModel Label TextField
body: A Wicket component does not hold the value it shows. A Label does not keep its text, and a TextField does not keep the value it edits. Each one holds a model: an object the component asks for the value whenever it needs it, and hands a new value to when the user submits one. The model is all the component knows about its data. Whether that data lives in a field, a database or a resource bundle is the model’s business.

title: A page outlives the request that built it
text: A Wicket page lives longer than a request. Its constructor runs once. After that, the same page handles every click, form submit and Ajax call on it, sometimes
body: A Wicket page lives longer than a request. Its constructor runs once. After that, the same page handles every click, form submit and Ajax call on it, sometimes for an hour. A component that copied its value in the constructor would show that value for the life of the page. // The text is fixed when the constructor runs add(new Label("total", order.getTotal())); // The model is asked again every time the label renders add(new Label("total", orderModel.map(Order::getTotal))); The second label shows the current total after a form on the same page changed the order. That is the point of the indirection: the component asks late, at the moment it renders or processes input, and the model decides what “the current value” means.

title: Between requests the page is serialized
text: At the end of a request, Wicket stores every stateful page that took part in it, so that the next request and the back button can find it again. Storing means s
body: At the end of a request, Wicket stores every stateful page that took part in it, so that the next request and the back button can find it again. Storing means serializing: Wicket writes the page and everything reachable from it to the page store. That includes the components, their behaviors, their models and the objects the models hold. How pages are stored describes where they go. Two things follow from this. The objects your models hold must be serializable, which is why Model only accepts Serializable values and why a NotSerializableException usually names a field in one of your components. And whatever a model holds is copied to the store after every request: a list of ten thousand rows in a Model is written to disk each time the user clicks.

title: Detaching: drop the data, keep the key
text: Before the page is stored, Wicket detaches it. It calls detach() on every component, and each component detaches its model and its behaviors. A model that can f
body: Before the page is stored, Wicket detaches it. It calls detach() on every component, and each component detaches its model and its behaviors. A model that can find its data again uses this moment to let go of it. LoadableDetachableModel works this way. It keeps the loaded object in a transient field, clears that field on detach, and calls load() again the first time it is asked for the object in a later request. Only what load() needs is serialized, usually an id. Over two requests, a detachable model that shows person 42 goes through these steps: Request 1: the label renders and calls getObject(). The model loads person 42 from the database. End of request 1: detach() clears the person. The page is stored with the id 42 and nothing else. Request 2: the page is read back. The first getObject() loads person 42 again, as the database has it now. Every model is detachable, since IModel extends IDetachable, but not every model has something to drop. Model keeps its value. A lambda model keeps what the lambda captured. A model that derives from another model, such as one made with map, passes the detach on to the model it came from.

title: Models a component finds on its own
text: A component created without a model asks its parents for one. When a parent holds a model that implements IComponentInheritedModel, the component gets a model d
body: A component created without a model asks its parents for one. When a parent holds a model that implements IComponentInheritedModel, the component gets a model derived from it. CompoundPropertyModel is the common case: it gives each child a model for the property named by the child’s id. A form with a CompoundPropertyModel of a person and a TextField with id email edits the person’s email without any model code on the field. Bind components to a JavaBean shows this in a form.

title: Static and dynamic models
text: A model that holds a value, like Model, is static: getObject() returns what was put in. A model that computes its value each time from something else is dynamic
body: A model that holds a value, like Model, is static: getObject() returns what was put in. A model that computes its value each time from something else is dynamic. Lambda models, LambdaModel, PropertyModel and models made with map read their source at every call, and LoadableDetachableModel reads it once per request. When a value shown on a page must follow changes to other data, it needs a dynamic model. The choice comes down to where the data lives: A value the page owns: Model, or a lambda on a field of the page. A property of an object another model holds: lambda models or property models. Data from a database or service: a detachable model. A value that depends on another model’s current value: a chained model. Model classes lists every model class in wicket-core.

title: The IModel interface
text: A model is any implementation of IModel<T>. It has one abstract method, getObject(). setObject(T) has a default implementation that throws UnsupportedOperationE
apis: IModel UnsupportedOperationException Label LocalTime GenericPanel GenericWebPage
body: A model is any implementation of IModel<T>. It has one abstract method, getObject(). setObject(T) has a default implementation that throws UnsupportedOperationException, so a model is read-only unless it overrides it. detach() has an empty default. The other methods, such as map, filter and orElse, are defaults that build new models from an existing one. Because IModel has a single abstract method, a lambda is a model: add(new Label("now", () -> LocalTime.now())); A component has at most one model of its own, its default model (getDefaultModel(), setDefaultModel()). GenericPanel and GenericWebPage add typed versions, getModel() and getModelObject(). One model can serve several components: a form and its fields share the form’s object, and a label and a link can show and act on the same person. Components use the model at fixed moments. A Label calls getObject() while it renders and converts the result to text. A form component calls setObject() when its form is submitted and the input is valid. Between those moments the component does not touch the data. See How a form is processed for the order of those calls in a submit.

title: Why new Model<>(entity) goes wrong
text: This code works on the first render: Person person = personService.findById(id); add(new PersonPanel("person", Model.of(person))); The trouble starts after the
body: This code works on the first render: Person person = personService.findById(id); add(new PersonPanel("person", Model.of(person))); The trouble starts after the first request: The whole entity is serialized with the page, along with everything it references: lazily loaded collections, proxies, sometimes a reference to the persistence session. You get a NotSerializableException, or pages that are much larger than they need to be. On the next request the panel works with a deserialized copy that belongs to no persistence context. Touching a lazy collection throws LazyInitializationException, and saving the copy can overwrite what another user changed in the meantime. The copy never changes. When someone else edits the person, this page keeps showing the old values until the user opens a new page. Passing the entity to a component’s constructor and keeping it in a field has the same effect, because the field is serialized in the same way, and the component can no longer get at fresh data. Give the component a model instead, and make that model one that loads the entity by its id. Load data once per request with detachable models shows how. Model is the right choice for values that belong to the page itself: the search term the user typed, the selected tab, a small value object.

title: How Wicket serves resources
text: What resources and resource references are, why components carry their own CSS and JavaScript, and how Wicket gives every file a cacheable URL.
keywords: static files assets static vs dynamic resource URL wicket/resource caching cache busting versioning -ver- header contribution
apis: IResource ResourceReference PackageResourceReference AbstractResource IHeaderResponse ResourceAggregator ResourceReferenceRegistry
body: A web page is more than its HTML. The browser also fetches stylesheets, scripts, images and fonts, and an application often hands out files it builds on request: a CSV export, a PDF invoice, a chart. Wicket calls all of these resources, and it serves them through the same request handling that serves pages.

title: A resource answers a request of its own
text: A resource is an object that implements IResource. That interface has one method, respond(IResource.Attributes), and the attributes give the resource the reques
apis: IResource Attributes PackageResource ContextRelativeResource FileSystemResource CaptchaImageResource AbstractResource Content Disposition Last Modified ResourceResponse
body: A resource is an object that implements IResource. That interface has one method, respond(IResource.Attributes), and the attributes give the resource the request, the response and the page parameters. Whatever the resource writes to the response is what the browser receives. Resources come in two flavours, and the difference is only in how much work respond does: A static resource sends a file that already exists, such as a stylesheet on the classpath or an image in the web application folder. Wicket ships these as PackageResource, ContextRelativeResource and FileSystemResource. A dynamic resource builds its content when the request comes in. CaptchaImageResource in wicket-extensions draws a new captcha image every time, and an export that writes the rows of a database query is dynamic too. You build these by extending AbstractResource, see Generate a resource in code. AbstractResource handles the HTTP side for both: content type, Content-Disposition, Last-Modified, cache headers and byte ranges for media files. A subclass only describes the response in a ResourceResponse and supplies the bytes.

title: Components ask for what they need
text: A component declares the files it needs in renderHead(IHeaderResponse), and a behavior does the same in renderHead(Component, IHeaderResponse). They do not writ
body: A component declares the files it needs in renderHead(IHeaderResponse), and a behavior does the same in renderHead(Component, IHeaderResponse). They do not write <link> or <script> tags; they hand header items to the header response, and Wicket decides what ends up in the page. Behind the header response sits the ResourceAggregator. It collects the items of every visible component on the page and then: renders each file once, however many components ask for it; renders the dependencies of an item before the item itself, see Declare dependencies between resources; swaps members of a bundle for the bundle, see Combine resources into one bundle; sorts the items, with priority items first, see Control the order of header items. Because the header is assembled from items rather than written as text, Wicket can also secure it. Its default Content Security Policy allows only scripts and styles that carry the nonce of the current response, and Wicket adds that nonce to every script and style item it renders. A <script> you type into the markup gets no nonce, and the browser blocks it. That is why the pages in this topic add JavaScript through header items; see Configure the Content Security Policy. The full list of items is in Header items. During an Ajax request the same mechanism runs for the components being updated. Wicket sends their header items along with the new markup, and the browser loads only the files that the page does not have yet.

title: Package resources make components self-contained
text: The usual home for a component’s CSS, JavaScript and images is its own Java package, next to its class and its markup. These are package resources, served throu
body: The usual home for a component’s CSS, JavaScript and images is its own Java package, next to its class and its markup. These are package resources, served through PackageResourceReference and its subclasses CssResourceReference and JavaScriptResourceReference. When a component brings its own files, using it means adding it to a page and nothing more. Nobody has to know which stylesheet a date picker needs or copy files into the web application folder. The files travel inside the JAR with the class, and a component library is one dependency. See Serve files from your Java packages. A package also holds class files and configuration that must never reach a browser. The package resource guard decides which files Wicket serves at all; by default only common web file types such as .css, .js, .png and .woff2 pass. See Control which package resources are served.

title: Resource references name a resource
text: Components rarely hold a resource directly. They hold a ResourceReference: a small, serializable name for a resource, made of a scope class, a name, and optiona
body: Components rarely hold a resource directly. They hold a ResourceReference: a small, serializable name for a resource, made of a scope class, a name, and optionally a locale, a style and a variation. The reference creates the actual resource only when it is needed, in getResource(). Separating the name from the thing has three effects: Wicket can write a URL for a resource while it renders a page, without loading or generating the resource. The URL contains the scope and the name, so a later request for that URL can find the reference again. The application keeps references in its ResourceReferenceRegistry, and for package files it creates a reference on the fly when a request names one it has not seen yet. A URL for a package resource keeps working after a restart. Pages stay small when they are serialized: a component stores a few strings, not file contents.

title: Resources and page state
text: A URL for a resource reference does not involve a page: Wicket finds the reference by its key and lets the resource respond. Such URLs work on stateless pages a
body: A URL for a resource reference does not involve a page: Wicket finds the reference by its key and lets the resource respond. Such URLs work on stateless pages and from anywhere, including another site. A ResourceLink that you give an IResource object instead of a reference works differently. The resource is stored in the link, the link’s URL points at the page instance, and the page becomes stateful. Use a reference, a mount or a shared resource when the page must stay stateless; Stateful and stateless pages explains the difference. A mounted or shared resource is one object for the whole application, used by all users and threads at once. It must not keep state about the current user in its fields; it reads what it needs from the request, the session or a service while it responds.

title: URLs that browsers can cache forever
text: The URL of a package resource looks like this: ./wicket/resource/com.example.CalendarPanel/calendar-ver-1712345678000.css After the wicket/resource prefix come
body: The URL of a package resource looks like this: ./wicket/resource/com.example.CalendarPanel/calendar-ver-1712345678000.css After the wicket/resource prefix come the scope class and the file name, and Wicket inserts a version into the file name. In development mode the version is the file’s last-modified time; in deployment mode it is an MD5 digest of the content, computed once. When a request carries the current version, Wicket answers with headers that let browsers and proxies cache the file for a year. The version makes that long cache safe. A changed file gets a new version and so a new URL, and the browser fetches it on the next page view. You never rename files to break a cache, and a deployment never serves a stale stylesheet. The caching strategy is a setting, ResourceSettings#setCachingStrategy, if you need a different scheme.

page: Show that a request is running
title: Show that a request is running
text: Show a busy indicator while an Ajax request runs, with the indicating components, your own component or your own spinner element.
keywords: spinner loading indicator busy indicator throbber progress disable button while submitting double submit
apis: IndicatingAjaxLink IndicatingAjaxButton IndicatingAjaxFallbackLink IAjaxIndicatorAware AjaxIndicatorAppender AjaxDisableComponentListener
body: Use this when an Ajax request can take long enough for the user to wonder whether the click registered. Wicket shows an element while the request runs and hides it when the response is in.

page: Show that a request is running
title: Add the indicator to your own component
text: Any component with an Ajax behavior gets an indicator when it implements IAjaxIndicatorAware and returns the markup id of the indicator element. AjaxIndicatorAp
apis: IAjaxIndicatorAware AjaxIndicatorAppender RefreshPanel Panel String AjaxLink Void Override AjaxRequestTarget ResourceReference
body: Any component with an Ajax behavior gets an indicator when it implements IAjaxIndicatorAware and returns the markup id of the indicator element. AjaxIndicatorAppender renders the default image and gives you that id: public class RefreshPanel extends Panel implements IAjaxIndicatorAware { private final AjaxIndicatorAppender indicator = new AjaxIndicatorAppender(); public RefreshPanel(String id) { super(id); add(indicator); add(new AjaxLink<Void>("refresh") { @Override public void onClick(AjaxRequestTarget target) { // ... } }); } @Override public String getAjaxIndicatorMarkupId() { return indicator.getMarkupId(); } } Wicket looks for an IAjaxIndicatorAware on the component that has the Ajax behavior, then on the behavior itself, then on each parent up to the page. That is why the link inside RefreshPanel shows the panel’s indicator: one implementation covers every Ajax component in the panel. For a different image, pass a ResourceReference to the AjaxIndicatorAppender constructor, or override its getIndicatorUrl().

page: Show that a request is running
title: Disable the button while the request runs
text: AjaxDisableComponentListener from wicket-extensions sets the disabled attribute on the component during the request and removes it afterwards: add(new AjaxButto
body: AjaxDisableComponentListener from wicket-extensions sets the disabled attribute on the component during the request and removes it afterwards: add(new AjaxButton("save") { @Override protected void updateAjaxAttributes(AjaxRequestAttributes attributes) { super.updateAjaxAttributes(attributes); attributes.getAjaxCallListeners().add(new AjaxDisableComponentListener()); } @Override protected void onSubmit(AjaxRequestTarget target) { // ... } }); This works for elements that have a disabled attribute, such as buttons and inputs. How call listeners work is described in React to Ajax requests in JavaScript.

page: Show that a request is running
title: Use an indicating link or button
text: wicket-extensions has variants of the Ajax link and button that render a small animated image after themselves: add(new IndicatingAjaxButton("save") { @Override
apis: IndicatingAjaxButton Override AjaxRequestTarget IndicatingAjaxLink IndicatingAjaxFallbackLink AjaxLink AjaxFallbackLink AjaxButton
body: wicket-extensions has variants of the Ajax link and button that render a small animated image after themselves: add(new IndicatingAjaxButton("save") { @Override protected void onSubmit(AjaxRequestTarget target) { reportService.generate(form.getModelObject()); target.add(result); } }); IndicatingAjaxLink, IndicatingAjaxFallbackLink and IndicatingAjaxButton have the same callbacks as AjaxLink, AjaxFallbackLink and AjaxButton. The image sits in a span with the CSS class wicket-ajax-indicator, which you can style.

page: Show that a request is running
title: Use your own spinner element
text: getAjaxIndicatorMarkupId() can return the id of any element on the page. Wicket removes its hidden attribute when the request starts and sets it again when the
apis: Saving OrderPage WebPage IAjaxIndicatorAware Override String
body:
getAjaxIndicatorMarkupId() can return the id of any element on the page. Wicket removes its hidden attribute when the request starts and sets it again when the request ends, so start with the element hidden: OrderPage.html
Saving your order...
OrderPage.java public class OrderPage extends WebPage implements IAjaxIndicatorAware { @Override public String getAjaxIndicatorMarkupId() { return "order-spinner"; } } Because the page is the last parent Wicket checks, every Ajax component on the page without an indicator of its own uses this one. Wicket counts the running requests, so the element stays visible until the last one is done.

page: Add behavior to a component with a Behavior
title: Add behavior to a component with a Behavior
text: Write a Behavior that changes a component's tag, adds markup around it or contributes CSS and JavaScript, and reuse it on any kind of component.
keywords: mixin decorator onComponentTag beforeRender afterRender renderHead reusable logic cross-cutting add behavior remove behavior isTemporary
body: Use a behavior when the same addition applies to components of different kinds: a CSS class on every required field, a tooltip, a JavaScript widget, a confirmation prompt. Subclassing each component type would mean one subclass per type; a behavior is written once and added to any component with add.

page: Add behavior to a component with a Behavior
title: Add a behavior to many components
text: Behaviors combine with visitors and with your own base classes. To mark every form component in a form: form.visitChildren(FormComponent.class, (component, visi
body: Behaviors combine with visitors and with your own base classes. To mark every form component in a form: form.visitChildren(FormComponent.class, (component, visit) -> component.add(new RequiredMarker())); Run this in onInitialize of the page or form, after the fields have been added.

page: Add behavior to a component with a Behavior
title: Add and remove a behavior
text: TextField<String> name = new TextField<>("name", nameModel); name.setRequired(true); name.add(new RequiredMarker()); add takes several behaviors at once. remove
body: TextField<String> name = new TextField<>("name", nameModel); name.setRequired(true); name.add(new RequiredMarker()); add takes several behaviors at once. remove(behavior) takes one off again; keep a reference to the instance if you need that. getBehaviors(RequiredMarker.class) finds the behaviors of a type on a component.

page: Add behavior to a component with a Behavior
title: Choose the right method to override
text: Method Called bind(Component) when the behavior is added to a component unbind(Component) when the behavior is removed onConfigure(Component) after the componen
body: Method Called bind(Component) when the behavior is added to a component unbind(Component) when the behavior is removed onConfigure(Component) after the component’s own onConfigure, once per request beforeRender(Component) just before the component renders onComponentTag(Component, ComponentTag) while the component’s tag is written afterRender(Component) just after the component rendered renderHead(Component, IHeaderResponse) while Wicket collects the page’s header contributions onEvent(Component, IEvent<?>) when the component receives an event detach(Component) at the end of every request; release models and caches here onRemove(Component) when the component is removed from its parent onException(Component, RuntimeException) when an exception occurs in one of the other methods isEnabled(Component) before each of the above; return false to skip the behavior isTemporary(Component) return true to have the behavior removed at the end of the request getStatelessHint(Component) return false if the behavior makes the page stateful canCallListener(Component) for behaviors with a callback URL: whether a request to it is accepted A behavior that holds no state can be shared: add one instance to many components. Ajax behaviors are bound to a single component and throw an exception when you add them to a second one. For Ajax behaviors, see Ajax behaviors.

page: Add behavior to a component with a Behavior
title: Contribute CSS and JavaScript
text: Override renderHead to add resources to the page when the component is on it. Wicket renders each header item once per page, however many components carry the b
apis: CssResourceReference RequiredMarker Override Component IHeaderResponse CssHeaderItem
body: Override renderHead to add resources to the page when the component is on it. Wicket renders each header item once per page, however many components carry the behavior. private static final CssResourceReference CSS = new CssResourceReference(RequiredMarker.class, "required-marker.css"); @Override public void renderHead(Component component, IHeaderResponse response) { response.render(CssHeaderItem.forReference(CSS)); } For JavaScript that needs the component’s element, call component.setOutputMarkupId(true) in bind and use component.getMarkupId() in renderHead. See Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component.

page: Add behavior to a component with a Behavior
title: Write a behavior
text: Extend Behavior and override the methods for the moments you need. Every method gets the component the behavior is attached to. This one marks required form com
apis: Behavior RequiredMarker Override Component ComponentTag FormComponent
body: Extend Behavior and override the methods for the moments you need. Every method gets the component the behavior is attached to. This one marks required form components: it adds a CSS class to the tag and writes an asterisk after it. RequiredMarker.java public class RequiredMarker extends Behavior { @Override public void onComponentTag(Component component, ComponentTag tag) { if (isRequired(component)) { tag.append("class", "is-required", " "); } } @Override public void afterRender(Component component) { if (isRequired(component)) { component.getResponse().write("*"); } } private boolean isRequired(Component component) { return component instanceof FormComponent field && field.isRequired(); } } beforeRender and afterRender write to the response just before and after the component’s markup. onComponentTag changes the component’s own tag.

A media query goes in a second argument: CssHeaderItem.forReference(CSS, "print"). A reference is a small immutable name, so one static instance per file is enough.

body: A panel, border or page can also put markup into the page header with <wicket:head>. Wicket adds its content once per component class, however many instances are on the page. Inline <script> and <style> in it get no nonce and are blocked like any other inline code, so use it for tags that load files, and wrap those in <wicket:link> so Wicket writes the URLs and the nonce: CalendarPanel.html <wicket:head> <wicket:link> <link rel="stylesheet" href="calendar.css"/> </wicket:link> </wicket:head> <wicket:panel> … </wicket:panel> Header items from renderHead take part in dependencies, ordering and bundles; the content of <wicket:head> does not.

Use it to add a script to any component without subclassing it: public class AutoGrowBehavior extends Behavior { private static final JavaScriptResourceReference JS = new JavaScriptResourceReference(AutoGrowBehavior.class, "autogrow.js"); @Override public void bind(Component component) { component.setOutputMarkupId(true); } @Override public void renderHead(Component component, IHeaderResponse response) { response.render(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(JS)); response.render(OnDomReadyHeaderItem.forScript( "AutoGrow.attach('" + component.getMarkupId() + "');")); } } add(new TextArea<>("comment", commentModel).add(new AutoGrowBehavior())); See Add behavior to a component with a Behavior.

page: Add CSS and JavaScript to a page
title: Keep scripts out of the markup
text: Wicket’s default Content Security Policy only lets the browser run scripts and apply styles that carry the nonce of the current response. Wicket adds the nonce
apis: OnDomReadyHeaderItem JavaScriptHeaderItem Content Security Policy Calendar Today OnEventHeaderItem
body:
Wicket’s default Content Security Policy only lets the browser run scripts and apply styles that carry the nonce of the current response. Wicket adds the nonce to every script and style it renders from a header item, including OnDomReadyHeaderItem and JavaScriptHeaderItem.forScript. Tags you type yourself get no nonce:
…
The browser refuses to run the script and the onclick handler, ignores the style attribute, and reports a violation in its console. Move the code into a file and an OnDomReadyHeaderItem, attach handlers with OnEventHeaderItem or an Ajax behavior, and put styles in a stylesheet with a class. Configure the Content Security Policy shows how to relax the policy if you cannot avoid inline code.

page: Add CSS and JavaScript to a page
title: Run JavaScript when the page is ready
text: Code that sets up the component goes in an OnDomReadyHeaderItem. Give the component a markup id so the script can find its element: public CalendarPanel(String
apis: OnDomReadyHeaderItem CalendarPanel String Override IHeaderResponse JavaScriptHeaderItem Calendar JavaScriptUtils OnLoadHeaderItem OnEventHeaderItem
body: Code that sets up the component goes in an OnDomReadyHeaderItem. Give the component a markup id so the script can find its element: public CalendarPanel(String id) { super(id); setOutputMarkupId(true); } @Override public void renderHead(IHeaderResponse response) { super.renderHead(response); response.render(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(JS)); response.render(OnDomReadyHeaderItem.forScript( "Calendar.init('" + getMarkupId() + "');")); } Wicket collects the ready scripts of all components into one inline script that runs when the DOM is loaded. When an Ajax request replaces the component, the script runs again after the new markup is in place, so the widget is set up again. Escape values from users before you put them in a script, for example with JavaScriptUtils.escapeQuotes. OnDomReadyHeaderItem depends on Wicket’s JavaScript library, which Wicket renders first. By default that library is built on jQuery, so the page also loads jQuery: version 3.7.1. To run code after images and other files have loaded, use OnLoadHeaderItem. To attach a handler to an event of an element, use OnEventHeaderItem.forComponent(component, "click", script). All header item types are listed in Header items.

title: Event and form behaviors
text: All in wicket-core, package org.apache.wicket.ajax and its form subpackage. Class What it does Callback you override AjaxEventBehavior Calls the server when a b
apis: AjaxEventBehavior AjaxRequestTarget AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior RuntimeException OnChangeAjaxBehavior AjaxFormChoiceComponentUpdatingBehavior RadioChoice CheckBoxMultipleChoice RadioGroup CheckGroup AjaxFormSubmitBehavior AjaxFormValidatingBehavior FilesSelectedBehavior FileUploadField List FileDescription AjaxPreventSubmitBehavior AbstractDefaultAjaxBehavior CallbackParameter AjaxButton AjaxFallbackButton
body: All in wicket-core, package org.apache.wicket.ajax and its form subpackage. Class What it does Callback you override AjaxEventBehavior Calls the server when a browser event, such as click or keyup, fires on the component. Takes the event name; an on prefix is cut off. onEvent(AjaxRequestTarget) AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior On the given event, converts and validates the input of its form component and updates the model, without submitting the form. onUpdate(AjaxRequestTarget), onError(AjaxRequestTarget, RuntimeException) OnChangeAjaxBehavior AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior on input and change for text fields and text areas, on change for other components. onUpdate(AjaxRequestTarget) AjaxFormChoiceComponentUpdatingBehavior Updates the model of a group of choices on change: RadioChoice, CheckBoxMultipleChoice, RadioGroup, CheckGroup. onUpdate(AjaxRequestTarget) AjaxFormSubmitBehavior Submits a form with Ajax when the event fires. Without a form argument it submits the form the component is in. onSubmit(AjaxRequestTarget), onError(AjaxRequestTarget), onAfterSubmit(AjaxRequestTarget) AjaxFormValidatingBehavior Submits the form on the given event and refreshes every feedback panel on the page. Add it to a form or to a component in a form. onSubmit, onError, onAfterSubmit, all with an AjaxRequestTarget, optional FilesSelectedBehavior Reports the files picked in a FileUploadField, before they are uploaded. onSelected(AjaxRequestTarget, List<FileDescription>) AjaxPreventSubmitBehavior Stops Enter in a text field from submitting the form. Runs in the browser only. none AbstractDefaultAjaxBehavior Base class for your own Ajax behavior. getCallbackScript() and getCallbackFunction(CallbackParameter...) give the JavaScript that calls it. respond(AjaxRequestTarget) AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior does not work for radio buttons and check boxes in a group; use AjaxFormChoiceComponentUpdatingBehavior there. Override its getUpdateModel() to return false when you want the input validated but the model left alone. AjaxFormSubmitBehavior does not prevent the browser’s default action. On an <input type="submit"> or a <button> in the form, call attributes.setPreventDefault(true) in updateAjaxAttributes, or the form is submitted twice. When shouldTriggerJavaScriptSubmitEvent() returns true, on AjaxFormSubmitBehavior, AjaxButton or AjaxFallbackButton, the behavior fires a JavaScript submit event on the form before it sends the request, so that the form’s submit handlers run. A handler that cancels the event cancels the Ajax request. The default is false.

title: React to Ajax requests in JavaScript
text: Run your own JavaScript before, during and after Ajax requests, for one component with a call listener or for the whole page with global events.
keywords: confirm dialog are you sure precondition beforeSend success handler failure handler Wicket.Event.subscribe /ajax/call/complete /dom/node/removing jqXHR
body: Use this when the browser has to do something around an Ajax request: ask for confirmation first, mark a part of the page as busy, or clean up a JavaScript widget before its markup is replaced. A call listener does this for the requests of one component; global events do it for every request on the page.

page: React to Ajax requests in JavaScript
title: Ask for confirmation before the request
text: Add an AjaxCallListener in updateAjaxAttributes. A precondition that returns false cancels the request: add(new AjaxLink<Void>("delete") { @Override protected v
apis: AjaxCallListener AjaxLink Void Override AjaxRequestAttributes Delete AjaxRequestTarget
body: Add an AjaxCallListener in updateAjaxAttributes. A precondition that returns false cancels the request: add(new AjaxLink<Void>("delete") { @Override protected void updateAjaxAttributes(AjaxRequestAttributes attributes) { super.updateAjaxAttributes(attributes); attributes.getAjaxCallListeners().add(new AjaxCallListener() .onPrecondition("return confirm('Delete this order?');")); } @Override public void onClick(AjaxRequestTarget target) { orders.delete(orderId); target.add(orderList); } }); Each on... method takes the body of a JavaScript function. Wicket wraps it in a function with the arguments listed below and calls it at that stage of the request.

page: React to Ajax requests in JavaScript
title: Clean up a widget before its markup is replaced
text: When a component that a JavaScript library has decorated is refreshed through Ajax, its old element is thrown away and the library is not told. Use /dom/node/re
body: When a component that a JavaScript library has decorated is refreshed through Ajax, its old element is thrown away and the library is not told. Use /dom/node/removing to tear the widget down. The event fires for the replaced element only, so also look inside it: Wicket.Event.subscribe('/dom/node/removing', function (event, element) { var pickers = element.matches('.datepicker') ? [element] : []; element.querySelectorAll('.datepicker').forEach(function (e) { pickers.push(e); }); pickers.forEach(function (picker) { if (picker._flatpickr) { picker._flatpickr.destroy(); } }); }); Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component shows the component side of this.

page: React to Ajax requests in JavaScript
title: Listen to every Ajax request on the page
text: Global events fire for all Ajax requests. Subscribe to them in JavaScript with Wicket.Event.subscribe: Wicket.Event.subscribe('/ajax/call/failure', function (ev
body: Global events fire for all Ajax requests. Subscribe to them in JavaScript with Wicket.Event.subscribe: Wicket.Event.subscribe('/ajax/call/failure', function (event, attrs, jqXHR, errorMessage, textStatus) { console.warn('Ajax request failed', attrs.u, textStatus); }); The first argument is a small event object; the others are the arguments of the matching stage in the table above. Event Fires /ajax/call/init At the init stage. /ajax/call/before At the before stage. /ajax/call/precondition At the precondition stage. /ajax/call/beforeSend Just before the request is sent. /ajax/call/after After the request is sent. /ajax/call/success When the response has been processed. /ajax/call/failure When the request failed. /ajax/call/complete After success or failure. /ajax/call/done At the end of every request. /dom/node/removing Before an element is replaced or removed by an Ajax update. Argument: the element. /dom/node/added After an element was inserted by an Ajax update. Argument: the new element. Render the subscription with the component or page that needs it, for example from renderHead with an OnDomReadyHeaderItem or in a script file, so it runs once per page. Wicket.Event.unsubscribe(topic, handler) removes a subscriber.

page: React to Ajax requests in JavaScript
title: The stages of a request
text: Stage AjaxCallListener method Function arguments Runs init onInit attrs Right after the event, before anything else. before onBefore attrs Before the preconditi
body: Stage AjaxCallListener method Function arguments Runs init onInit attrs Right after the event, before anything else. before onBefore attrs Before the preconditions. precondition onPrecondition attrs Returning false cancels the request and the handlers after it. beforeSend onBeforeSend attrs, jqXHR, settings Just before the request is sent, when all preconditions passed. after onAfter attrs Right after the request is sent, before the response arrives. success onSuccess attrs, jqXHR, data, textStatus When the response has been processed. failure onFailure attrs, jqXHR, errorMessage, textStatus When the request failed or timed out. complete onComplete attrs, jqXHR, textStatus After success or failure. done onDone attrs At the very end, also when a precondition cancelled the request. attrs is the attributes object of the request, the same JSON that is passed to Wicket.Ajax.ajax; attrs.c is the markup id of the component. jqXHR is the request object.

title: Write a reusable listener
text: For a listener you use in several places, extend AjaxCallListener and override the getters. AjaxCallListener also implements IComponentAwareHeaderContributor, s

body: For a listener you use in several places, extend AjaxCallListener and override the getters. AjaxCallListener also implements IComponentAwareHeaderContributor, so the listener can bring its own script: BusyListener.java public class BusyListener extends AjaxCallListener { private static final ResourceReference SCRIPT = new JavaScriptResourceReference(BusyListener.class, "busy.js"); private final Component region; public BusyListener(Component region) { this.region = region; region.setOutputMarkupId(true); } @Override public CharSequence getBeforeHandler(Component component) { return "Busy.start('" + region.getMarkupId() + "');"; } @Override public CharSequence getCompleteHandler(Component component) { return "Busy.stop('" + region.getMarkupId() + "');"; } @Override public void renderHead(Component component, IHeaderResponse response) { response.render(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(SCRIPT)); } } busy.js var Busy = { start: function (id) { document.getElementById(id).classList.add('busy'); }, stop: function (id) { document.getElementById(id).classList.remove('busy'); } }; Add it with attributes.getAjaxCallListeners().add(new BusyListener(form)). title: How markup becomes components
text: How Wicket loads, parses and caches markup, and how Wicket tags turn into auto components that you never add yourself.
keywords: auto component autoAdd component resolver markup filter markup parser markup cache wicket tags enclosure hierarchy isAuto custom wicket tag
apis: MarkupFactory MarkupParser IMarkupFilter IComponentResolver ComponentResolvers MarkupCache PageSettings WicketTagIdentifier
body: You add components in Java and attach them to tags with wicket:id. Yet a rendered page contains components you never created: one for every <wicket:message>, every <wicket:enclosure>, every link inside <wicket:link>, every <label wicket:for>, and the <head> of the page. These are auto components. They come from two steps: parsing the markup, which turns the file into a list of tags Wicket understands, and resolving, which finds a component for each tag that needs one.

title: Loading and caching markup
text: Wicket loads a component’s markup the first time the component renders, not when it is created. The MarkupFactory, found in the application’s markup settings, l
body: Wicket loads a component’s markup the first time the component renders, not when it is created. The MarkupFactory, found in the application’s markup settings, locates the file for the component’s class, locale, style and variation, parses it and stores the result in the application-wide MarkupCache. Every later instance of the class, in any session, uses the cached markup. In development mode Wicket watches the files and drops a cache entry when its file changes, which is why editing HTML needs no restart. Because markup is shared between all instances, it is read-only at runtime. Anything that differs per instance or per request, such as a value, an attribute or visibility, lives in components, not in the markup.

title: Parsing: a chain of markup filters
text: The MarkupParser reads the file with an XML pull parser and passes every element through a chain of IMarkupFilters. Each filter handles one concern and can chan
apis: MarkupParser IMarkupFilter WicketTagIdentifier WicketRemoveTagHandler WicketLinkTagHandler AutoLabelTagHandler WicketNamespaceHandler WicketMessageTagHandler HtmlHeaderSectionHandler EnclosureHandler InlineEnclosureHandler MarkupFactory
body: The MarkupParser reads the file with an XML pull parser and passes every element through a chain of IMarkupFilters. Each filter handles one concern and can change, mark or drop what passes through. Among the default filters: Filter What it does WicketTagIdentifier Recognizes wicket:id attributes and tags in the Wicket namespace, and gives every Wicket tag without an id a generated one. Rejects unknown Wicket tags. WicketRemoveTagHandler Drops <wicket:remove> regions entirely. WicketLinkTagHandler Inside <wicket:link>, marks tags with a relative href or src as auto components. AutoLabelTagHandler Marks <label wicket:for> tags as auto components. WicketNamespaceHandler Reads the namespace prefix from xmlns:...="http://wicket.apache.org". WicketMessageTagHandler Handles wicket:message attributes, on plain tags as well as component tags. HtmlHeaderSectionHandler In page markup, makes <head> (or <wicket:header-items/>) a component tag, and adds a <head> when the markup has a <body> but no <head>. EnclosureHandler, InlineEnclosureHandler Work out the controlling child of each enclosure. What comes out is a sequence of two kinds of elements: raw markup, which Wicket writes to the response as is, and component tags, which need a component. A tag becomes a component tag because it has a wicket:id, because it is a Wicket tag, or because a filter marked it. The chain is open: a MarkupFactory subclass can add filters in newMarkupParser, and an application can register it with getMarkupSettings().setMarkupFactory(...). Few applications need this. Some Wicket tags never become components. <wicket:remove> is gone after parsing. <wicket:child> and <wicket:extend> serve to merge a parent’s and a subclass’s markup when it is loaded; see Markup inheritance. <wicket:panel> and <wicket:border> tell a panel or border which part of its file to use.

title: Resolving: finding a component for each tag
text: When a container renders, it walks through its markup. For each component tag it looks for a child with the tag’s id. For tags with a wicket:id, that child is n
apis: IComponentResolver Border TransparentWebMarkupContainer Enclosure HtmlHeaderResolver WicketMessageResolver EnclosureHandler InlineEnclosureHandler WicketContainerResolver AutoLinkResolver AutoLabelResolver AutoLabelTextResolver ComponentResolvers
body: When a container renders, it walks through its markup. For each component tag it looks for a child with the tag’s id. For tags with a wicket:id, that child is normally the component you added. For a Wicket tag, there usually is none, so the container asks the component resolvers, the IComponentResolvers, to supply one. It asks in this order: The container itself and its parents, up to the page, if they implement IComponentResolver. A Border resolves <wicket:body> this way, a TransparentWebMarkupContainer lets its parent’s children render inside its tag, and an Enclosure finds the children in its markup. The application-wide resolvers in getPageSettings().getComponentResolvers(), in the order they were registered. The first resolver that returns a component wins. The default application-wide resolvers include HtmlHeaderResolver for <head> and <wicket:head>, WicketMessageResolver for <wicket:message>, EnclosureHandler and InlineEnclosureHandler for enclosures, WicketContainerResolver for <wicket:container>, and, in a web application, AutoLinkResolver, AutoLabelResolver and AutoLabelTextResolver. ComponentResolvers.resolve runs this lookup and is what you call if you write a component that renders unusual markup itself. A resolved component is added to the container with autoAdd and marked as auto. Auto components are exempt from two rules that apply to your own components: they can be added while the page renders, and changes to them are not recorded in the page’s version history. They are created from the markup, so treat them as stateless: whatever they need comes from the tag and from the components around them.

title: Why enclosures are siblings, not parents
text: Resolving explains the one surprise in this mechanism. In the markup, <wicket:enclosure> contains the components inside it. In Java, it does not: the Enclosure
body: Resolving explains the one surprise in this mechanism. In the markup, <wicket:enclosure> contains the components inside it. In Java, it does not: the Enclosure is created by a resolver while its container renders, and is added to that same container, next to the components it encloses. The enclosure finds its controlling child by id in its parent and asks it whether it is visible. So the markup hierarchy and the component hierarchy differ. When the enclosure is hidden, the components inside it are not hidden in Java: they are still configured, onBeforeRender may be called on them, and form components in a hidden enclosure are still validated when the form is submitted. WicketTester cannot see that they are hidden either. Component queueing removes the difference. When you queue components instead of adding them, Wicket builds the hierarchy from the markup before rendering. When it meets a tag that has an auto component factory, such as an enclosure, it creates the component right there and places the queued components inside it. The enclosure becomes a real parent, and hiding it hides its children. See Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy. Where you cannot queue, an EnclosureContainer that you add yourself gives the same result; see Hide surrounding markup with wicket:enclosure.

title: Your own tags
text: The same mechanism is available to applications. A class implementing IComponentResolver, registered with getPageSettings().addComponentResolver(...), can suppl
body: The same mechanism is available to applications. A class implementing IComponentResolver, registered with getPageSettings().addComponentResolver(...), can supply components for tags that have no component in Java. A new tag name in the Wicket namespace also needs WicketTagIdentifier.registerWellKnownTagName(...), or the parser rejects it. This is a trade-off. A custom tag lets markup authors use a feature without touching Java, but it hides where the component comes from: someone reading the Java code does not see it, and someone reading the markup has to know the tag. Wicket’s own tags are few for that reason, and most features that could be tags are components or behaviors instead. The complete list of tags is in Wicket tags and attributes.

body: You need this when your domain classes already carry Jakarta Bean Validation annotations such as @NotNull and @Size, and you want the form to enforce them instead of repeating each rule with Wicket validators.

body: A PropertyValidator finds the property behind the field and runs that property’s constraints on the converted input. It reads the property from a PropertyModel or from an inherited CompoundPropertyModel: PersonPage.java Form<Person> form = new Form<>("form", new CompoundPropertyModel<>(new Person())); add(form); form.add(new TextField<String>("name").add(new PropertyValidator<>())); form.add(new TextField<String>("email").add(new PropertyValidator<>())); form.add(new TextField<Integer>("age").add(new PropertyValidator<>())); form.add(new TextField<LocalDate>("birthday").add(new PropertyValidator<>())); form.add(new TextField<String>("postcode").add(new PropertyValidator<>())); form.add(new FeedbackPanel("feedback")); The validator also changes the field to match its constraints: @NotNull and @NotEmpty make the field required. @Size(max = ...) adds a maxlength attribute to the input.

It also needs a Jakarta Expression Language implementation; its documentation names the one that matches your version. pom.xml <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-bean-validation</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.hibernate.validator</groupId> <artifactId>hibernate-validator</artifactId> <version>${hibernate-validator.version}</version> </dependency>

text: Person.java public class Person implements Serializable { @NotNull @Size(max = 50) private String name; @Email private String email; @Min(18) private int age; @

body: Person.java public class Person implements Serializable { @NotNull @Size(max = 50) private String name; @Email private String email; @Min(18) private int age; @Past private LocalDate birthday; @Pattern(regexp = "\\d{4}\\s?[A-Z]{2}", message = "{person.invalidPostcode}") private String postcode; // getters and setters }

title: Change the message text
text: Wicket ships messages for the standard constraints, keyed by the constraint’s message key, such as jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull.message. They use ${la
body: Wicket ships messages for the standard constraints, keyed by the constraint’s message key, such as jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull.message. They use ${label} like the other form messages. Define the same key in a properties file of your page or application to replace one. For a message of your own, put a key in braces in the annotation, as {person.invalidPostcode} above, and define that key: PersonPage.properties person.invalidPostcode=${label} must be a Dutch postcode, such as 1234 AB. Wicket tries the key with the type of the rejected value appended first (person.invalidPostcode.String), then the key itself. The attributes of the annotation are available as variables, so a message for @Size can use ${max}.

body: PropertyValidator checks one property at a time, before the model is updated. A constraint that compares properties, declared on the class, needs the updated object. Check it in onValidateModelObjects() of the form, which runs after the model update; see How a form is processed for what that means for your model.

body: A lambda model does not tell which property it reads, so name it with a Property: TextField<String> name = new TextField<>("name", LambdaModel.of(person, Person::getName, Person::setName)); name.add(new PropertyValidator<>(new Property(Person.class, "name")));
