title: Test a page with WicketTester
text: Write JUnit tests that render your pages, click links, submit the guestbook form and check Ajax updates, without a browser or a server.
keywords: unit test JUnit test page assertLabel clickLink assertRenderedPage assertErrorMessages executeAjaxEvent assertComponentOnAjaxResponse mvn test
body: In this tutorial you write tests for the application you built in the previous tutorials. The tests render the home page, click its links, submit the guestbook form and check what Ajax redraws. They run in JUnit, without a browser and without starting a server. Start from the myapp project as you left it at the end of Update a page with Ajax. The quickstart already put the test dependencies in pom.xml: wicket-tester and JUnit.

title: 1. Run the test you already have
text: The quickstart generated TestHomePage.java in src/test/java/com/example: public class TestHomePage { private WicketTester tester; @BeforeEach public void setUp(
apis: TestHomePage WicketTester BeforeEach WicketApplication Test HomePage Tests Failures
body: The quickstart generated TestHomePage.java in src/test/java/com/example: public class TestHomePage { private WicketTester tester; @BeforeEach public void setUp() { tester = new WicketTester(new WicketApplication()); } @Test public void homepageRendersSuccessfully() { tester.startPage(HomePage.class); tester.assertRenderedPage(HomePage.class); } } WicketTester runs your application in memory, with a fake request, response and session. startPage renders a page the way a browser request would. assertRenderedPage checks which page came out. Run the tests from the project folder: mvn test Maven reports Tests run: 1, Failures: 0. The test still passes after all your changes, so the home page, the base page and both panels render without errors. A test like this catches a wicket:id in the HTML without a component in Java, and the other way around.

title: 2. Check what a label shows
text: Add a test to TestHomePage that checks the greeting: @Test public void greetsTheVisitor() { tester.startPage(HomePage.class); tester.assertLabel("greeting", "He
body: Add a test to TestHomePage that checks the greeting: @Test public void greetsTheVisitor() { tester.startPage(HomePage.class); tester.assertLabel("greeting", "Hello, Wicket!"); } The first argument is the path of the component: its id, prefixed with the ids of the containers it sits in, separated by colons. The greeting is added straight to the page, so its path is its id. Run mvn test. Two tests pass. Change the expected text to Hello! and run again: the test fails and tells you what the label showed instead. Change it back.

body: clickLink clicks a link. For an AjaxLink it sends an Ajax request, as the browser would. Add: @Test public void countsClicks() { tester.startPage(HomePage.class); tester.assertLabel("clicks", "0"); tester.clickLink("count"); tester.assertLabel("clicks", "1"); tester.assertComponentOnAjaxResponse("clicks"); } assertComponentOnAjaxResponse checks that the label was part of the Ajax response, so the browser would have redrawn it. Run mvn test: three tests pass.

title: 4. Follow a link to another page
text: The links in the header sit inside the HeaderPanel, which has the id header. Their paths start with that id: @Test public void navigatesToTheAboutPage() { teste
body: The links in the header sit inside the HeaderPanel, which has the id header. Their paths start with that id: @Test public void navigatesToTheAboutPage() { tester.startPage(HomePage.class); tester.clickLink("header:about"); tester.assertRenderedPage(AboutPage.class); } Run mvn test: four tests pass.

title: 5. Test that the form opens
text: The guestbook form is hidden until the visitor clicks “Write a message”. Create TestGuestbookPage.java in src/test/java/com/example, and test that link first. K
apis: Assertions FormTester WicketTester AfterEach BeforeEach Test TestGuestbookPage WicketApplication GuestbookPage
body: The guestbook form is hidden until the visitor clicks “Write a message”. Create TestGuestbookPage.java in src/test/java/com/example, and test that link first. Keep the application in a field, so later tests can look at its guestbook: package com.example; import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals; import org.apache.wicket.util.tester.FormTester; import org.apache.wicket.util.tester.WicketTester; import org.junit.jupiter.api.AfterEach; import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach; import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test; public class TestGuestbookPage { private WicketApplication application; private WicketTester tester; @BeforeEach public void setUp() { application = new WicketApplication(); tester = new WicketTester(application); } @AfterEach public void tearDown() { tester.destroy(); } @Test public void opensTheForm() { tester.startPage(GuestbookPage.class); tester.assertInvisible("form"); tester.clickLink("write"); tester.assertVisible("form"); tester.assertInvisible("write"); tester.assertComponentOnAjaxResponse("form"); } } Each test gets a new application and so a new guestbook, and destroy() cleans up after each test. assertInvisible and assertVisible check the visibility that onConfigure() decided. Run mvn test: five tests pass.

title: 6. Test that the guestbook rejects empty input
text: newFormTester gives you a FormTester for the form at that path. Its submit() sends the form with the fields as they are. Add a test that submits the form empty:
body: newFormTester gives you a FormTester for the form at that path. Its submit() sends the form with the fields as they are. Add a test that submits the form empty: @Test public void requiresNameAndMessage() { tester.startPage(GuestbookPage.class); tester.clickLink("write"); FormTester form = tester.newFormTester("form"); form.submit(); tester.assertErrorMessages("'Name' is required.", "'Message' is required."); assertEquals(1, application.getGuestbook().getEntries().size()); } assertErrorMessages checks the error messages the submit produced. The guestbook still holds only its welcome entry. Run mvn test: six tests pass.

title: 7. Test that the guestbook saves an entry
text: setValue fills in a field. Its first argument is the path of the field relative to the form. Add: @Test public void savesAnEntry() { tester.startPage(GuestbookP
apis: Test GuestbookPage FormTester Ann Nice Thanks
body: setValue fills in a field. Its first argument is the path of the field relative to the form. Add: @Test public void savesAnEntry() { tester.startPage(GuestbookPage.class); tester.clickLink("write"); FormTester form = tester.newFormTester("form"); form.setValue("name", "Ann"); form.setValue("text", "Nice site!"); form.submit(); tester.assertNoErrorMessage(); tester.assertInfoMessages("Thanks for signing, Ann!"); assertEquals("Ann", application.getGuestbook().getEntries().get(0).getName()); } Run mvn test: seven tests pass.

title: 8. Submit through the Ajax button
text: form.submit() submits the form as a plain request. To test the Ajax button, fill in the fields and fire the button’s click event with executeAjaxEvent. Wicket t
apis: Test GuestbookPage FormTester Bob Hello Ajax
body: form.submit() submits the form as a plain request. To test the Ajax button, fill in the fields and fire the button’s click event with executeAjaxEvent. Wicket then submits the form over Ajax, as the browser does: @Test public void savesAnEntryWithAjax() { tester.startPage(GuestbookPage.class); tester.clickLink("write"); FormTester form = tester.newFormTester("form"); form.setValue("name", "Bob"); form.setValue("text", "Hello from Ajax."); tester.executeAjaxEvent("form:save", "click"); tester.assertComponentOnAjaxResponse("entries"); tester.assertComponentOnAjaxResponse("feedback"); assertEquals("Bob", application.getGuestbook().getEntries().get(0).getName()); } Run mvn test: eight tests pass.

title: 9. Fire the timer
text: A test does not wait ten seconds for the timer. executeAllTimerBehaviors fires every timer on a page at once. Add an entry to the guestbook behind the page’s ba
body: A test does not wait ten seconds for the timer. executeAllTimerBehaviors fires every timer on a page at once. Add an entry to the guestbook behind the page’s back, as another visitor would, and fire the timers: @Test public void refreshesTheList() { tester.startPage(GuestbookPage.class); application.getGuestbook().add(new Entry("Cid", "Signed in another browser.")); tester.executeAllTimerBehaviors(tester.getLastRenderedPage()); tester.assertComponentOnAjaxResponse("entries"); tester.assertContains("Signed in another browser."); } assertContains searches the last response, here the Ajax response with the redrawn list. Run mvn test: all nine tests pass. Together they cover every page, the counter, the navigation, the hidden form, both ways of submitting the guestbook and the timer, and none of them needs a browser or a server.

page: Combine fields into one form component
title: Combine fields into one form component
text: Build a FormComponentPanel that shows several inputs but converts, validates and stores them as one value.
keywords: compound field composite input custom form component convertInput setConvertedInput reusable input
body: You need this when one value in your model takes more than one input to enter, such as an amount with a currency, or a date split into day, month and year. A plain Panel can hold those inputs, but it is not a form component: it cannot be required, have validators, or write one combined value to its model. A FormComponentPanel is a panel with its own markup that is also a FormComponent.

page: Combine fields into one form component
title: Build the panel
text: Take a field for an amount of money in a currency. The model holds one Money value; the panel shows a number input and a currency list. Money.java public record
apis: Money BigDecimal Currency Serializable MoneyField FormComponentPanel NumberTextField DropDownChoice String IModel Model List LambdaChoiceRenderer
body: Take a field for an amount of money in a currency. The model holds one Money value; the panel shows a number input and a currency list. Money.java public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) implements Serializable { } MoneyField.java public class MoneyField extends FormComponentPanel<Money> { private final NumberTextField<BigDecimal> amount; private final DropDownChoice<Currency> currency; public MoneyField(String id, IModel<Money> model) { super(id, model); amount = new NumberTextField<>("amount", Model.of(), BigDecimal.class); amount.setStep(new BigDecimal("0.01")); add(amount); List<Currency> currencies = List.of( Currency.getInstance("EUR"), Currency.getInstance("USD"), Currency.getInstance("GBP")); currency = new DropDownChoice<>("currency", Model.of(), currencies, new LambdaChoiceRenderer<>(Currency::getCurrencyCode, Currency::getCurrencyCode)); add(currency); } MoneyField.html <wicket:panel> <input type="number" wicket:id="amount"> <select wicket:id="currency"></select> </wicket:panel> The inner fields get models of their own. The panel copies values between those models and its own model in two methods.

page: Combine fields into one form component
title: Combine the input in convertInput
text: When the form is processed, Wicket converts the inner fields before the panel. In convertInput(), read their converted input and set the combined value with set
body: When the form is processed, Wicket converts the inner fields before the panel. In convertInput(), read their converted input and set the combined value with setConvertedInput(): @Override public void convertInput() { BigDecimal value = amount.getConvertedInput(); Currency unit = currency.getConvertedInput(); setConvertedInput(value == null || unit == null ? null : new Money(value, unit)); } The panel’s validators then run on that Money value, and if the whole form is valid, Wicket writes it to the panel’s model. If the panel is required and convertInput() produces null, the panel fails with the Required message.

page: Combine fields into one form component
title: Split the value in onBeforeRender
text: Before the panel renders, copy the parts of the model value into the inner fields: @Override protected void onBeforeRender() { Money money = getModelObject(); a
body: Before the panel renders, copy the parts of the model value into the inner fields: @Override protected void onBeforeRender() { Money money = getModelObject(); amount.setModelObject(money == null ? null : money.amount()); currency.setModelObject(money == null ? null : money.currency()); super.onBeforeRender(); } } When the form has errors, the inner fields show what the user typed rather than their models, so this does not overwrite the user’s input.

page: Combine fields into one form component
title: Update the panel with Ajax
text: An AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior on the panel processes only the panel itself, not the inner fields. To react when any of its inputs changes, attach the beh
body: An AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior on the panel processes only the panel itself, not the inner fields. To react when any of its inputs changes, attach the behavior to the inner fields instead, and call processInput() on the panel in onUpdate(). processInput() runs the required check, conversion, validation and model update of the panel.

page: Combine fields into one form component
title: Use the panel in a form
text: Bind the panel to any tag; Wicket renders the panel’s markup inside it. form.add(new MoneyField("price", LambdaModel.of(product, Product::getPrice, Product::set
body:
Bind the panel to any tag; Wicket renders the panel’s markup inside it. form.add(new MoneyField("price", LambdaModel.of(product, Product::getPrice, Product::setPrice)).setRequired(true));
Messages about the inner fields, such as an amount that is not a number, are reported on the inner fields and use their labels. Give them a label with setLabel() or a resource keyed by their id.

title: How a form is processed
text: The order in which Wicket checks, converts, validates and stores submitted input, and why a form updates all its models or none.
keywords: form submission onSubmit onError model update validation order conversion raw input process
apis: Form FormComponent IFormSubmitter IFormValidator IConverter IValidator LocalDate Integer
body: A browser submits a form as a set of strings, one per field. Your code wants typed values in its models: a LocalDate in the order, an Integer in the quantity. Between the two, Wicket runs every field through the same stages in a fixed order, and it only touches your models when every field has passed.

title: Conversion before validation
text: Validators run after conversion so that they can work with your types. A RangeValidator<Integer> compares integers, a RangeValidator<LocalDate> compares dates.
body: Validators run after conversion so that they can work with your types. A RangeValidator<Integer> compares integers, a RangeValidator<LocalDate> compares dates. If conversion came after validation, every validator would have to parse the string itself, and each would do it slightly differently. The type comes from the component: set it with setType(), or let the component take it from a model that knows its object class, such as PropertyModel. Without a type, the input stays a String. Convert input to your types shows how to plug in your own converter.

title: Skipping the stages
text: Sometimes a submit should not validate anything. A “Cancel” button has to work even when required fields are empty. Call setDefaultFormProcessing(false) on the
body: Sometimes a submit should not validate anything. A “Cancel” button has to work even when required fields are empty. Call setDefaultFormProcessing(false) on the submitting component, and Wicket skips all four stages: it only calls the submitter’s onSubmit() and onAfterSubmit(). The user’s input is neither checked nor stored. See Use more than one submit button. Ajax narrows the stages instead of skipping them. An AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior runs required check, conversion, validators and model update for the one component it is attached to, without touching the rest of the form. That lets you store a field as the user leaves it, at the price of the all-or-nothing guarantee for that field. See Ajax behaviors.

title: The exception: late validation
text: onValidateModelObjects() runs after the models are updated, so it breaks the all-or-nothing rule on purpose. It exists for checks that need the complete object,
body: onValidateModelObjects() runs after the models are updated, so it breaks the all-or-nothing rule on purpose. It exists for checks that need the complete object, such as class-level constraints in Bean Validation. If such a check fails, the model objects already contain the new values. Your onError() should then discard or reload them, for example by not saving and detaching a loadable model.

title: The stages of a form submit
text: When the request arrives, the Form first finds out what submitted it. That is a submitting component such as a Button or SubmitLink (an IFormSubmitter), or noth
apis: Form Button SubmitLink IFormSubmitter Required IConverter INullAcceptingValidator IFormValidator FormComponentPanel
body: When the request arrives, the Form first finds out what submitted it. That is a submitting component such as a Button or SubmitLink (an IFormSubmitter), or nothing when the user pressed Enter or clicked a plain <input type="submit"> without a wicket:id. The submitter decides which form is processed, which matters for nested forms. Then the form is processed in four stages. Validation. Every visible and enabled form component goes through three checks, in this order: Required. If the component is required and the user left it empty, it gets the Required error and the other checks are skipped. Conversion. The component converts its input string to the type of its model, usually through an IConverter. If that fails, it gets a conversion error and its validators are skipped. Validators. The component’s validators run on the converted value, in the order you added them, until one reports an error. Validators do not run when the value is null, unless they implement INullAcceptingValidator. After the components, the form runs its form validators (IFormValidator), which compare several fields, and then calls its own onValidate(). A form validator only runs when all the components it depends on passed their own checks. Decision. If any component or validator reported an error, processing stops here. The submitter’s onError() is called, then onError() of each form that has errors. No model is changed. Model update. If nothing failed, every component writes its converted value to its model. After that the form calls onValidateModelObjects(), a late check that can look at the updated model objects. An error there still leads to onError(). Submit. The submitter’s onSubmit() runs, then onSubmit() of each processed form, then the submitter’s onAfterSubmit(). Nested forms are visited innermost first, both when validating and when calling onSubmit() and onError(). Inside a form, children are visited before their parents. That is why a FormComponentPanel can read the converted input of its inner fields in its own convertInput(): they have already been converted.

title: Where the messages come from
text: Every error in the stages above becomes a feedback message on the component that failed. The text is looked up in resource bundles by a key: Required for the re
body: Every error in the stages above becomes a feedback message on the component that failed. The text is looked up in resource bundles by a key: Required for the required check, IConverter for a failed conversion, and the validator’s class name for a validator. Wicket fills in variables such as ${label} and ${input}. Validate input and show errors shows how to display these messages and replace their text; Validators and converters lists the keys.

title: Why a form updates all models or none
text: Wicket could store each valid field as soon as it passed its checks. It does not, for two reasons. The first is your data. Form components are often bound to a
body: Wicket could store each valid field as soon as it passed its checks. It does not, for two reasons. The first is your data. Form components are often bound to a live object: a PropertyModel on an entity, or a CompoundPropertyModel on the bean the form edits. If the start date of a booking is valid and the end date is not, storing only the start date leaves the booking in a state that neither the user nor your code asked for. If that object is shared, or flushed to a database at the end of the request, the half-edited state escapes. By holding back every update until the whole form is valid, Wicket keeps your objects as they were before the submit, or as the user wants them after. The second is the user’s input. When a field fails, the form is rendered again with the error. The user expects to see what they typed, including the mistake, not the old model value. Wicket keeps the raw input of every component until the form is valid. A component that has raw input renders that instead of its model value. When the form succeeds, the raw input is cleared and the components render their models again. This has consequences for your code: In onError(), the models still hold the old values. To see what the user typed, call getInput() on the component, or getConvertedInput() if conversion succeeded. In onSubmit(), every model holds its new value. That is the place to save, call services and navigate. A validator never sees a half-converted form. It gets one typed value; a form validator gets the converted input of the components it depends on.

title: Generate markup from code
text: Give a panel or page markup built in Java instead of an HTML file, and control whether Wicket caches it.
keywords: dynamic markup markup without html file markup from database template from string markup cache getMarkupResourceStream getCacheKey CMS
body: Use this when a component’s markup cannot be a file next to its class: it comes from a database or a CMS, is assembled from configuration, or differs per customer. A page, panel or border can supply its own markup by implementing IMarkupResourceStreamProvider.

title: Cache the markup per variant
text: Wicket caches markup per class, locale, style and variation, and asks for the markup stream only once per cache key. A component whose markup depends on other s
apis: IMarkupCacheKeyProvider TenantPanel Panel IMarkupResourceStreamProvider String Override IResourceStream MarkupContainer Class StringResourceStream
body: Wicket caches markup per class, locale, style and variation, and asks for the markup stream only once per cache key. A component whose markup depends on other state must tell Wicket how to tell the versions apart. Implement IMarkupCacheKeyProvider and return a key that differs for each version of the markup: public class TenantPanel extends Panel implements IMarkupResourceStreamProvider, IMarkupCacheKeyProvider { private final String tenant; public TenantPanel(String id, String tenant) { super(id); this.tenant = tenant; } @Override public IResourceStream getMarkupResourceStream(MarkupContainer container, Class<?> containerClass) { return new StringResourceStream(templates.panelFor(tenant)); } @Override public String getCacheKey(MarkupContainer container, Class<?> containerClass) { return containerClass.getName() + "_" + tenant + "_" + container.getLocale(); } } Include the locale (and the style, if you use styles) in the key when the markup depends on them.

title: Change how all markup is loaded
text: IMarkupResourceStreamProvider works per component. To change where Wicket looks for the markup of every component, for example to load all templates from a dire
body: IMarkupResourceStreamProvider works per component. To change where Wicket looks for the markup of every component, for example to load all templates from a directory outside the classpath, configure the resource stream locator in the resource settings instead; see Customize where resources are loaded from. How Wicket loads, parses and caches markup is described in How markup becomes components.

title: Keep user content out of the markup
text: Generated markup is parsed as a template, not escaped. Never paste user input or other untrusted text into it: it could add tags, scripts or wicket: tags. Put s
body: Generated markup is parsed as a template, not escaped. Never paste user input or other untrusted text into it: it could add tags, scripts or wicket: tags. Put such content in a component, such as a Label, which escapes it. To show trusted HTML from a CMS without Wicket tags, a Label with setEscapeModelStrings(false) is simpler than generating markup.

title: Return the markup from the component
text: Implement getMarkupResourceStream and return the markup as an IResourceStream. For markup in a string, wrap it in a StringResourceStream. The markup follows the
apis: IResourceStream StringResourceStream NoticePanel Panel IMarkupResourceStreamProvider String IModel Label Override MarkupContainer Class
body:
Implement getMarkupResourceStream and return the markup as an IResourceStream. For markup in a string, wrap it in a StringResourceStream. The markup follows the same rules as a file: a panel’s markup needs , a border’s . public class NoticePanel extends Panel implements IMarkupResourceStreamProvider { public NoticePanel(String id, IModel text) { super(id); add(new Label("text", text)); } @Override public IResourceStream getMarkupResourceStream(MarkupContainer container, Class containerClass) { return new StringResourceStream("""

"""); } } The markup can contain wicket:id tags; the component adds the matching components as usual. No NoticePanel.html is needed.

title: Turn caching off
text: Return null from getCacheKey and Wicket does not cache the markup: it asks for the stream and parses it every time it needs the markup. Use this only for markup
body: Return null from getCacheKey and Wicket does not cache the markup: it asks for the stream and parses it every time it needs the markup. Use this only for markup that really changes between renders. Parsing on every render costs time, and markup that changes between requests can break pages that are already in the browser, for example when an Ajax request refers to a component whose tag has gone. @Override public String getCacheKey(MarkupContainer container, Class<?> containerClass) { return null; }

title: Glossary
text: Plain-English definitions of the Wicket terms used in this guide, each compared with what other web frameworks call it.
keywords: terminology vocabulary definitions terms concepts compare frameworks JSF Spring MVC React Vue Thymeleaf
apis: Application Behavior Border Component CompoundPropertyModel IConverter LoadableDetachableModel FeedbackPanel Form Fragment IModel LambdaModel ListView Page PageParameters Panel RequestCycle IResource ResourceReference Session WicketTester AjaxRequestTarget IRequestMapper IValidator HeaderItem WebApplication AbstractAjaxBehavior UIComponent MarkupContainer ConverterLocator Converter Formatter Development Production PostMapping TextField CheckBox DropDownChoice FormComponent Person ProductPage GetMapping WebPage PathVariable
body: The definitions use plain words first and the Wicket class second. “Similar to” names the closest idea in other frameworks; the comparison is never exact. Ajax request target The list of components to redraw in response to an Ajax request, plus any JavaScript to run. Ajax callbacks such as onClick(AjaxRequestTarget) receive one; AjaxRequestTarget.add() puts a component in it. Similar to: the render attribute of JSF’s <f:ajax>, or out-of-band swaps (hx-swap-oob) in htmx. Application The object that represents your web application, one per deployment. You subclass WebApplication to name the home page and configure everything else in init(). Similar to: a Spring Boot application class with its configuration, or faces-config.xml in JSF. Behavior An add-on you attach to a component to change its tag, contribute CSS or JavaScript, or react to browser events, without subclassing the component. Behaviors extend Behavior; Ajax behaviors extend AbstractAjaxBehavior. Similar to: attribute directives in Angular, custom directives in Vue. Border A component that wraps markup around its children: the border provides the frame, and <wicket:body> marks where the children go. Similar to: a React component that renders its children inside a frame, or a layout decorator in Thymeleaf. Component A Java object that renders one part of a page and handles the events for it, such as a label, a link or a text field. It is tied to a tag in the markup through wicket:id. All components extend Component. Similar to: a JSF UIComponent, a Vaadin component, or a React or Vue component rendered on the server. Component tree The hierarchy of components that make up a page. Containers (MarkupContainer), such as pages, panels and forms, hold child components, and the hierarchy matches the nesting of the wicket:id tags in the markup. Similar to: the JSF component tree, or a DOM that lives on the server. CompoundPropertyModel A model for a container whose children use their own wicket:id as the name of the property they read and write on the model’s object. Similar to: Spring MVC form binding with th:field, which binds inputs to bean properties by name. Converter An object that turns submitted text into a Java value and a value back into text, for numbers, dates and the other types it knows. Converters implement IConverter; you register your own on the ConverterLocator. Similar to: a JSF Converter, or a Spring Formatter. Deployment mode, development mode The two runtime configuration types of an application. Development mode adds checks, reloads changed markup and shows stack traces; deployment mode leaves those out for speed and safety. See Switch between development and deployment mode. Similar to: the Development and Production project stages of JSF, or Spring profiles. Detach The cleanup step at the end of every request, in which components and models drop data they can load again, before Wicket stores the page. Similar to: releasing request-scoped beans at the end of a request. Detachable model A model that loads its object when it is first asked for it in a request, and forgets it when the request ends, so the stored page keeps only what it needs to load it again, such as an id. LoadableDetachableModel is the usual base class. Similar to: loading an entity by id in every Spring MVC request instead of keeping it in the session. Enclosure A <wicket:enclosure> tag around markup that is shown only when a chosen child component is visible, so its label and surrounding tags disappear with it. Similar to: th:if in Thymeleaf or v-if in Vue on a wrapping element. Feedback message, FeedbackPanel A message for the user, such as a validation error or a confirmation, with a level: error, warning, info, success. Components record them with error(), info() and similar methods, and a FeedbackPanel shows them. Similar to: <h:messages> in JSF, or flash messages in Spring MVC. Form A component for an HTML <form> that runs the submit: it converts and validates the input of its form components, updates their models, and calls onSubmit() or onError(). Similar to: <h:form> in JSF, or a Spring MVC form with its @PostMapping handler. Form component A component that takes user input, such as TextField, CheckBox or DropDownChoice. Form components extend FormComponent. Similar to: JSF input components such as <h:inputText>. Fragment A piece of markup defined inside the markup file of a page or panel with <wicket:fragment>, and shown by a Fragment component, so small variations need no file of their own. Similar to: a th:fragment defined in the same Thymeleaf template, or a named template block. Header item A reference to CSS, JavaScript or other content for the <head> of a page, which a component contributes in renderHead(). Wicket includes each item once, in dependency order. HeaderItem is the base class. Similar to: <h:outputScript> in JSF. LambdaModel A model built from a getter and a setter, often two method references such as Person::getName and Person::setName. The compiler checks it, unlike a property expression in a string. Similar to: a computed property with a getter and setter in Vue. Markup The HTML file of a page, panel or border, kept next to its Java class. It is plain HTML with wicket:id attributes and a few wicket: tags. Similar to: a Thymeleaf template or a JSF Facelets file, without an expression language. Markup id The id attribute Wicket writes on a component’s tag when you call setOutputMarkupId(true). Ajax needs it to find the tag to replace. Similar to: the generated client id of a JSF component. Markup inheritance A page or panel subclass inherits the markup of its parent class. The parent marks one place with <wicket:child/>, and the subclass fills it with the content of its <wicket:extend> tag. Similar to: template inheritance with the Thymeleaf Layout Dialect, or a Facelets template with <ui:composition>. Model The object a component asks for the value it shows, and hands a new value to when the user submits one. Models implement IModel, which has getObject() and setObject(). Because IModel has only one abstract method, a lambda is a read-only model. Similar to: a property in JavaFX, or a computed property with a getter and setter in Vue. Mount Giving a page or resource a fixed, readable URL path in init(), for example mountPage("/products/${id}", ProductPage.class). Similar to: @GetMapping("/products/{id}") in Spring MVC. Package resource A file, such as CSS, JavaScript or an image, stored in a Java package next to the component that uses it, and served by Wicket with a URL that changes when the file does. Similar to: a resource library in META-INF/resources in JSF. Page A component that is a complete HTML document, with its own markup file. Every rendered HTML page in a Wicket application is an instance of a Page subclass, usually WebPage. Similar to: a JSF view, or a Spring MVC controller method together with its template. Page parameters The named and indexed values in the URL of a bookmarkable page, which the page receives as PageParameters in its constructor. Similar to: @PathVariable and @RequestParam in Spring MVC, or view parameters in JSF. Page store Where Wicket keeps the stateful pages of each session between requests: the most recent ones in memory, and serialized pages on disk. Similar to: server-side view state in JSF. Panel A reusable component with its own markup file, inside a <wicket:panel> tag. Panels are the usual way to build your own components. Similar to: a JSF composite component, or a React or Vue component with its own template. Repeater A component that renders its markup once for each item in a collection: RepeatingView, ListView, DataView and others. Similar to: th:each in Thymeleaf, v-for in Vue, or <ui:repeat> in JSF. Request cycle The processing of one request, from mapping the URL to a handler to writing the response and detaching. RequestCycle.get() returns the current one. Similar to: the JSF lifecycle, or what Spring’s DispatcherServlet does for one request. Request mapper An object that translates a URL into a request handler and the other way around, used for mounted pages and resources. Mappers implement IRequestMapper. Similar to: handler mappings in Spring MVC. Resource Anything Wicket serves that is not a page: a stylesheet, an image, a download, a generated PDF or a JSON response. Resources implement IResource. Similar to: a Spring MVC handler that returns a ResponseEntity with bytes, or a static resource handler. Resource reference A named, serializable pointer to a resource, which Wicket turns into a URL and resolves when the URL is requested. Similar to: a JSF resource identified by library and name. Session The Wicket object for one visitor, kept in the HTTP session once something needs to be remembered: the locale, the signed-in user, feedback messages, and the visitor’s stateful pages. You can subclass WebSession for typed fields. Similar to: a session-scoped bean in Spring or CDI. Stateful page, stateless page A stateful page is stored after it renders, so later requests, such as link clicks and form submits, go to the same page object. A stateless page is created anew for every request and needs no session. Wicket makes a page stateful as soon as one of its components needs that. Similar to: JSF views with view state versus transient views; every Spring MVC page is stateless. Validator An object that checks the converted input of a form component and records an error when it fails, such as StringValidator or EmailAddressValidator. Validators implement IValidator. Similar to: a JSF Validator, or a Spring Validator. WicketTester A test helper that runs your application in memory, so a JUnit test can render pages, click links, submit forms and check the result without a browser or server. Similar to: Spring’s MockMvc. wicket:id The attribute that ties a tag in the markup to the component with the same id in Java. body: Wicket shows three pages for the exceptions it expects. Set your own in Application.init(): @Override protected void init() { super.init(); getApplicationSettings() .setInternalErrorPage(ErrorPage.class) .setPageExpiredErrorPage(SessionExpiredPage.class) .setAccessDeniedPage(NoAccessPage.class); } Setting Shown for setInternalErrorPage Unexpected exceptions, in deployment mode. setPageExpiredErrorPage PageExpiredException: the page a link or form belongs to is no longer in the page store, usually because the session expired. setAccessDeniedPage AuthorizationException, for example from a role check, and listener calls on components that are disabled or invisible. body: To send one kind of exception to its own page, register a request cycle listener and return a handler from onException(). Returning null leaves the exception to Wicket. getRequestCycleListeners().add(new IRequestCycleListener() { @Override public IRequestHandler onException(RequestCycle cycle, Exception ex) { var notFound = Exceptions.findCause(ex, ProductNotFoundException.class); if (notFound != null) { return new RenderPageRequestHandler(new ProductNotFoundPage(notFound.getProductId())); } return null; } }); Wicket often wraps an exception, for example in a WicketRuntimeException when a component fails to render, so look for the cause with org.apache.wicket.util.lang.Exceptions.findCause instead of checking ex itself. title: Fix where Wicket inserts its items

body: Without further markup, the content of the page’s <head> is just one of the page’s items, so a <meta charset> you write there ends up after the stylesheets and scripts of the components. Wicket throws an exception when it loads markup with a second one or with one after </head>. The default Content Security Policy blocks a <script> or <link rel="stylesheet"> written directly in the markup, because it has no nonce. Wrap such tags in <wicket:link>, as in the example, so Wicket writes the URL of the package resource and adds the nonce; for files outside your packages, render a header item instead. The scripts of all OnLoadHeaderItem items, combined into one inline script. The dependencies of an item are written before the item.
