title: How Wicket Ajax works
text: What happens between a click in the browser and the updated components on the page, and why components need a markup id.
keywords: partial page update ajax-response callback url round trip XMLHttpRequest markup id placeholder wicket-ajax.js
body: Wicket Ajax lets a component handle a browser event on the server and send back new markup for only the parts of the page that changed. You write no JavaScript for this. The component and its behavior generate the script, a JavaScript library that comes with Wicket sends the request and applies the response, and the server side works with the same component tree that rendered the page.

title: Ordering, channels and state
text: The library sends Ajax requests one after the other per channel. By default all requests share one channel that queues them, so a second click waits until the f
body: The library sends Ajax requests one after the other per channel. By default all requests share one channel that queues them, so a second click waits until the first response has been applied. A channel can also drop all but the last waiting request, or discard a new request while one is running. Combined with the page lock on the server, this keeps the page instance and the DOM in step: the server never processes two requests for the same page at once, and the browser never applies two responses in an unknown order. Because the callback URL addresses a page instance, an Ajax behavior makes its page stateful: the page has to be kept in the page store so the next request can find it. This is the same reason a Link makes a page stateful; see Stateful and stateless pages. Ajax components and behaviors can be made stateless when the page can be rebuilt from its URL alone; see Use Ajax on stateless pages.

title: The pieces involved
text: Every Ajax component is built on an Ajax behavior. An AjaxLink is a link with an AjaxEventBehavior for the click event; an AjaxButton carries an AjaxFormSubmitB
apis: AjaxLink AjaxEventBehavior AjaxButton AjaxFormSubmitBehavior AbstractDefaultAjaxBehavior Wicket Ajax AjaxRequestAttributes
body: Every Ajax component is built on an Ajax behavior. An AjaxLink is a link with an AjaxEventBehavior for the click event; an AjaxButton carries an AjaxFormSubmitBehavior. All of them extend AbstractDefaultAjaxBehavior, which does three things: it makes its component output a markup id, so the browser can find the element; it contributes Wicket’s client library, wicket-ajax.js, to the page header; it renders a script that tells the library which event to listen to and which URL to call. That script is a single call with a JSON object of request attributes: Wicket.Ajax.ajax({"u":"./home?2-1.0-counter","c":"counter1","e":"click"}); u is the callback URL of the behavior, c the markup id of the element, e the event. The URL points at one behavior of one component in one page instance: page id 2, render count 1, behavior index 0, component path counter. Wicket renders this call as a DOM-ready script in the page header, so the library binds the event handler once the document is loaded. Other attributes, such as the HTTP method, a form to submit, throttling or JavaScript handlers, are only written when they differ from the default. You change them by overriding updateAjaxAttributes(AjaxRequestAttributes); see Change how an Ajax request is sent.

title: The round trip
text: When the user clicks, the library builds an XMLHttpRequest to the callback URL. It adds the header Wicket-Ajax: true and the base URL of the page in Wicket-Ajax
apis: XMLHttpRequest Wicket Ajax BaseURL AjaxRequestTarget AjaxRequestHandler Location
body: When the user clicks, the library builds an XMLHttpRequest to the callback URL. It adds the header Wicket-Ajax: true and the base URL of the page in Wicket-Ajax-BaseURL, and for a form submit it serializes the form fields into the request. On the server the request is an ordinary request to a page instance. Wicket fetches the page from the page store by its id, locks it so that no other request for the same page runs at the same time, and calls the behavior. The behavior calls its callback method, such as onClick or onEvent, with an AjaxRequestTarget. The AjaxRequestTarget collects what goes back to the browser. Your callback changes models and component state as in any other request, then adds the components that need to be rendered again with target.add(...), and adds JavaScript with appendJavaScript and prependJavaScript. Wicket’s default target is AjaxRequestHandler. Before it responds, it sends itself as an event payload to the application, which passes it on breadth-first to the session, the request cycle, the page and all its components. A component that should be refreshed after every Ajax request can add itself to the target in its onEvent, without the component that handled the click knowing about it. The response is XML: ... 3]]> ... ... Each added component renders on its own, with its complete tag, and ends up in a component element. The header contributions of those components, such as CSS and JavaScript references and their DOM-ready scripts, travel along; the library loads only the references the page does not have yet. Prepended JavaScript ends up in priority-evaluate and runs before the components are replaced; appended JavaScript ends up in evaluate and runs after. Back in the browser, the library finds each element by its id and replaces it with the new markup. It publishes the events /dom/node/removing and /dom/node/added while doing so, and runs the scripts. If the server answered with a redirect instead, the library follows the URL in the Ajax-Location header and the browser loads a new page.

title: Two implementations of the client library
text: The default client library is wicket-ajax-jquery.js, which uses jQuery for DOM manipulation and the request itself. The JavaScript API it offers (Wicket.Ajax, W
body: The default client library is wicket-ajax-jquery.js, which uses jQuery for DOM manipulation and the request itself. The JavaScript API it offers (Wicket.Ajax, Wicket.Event, Wicket.DOM and so on) is what the server-side code relies on, not jQuery.

title: Why components need a markup id
text: The browser knows nothing about the component tree. It only has the HTML, and the only way the library can find “the label” again is by its id attribute. Wicket
body: The browser knows nothing about the component tree. It only has the HTML, and the only way the library can find “the label” again is by its id attribute. Wicket does not render an id for every component, because ids it generates would clutter the markup and could clash with ids you write yourself. A component that is updated through Ajax has to render one, which you ask for with setOutputMarkupId(true), or by writing the id in the markup yourself. See Give a component a markup id. When a component is added to the target, Wicket switches the markup id on for it, but that is too late for the markup already in the browser: if the component did not render its id the first time, the library cannot find the element and logs that the component “was not found while trying to perform markup update”. An invisible component renders nothing at all, so there is no element to replace when it becomes visible. setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag(true) makes an invisible component render an empty, hidden tag with its id in its place: The next Ajax update replaces this placeholder with the real markup. Placeholder tags imply setOutputMarkupId(true). Repeaters such as ListView and RepeatingView have no tag of their own: their markup is the repeated markup of their items. AjaxRequestTarget refuses them with an exception. To refresh a list, you add a container around it. The same goes for a component with setRenderBodyOnly(true), which renders no tag either.

title: How native WebSockets work
text: How Wicket connects a page to a WebSocket, routes messages to components, pushes updates from other threads, and what that means for sessions and locking.
keywords: server push real-time full duplex jakarta websocket JSR 356 connection registry page lock request scoped beans session scoped beans
apis: WebSocketBehavior WebSocketResource WebSocketRequestHandler IWebSocketConnectionRegistry WebSocketPushBroadcaster IWebSocketPushMessage JavaxWebSocketFilter
body: With Ajax the browser always asks first: the server can only answer. A WebSocket is a connection that stays open after the page has loaded, over which both sides send messages whenever they like. Wicket’s native WebSocket support uses it to let the server update components on a page that nobody clicked on: a progress bar of a background job, a new chat message, a price that changed.

title: A connection per page, kept in a registry
text: You switch WebSockets on for a page by adding a WebSocketBehavior to the page or to any component on it. The behavior renders a small script that opens the conn
body: You switch WebSockets on for a page by adding a WebSocketBehavior to the page or to any component on it. The behavior renders a small script that opens the connection when the page is loaded, passing the page id and the application name in the URL. One connection serves the whole page, however many WebSocket behaviors it has. On the server, each open connection is stored in the application’s IWebSocketConnectionRegistry, under three keys: the application, the HTTP session id, and a key for the page. The page key is a PageIdKey holding the page id and the page class name. This registry is what makes pushing possible: code that wants to reach a page later looks the connection up by these keys, and code that wants to reach everyone asks for all connections of the application. A WebSocketResource is the alternative to the behavior: a shared resource that receives messages for connections opened under its resource name, keyed with a ResourceNameKey. It has no page, so it can push text and binary data but cannot re-render components.

title: Built on the servlet container’s WebSocket support
text: Wicket does not implement the WebSocket protocol. The module wicket-native-websocket-javax plugs into the Jakarta WebSocket API that every current servlet conta
body: Wicket does not implement the WebSocket protocol. The module wicket-native-websocket-javax plugs into the Jakarta WebSocket API that every current servlet container provides, such as Tomcat, Jetty and WildFly. The module and its filter still carry javax in their names, from the time the API lived in that namespace, but they work with jakarta.websocket. The module registers a WebSocket endpoint at /wicket/websocket with the container, which finds it on start-up. JavaxWebSocketFilter takes the place of WicketFilter: it handles normal requests the same way and leaves that path to the endpoint. A browser that opens a WebSocket connection to that path goes through an HTTP upgrade request, and from then on the connection belongs to the container’s WebSocket implementation, not to the servlet filter chain.

title: How a message reaches a component
text: Messages from the browser are text or binary frames. When one arrives, Wicket finds the page instance by the id the connection was opened with, takes the lock o
body: Messages from the browser are text or binary frames. When one arrives, Wicket finds the page instance by the id the connection was opened with, takes the lock on that page, and sends the message as an event through the page: every component and behavior can see it in onEvent. WebSocketBehavior unpacks the event and calls the matching method, such as onMessage with a TextMessage, onConnect or onClose. The handler these methods receive, a WebSocketRequestHandler, works like an AjaxRequestTarget. You can add components to it, and their new markup goes back over the connection as an <ajax-response>, which the client script applies exactly like an Ajax response. You can also push plain text with push(String), which the browser receives as a message event for your own JavaScript to handle.

title: Pushing from another thread
text: The interesting case is a message that does not come from the browser. A background job, a message queue listener or another user’s request wants to update a pa
body: The interesting case is a message that does not come from the browser. A background job, a message queue listener or another user’s request wants to update a page. That code holds no page and runs outside any Wicket request. It describes what happened in an object implementing IWebSocketPushMessage and hands it to a WebSocketPushBroadcaster, for one connection or for all of them. The broadcaster finds the connections in the registry and, for each, processes the message as if it had come in over the connection: page lookup, page lock, event through the page. Components receive a WebSocketPushPayload in onEvent, or WebSocketBehavior.onPush is called, with a handler to add components to. The push message is a plain Java object, so the background code never touches a component. Because every message takes the page lock, WebSocket traffic and Ajax requests for the same page are processed one at a time, in the same way two Ajax requests are. This keeps component code free of threading concerns, at the cost of throughput: a page that receives many messages per second keeps its lock busy. A WebSocketResource takes no page lock, which is why it suits high-volume streams that the browser renders itself.

title: What a WebSocket request does not have
text: A WebSocket message is not an HTTP request. It is not processed by servlet filters or listeners, so anything that relies on them is missing: request-scoped and
body: A WebSocket message is not an HTTP request. It is not processed by servlet filters or listeners, so anything that relies on them is missing: request-scoped and session-scoped beans of Spring or CDI do not work, and a security filter does not see the messages. Wicket gives the handler a copy of the HTTP request and session as they were when the connection was opened. The upgrade request is the only point where the usual web defences apply. Browsers send an Origin header with it, and WebSocketConnectionOriginFilter can reject connections from other origins. Frames sent after that carry no such headers; if the application uses a ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener against cross-site requests, it uses WebSocketAwareResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener, which lets WebSocket messages through. See Protect against cross-site request forgery. The connection also lives only as long as the page in the browser. A reload opens a new connection for the new page instance, and a push to a connection that has closed is silently dropped. Code that pushes has to cope with nobody listening.

title: Require HTTPS
text: Serve pages over HTTPS with HttpsMapper and @RequireHttps, and set up the container so redirects and absolute URLs use the right host.
keywords: TLS SSL secure page redirect to https port 8443 reverse proxy Host header HSTS X-Forwarded-Proto
body: You need this when pages must reach the browser over an encrypted connection. Most applications today serve everything over HTTPS and let the container or a reverse proxy redirect plain HTTP; then you do not need anything in Wicket. HttpsMapper is for applications that serve some pages over HTTP and others over HTTPS from the same container.

title: Create the session before switching to HTTPS
text: By default HttpsMapper creates the HTTP session before it redirects from HTTP to HTTPS, so that both schemes share one session. HttpsConfig.setPreferStateful(fa
body: By default HttpsMapper creates the HTTP session before it redirects from HTTP to HTTPS, so that both schemes share one session. HttpsConfig.setPreferStateful(false) turns this off. Do so only if you accept that a user can end up with two sessions, one per scheme, each with its own sign-in state.

title: Install HttpsMapper
text: HttpsMapper wraps the root request mapper. Install it last in init(), after mounting your pages, because it replaces the root mapper. HttpsConfig holds the HTTP
body: HttpsMapper wraps the root request mapper. Install it last in init(), after mounting your pages, because it replaces the root mapper. HttpsConfig holds the HTTP and HTTPS ports, 80 and 443 by default. WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); mountPage("/account", AccountPage.class); setRootRequestMapper(new HttpsMapper(getRootRequestMapper(), new HttpsConfig(8080, 8443))); }

title: Keep the other pages on HTTPS as well
text: HttpsMapper sends pages without @RequireHttps back to HTTP: a request for such a page over HTTPS is redirected to the HTTP port. If you want HTTPS everywhere, e
apis: HttpsMapper RequireHttps HttpsConfig Override Scheme Class IRequestablePage
body: HttpsMapper sends pages without @RequireHttps back to HTTP: a request for such a page over HTTPS is redirected to the HTTP port. If you want HTTPS everywhere, either annotate your base page, or override getDesiredSchemeFor so that every page asks for HTTPS: setRootRequestMapper(new HttpsMapper(getRootRequestMapper(), new HttpsConfig(8080, 8443)) { @Override protected Scheme getDesiredSchemeFor(Class<? extends IRequestablePage> pageClass) { return pageClass == null ? Scheme.ANY : Scheme.HTTPS; } }); Requests that do not concern a page, such as requests for resources, keep the scheme they arrived on.

title: Make the host in redirects trustworthy
text: The redirect to HTTPS uses the host name the servlet container reports, which is the Host header of the request. Every absolute URL Wicket renders uses it too.
body: The redirect to HTTPS uses the host name the servlet container reports, which is the Host header of the request. Every absolute URL Wicket renders uses it too. Wicket does not validate it, because only your deployment knows which host names are valid. Set up the deployment so that only expected values arrive: Configure the container or virtual host to reject requests with an unknown Host, with a 400 or 404 response. When a reverse proxy terminates TLS, let it set Host to the canonical name instead of passing on what the client sent. Do not serve the application from a catch-all or default virtual host. Serve over HTTPS and send an HSTS header, so plain HTTP requests are not part of normal traffic. External security checks shows how to add the header.

title: Mark the pages that need HTTPS
text: AccountPage.java @RequireHttps public class AccountPage extends WebPage { } A request for an annotated page over HTTP is redirected to the same URL over HTTPS.
apis: RequireHttps AccountPage WebPage HttpsMapper SecurePage PaymentPage
body: AccountPage.java @RequireHttps public class AccountPage extends WebPage { } A request for an annotated page over HTTP is redirected to the same URL over HTTPS. Links and form actions to the page are rendered with https:// and the HTTPS port. To protect many pages at once, annotate a base class or an interface. HttpsMapper looks for the annotation on the class, its superclasses and every interface they implement: @RequireHttps public interface SecurePage { } public class PaymentPage extends WebPage implements SecurePage { }

title: Run behind a proxy that terminates TLS
text: When a proxy talks plain HTTP to the container, Wicket sees every request as HTTP. Configure the container to take the scheme from the proxy, or install Wicket’
body: When a proxy talks plain HTTP to the container, Wicket sees every request as HTTP. Configure the container to take the scheme from the proxy, or install Wicket’s XForwardedRequestWrapperFactory, which reads X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For: getFilterFactoryManager().add(new XForwardedRequestWrapperFactory()); Only enable it when a trusted proxy strips any copies of these headers sent by the client; otherwise the client controls them. Wicket does not read X-Forwarded-Host: the host always comes from the container.

page: Add Wicket support to your IDE
title: Add Wicket support to your IDE
text: Install WicketForge in IntelliJ IDEA or QWickie in Eclipse to jump between Java and markup and complete wicket:id values.
keywords: IDE plugin IntelliJ IDEA Eclipse WicketForge QWickie WicketLambdaFold NetBeans VS Code navigate to markup wicket:id completion editor support
body: Every Wicket component in Java has a partner element in HTML, joined by its wicket:id. Any Java IDE edits both files, but it does not know they belong together. A Wicket plugin does: it takes you from a component to its markup and back, and completes wicket:id values while you type. The plugins are written and maintained by their own teams, not by the Wicket project, so report a problem with a plugin in its own issue tracker.

page: Add Wicket support to your IDE
title: Eclipse: QWickie
text: QWickie adds Wicket navigation and code assist to Eclipse. It needs the HTML editor of the Eclipse Web Tools Platform, which the Eclipse IDE for Enterprise Java
body: QWickie adds Wicket navigation and code assist to Eclipse. It needs the HTML editor of the Eclipse Web Tools Platform, which the Eclipse IDE for Enterprise Java and Web Developers already contains. Choose Help, Eclipse Marketplace. Search for qwickie and choose Install. Restart Eclipse when it asks. Without the Marketplace client, choose Help, Install New Software, and add the update site https://raw.githubusercontent.com/count-negative/qwickie/master/qwickie.updatesite/site.xml. With the plugin installed you can: jump from a wicket:id in Java to the element in the HTML file, and see that HTML fragment when you hover over the component; jump from a wicket:message key to its properties file; complete wicket:id values in Java with Ctrl+1; rename the HTML and properties files along with a page or panel class; create a new page with a wizard. Report problems in the QWickie issues.

page: Add Wicket support to your IDE
title: IntelliJ IDEA: WicketForge
text: WicketForge adds code completion, inspections and navigation for Wicket to IntelliJ IDEA. Open Settings, Plugins, and the Marketplace tab. Search for WicketForg
body: WicketForge adds code completion, inspections and navigation for Wicket to IntelliJ IDEA. Open Settings, Plugins, and the Marketplace tab. Search for WicketForge and choose Install. Restart the IDE when it asks. With the plugin installed you can: switch between a page or panel class and its HTML file; go from a component in Java to its wicket:id in the markup, and from a wicket:id to the component that renders it; complete wicket:id values in Java and in HTML; create a page or panel together with its markup file; complete and extract keys in the component’s properties files. The WicketForge wiki describes each feature and its shortcut. Report problems in the WicketForge issues. Shorter lambda models: WicketLambdaFold WicketLambdaFold folds the getter and setter references of a lambda model in the editor, so a line like LambdaModel.of(model, Person::getName, Person::setName) reads as the property it binds. It changes only how the code is shown, not the code itself. Install it from the Marketplace tab the same way.

page: Add Wicket support to your IDE
title: NetBeans and VS Code
text: There is no maintained Wicket plugin for NetBeans or VS Code. Wicket does not need one: a page is a Java class and an HTML file, and the Java support of either
body: There is no maintained Wicket plugin for NetBeans or VS Code. Wicket does not need one: a page is a Java class and an HTML file, and the Java support of either IDE handles both. Keep the HTML file next to its class, as the quickstart project does, and the IDE shows the pair together in the project tree.

page: Configure a module with an initializer
title: Configure a module with an initializer
text: Let a jar configure every Wicket application it is added to, with an IInitializer registered through the Java ServiceLoader.
keywords: ServiceLoader META-INF/services module-info provides library setup plugin auto configuration application startup shutdown
body: Use an initializer when you write a library of components and want it to set itself up in any application that puts the jar on its classpath: mount its resources, register listeners, add settings. Code for one application belongs in its init() method instead.

page: Configure a module with an initializer
title: Register it with the ServiceLoader
text: Wicket finds initializers with java.util.ServiceLoader. Create the file src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.apache.wicket.IInitializer and put the fully qu
body: Wicket finds initializers with java.util.ServiceLoader. Create the file src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.apache.wicket.IInitializer and put the fully qualified class name in it: com.example.charts.ChartsInitializer The file may list several initializers, one per line. If your library is a Java module with a module-info.java, declare the service there as well: module com.example.charts { requires org.apache.wicket.core; provides org.apache.wicket.IInitializer with com.example.charts.ChartsInitializer; }

page: Configure a module with an initializer
title: When the initializer runs
text: Application.initApplication() runs these steps in order: Wicket’s internal setup. The init() method of every initializer found. The application’s own init(). Be
body: Application.initApplication() runs these steps in order: Wicket’s internal setup. The init() method of every initializer found. The application’s own init(). Because the application’s init() runs last, an application can change any setting an initializer made. When the application is destroyed, Wicket calls destroy() on every initializer, after the application’s onDestroy(). Wicket uses the same mechanism for its own modules: wicket-jmx, for example, registers its MBeans from an initializer as soon as the jar is on the classpath (see Inspect and change settings with JMX). Each Wicket application in a web application runs every initializer once. Wicket does not read the META-INF/wicket/*.properties files with an initializer= entry that older documentation describes; only the ServiceLoader registration works.

page: Configure a module with an initializer
title: Write the initializer
text: Implement IInitializer. Wicket calls init() when the application starts and destroy() when it stops: ChartsInitializer.java package com.example.charts; public c
apis: IInitializer ChartsInitializer Override Application ChartDataResource ChartLicenseCheck String Charts
body: Implement IInitializer. Wicket calls init() when the application starts and destroy() when it stops: ChartsInitializer.java package com.example.charts; public class ChartsInitializer implements IInitializer { @Override public void init(Application application) { application.getSharedResources().add("chartData", new ChartDataResource()); application.getComponentInstantiationListeners().add(new ChartLicenseCheck()); } @Override public void destroy(Application application) { // release what init() acquired, such as threads or connections } @Override public String toString() { return "Charts library"; } } Wicket logs each initializer it runs at info level with its toString(), so a readable name helps.

page: Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component
title: Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component
text: Package a JavaScript library with a component, initialize it with the component's markup id, keep it working after Ajax updates and call back to the server.
keywords: javascript library widget datepicker flatpickr jquery plugin renderHead init script getCallbackFunction reusable component dhtml
apis: OnDomReadyHeaderItem JavaScriptResourceReference AbstractDefaultAjaxBehavior CallbackParameter JavaScriptLibrarySettings LocalDateTextField
body: Use this when you want a JavaScript widget, such as a date picker, to behave like any other Wicket component: added in Java, configured from Java, and working without setup in every page that uses it. The example wraps the flatpickr date picker around a LocalDateTextField; the same steps apply to any library that attaches itself to an element.

page: Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component
title: Call the server from the widget
text: To let the server react to the widget, add an Ajax behavior to the component and hand its callback function to the script. getCallbackFunction returns a JavaScr
apis: CallbackParameter AbstractDefaultAjaxBehavior Override AjaxRequestTarget String RequestCycle LocalDate DateField IModel OnDomReadyHeaderItem AjaxFormSubmitBehavior
body: To let the server react to the widget, add an Ajax behavior to the component and hand its callback function to the script. getCallbackFunction returns a JavaScript function; each CallbackParameter.explicit becomes an argument of that function and a request parameter of the same name: private final AbstractDefaultAjaxBehavior picked = new AbstractDefaultAjaxBehavior() { @Override protected void respond(AjaxRequestTarget target) { String date = RequestCycle.get().getRequest().getRequestParameters() .getParameterValue("date").toString(); onPicked(target, LocalDate.parse(date)); } }; public DateField(String id, IModel<LocalDate> model) { super(id, model, "yyyy-MM-dd"); setOutputMarkupId(true); add(picked); } protected void onPicked(AjaxRequestTarget target, LocalDate date) { } // in renderHead response.render(OnDomReadyHeaderItem.forScript("DateField.init('" + getMarkupId() + "', " + options + ", " + picked.getCallbackFunction(CallbackParameter.explicit("date")) + ");")); datefield.js var DateField = { init: function (id, options, onPick) { options.onChange = function (selectedDates, dateStr) { onPick(dateStr); }; flatpickr(document.getElementById(id), options); } }; The callback does not submit the form, so the field’s model is not updated by it. Read the value from the parameter, as above, or submit the form with an AjaxFormSubmitBehavior.

page: Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component
title: Initialize the widget from renderHead
text: The component renders the reference and a DOM-ready script that starts the widget on its own element. The element is found by its markup id, so switch that on.
apis: DateField LocalDateTextField String IModel LocalDate Override IHeaderResponse JavaScriptHeaderItem DateFieldJavaScript JSONObject OnDomReadyHeaderItem
body: The component renders the reference and a DOM-ready script that starts the widget on its own element. The element is found by its markup id, so switch that on. Pass options as JSON built in Java rather than by concatenating strings: DateField.java public class DateField extends LocalDateTextField { public DateField(String id, IModel<LocalDate> model) { super(id, model, "yyyy-MM-dd"); setOutputMarkupId(true); } @Override public void renderHead(IHeaderResponse response) { super.renderHead(response); if (!isEnabledInHierarchy()) { return; } response.render(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(DateFieldJavaScript.INSTANCE)); JSONObject options = new JSONObject() .put("dateFormat", "Y-m-d") .put("allowInput", true); response.render(OnDomReadyHeaderItem.forScript( "DateField.init('" + getMarkupId() + "', " + options + ");")); } } JSONObject is com.github.openjson.JSONObject, which wicket-core already depends on. The Java pattern yyyy-MM-dd and flatpickr’s Y-m-d must describe the same format, or the field cannot parse what the picker writes. A disabled field gets no picker. datefield.js var DateField = { init: function (id, options) { flatpickr(document.getElementById(id), options); } }; The init script carries a nonce when the content security policy is on, like every header item Wicket renders; see Configure the Content Security Policy.

page: Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component
title: Keep it working after an Ajax update
text: When the field, or a container around it, is added to an AjaxRequestTarget, Wicket replaces its element and calls renderHead again, so the init script runs on t
body: When the field, or a container around it, is added to an AjaxRequestTarget, Wicket replaces its element and calls renderHead again, so the init script runs on the new element. The old widget instance is never told and may leave elements and listeners behind. Destroy it when Wicket removes the element: datefield.js Wicket.Event.subscribe('/dom/node/removing', function (event, element) { var inputs = Array.from(element.querySelectorAll('input')); inputs.push(element); inputs.forEach(function (input) { if (input._flatpickr) { input._flatpickr.destroy(); } }); }); The event fires for the replaced element only, which can be a container around the field, so the script also looks inside it. React to Ajax requests in JavaScript lists the other events.

page: Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component
title: Libraries that need jQuery
text: A jQuery plugin needs jQuery on the page. Add getJavaScriptLibrarySettings().getJQueryReference() to the dependencies of your reference, before the plugin. Wick
body: A jQuery plugin needs jQuery on the page. Add getJavaScriptLibrarySettings().getJQueryReference() to the dependencies of your reference, before the plugin. Wicket’s own Ajax library does not guarantee jQuery is there. By default getJQueryReference() returns jQuery 3.7.1.

page: Wrap a JavaScript widget in a component
title: Package the library with the component
text: Put the library’s files in the component’s package, next to the class, and write a small script of your own that connects the library to Wicket: src/main/java/c
apis: DateField DateFieldJavaScript JavaScriptResourceReference Override List HeaderItem JavaScriptHeaderItem Application CssHeaderItem CssResourceReference
body: Put the library’s files in the component’s package, next to the class, and write a small script of your own that connects the library to Wicket: src/main/java/com/example/datefield/ DateField.java DateFieldJavaScript.java datefield.js flatpickr.min.js flatpickr.min.css Then make one resource reference that pulls in everything the script needs, so a page only has to render that one: DateFieldJavaScript.java public class DateFieldJavaScript extends JavaScriptResourceReference { public static final DateFieldJavaScript INSTANCE = new DateFieldJavaScript(); private DateFieldJavaScript() { super(DateFieldJavaScript.class, "datefield.js"); } @Override public List<HeaderItem> getDependencies() { List<HeaderItem> dependencies = super.getDependencies(); dependencies.add(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference( Application.get().getJavaScriptLibrarySettings().getWicketAjaxReference())); dependencies.add(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference( new JavaScriptResourceReference(DateFieldJavaScript.class, "flatpickr.min.js"))); dependencies.add(CssHeaderItem.forReference( new CssResourceReference(DateFieldJavaScript.class, "flatpickr.min.css"))); return dependencies; } } Wicket renders every reference once per page, however many date fields the page has. Declare dependencies between resources has more on dependencies.

page: Put JavaScript at the end of the body
title: Put JavaScript at the end of the body
text: Render all script header items in a container just before the closing body tag with JavaScriptFilteredIntoFooterHeaderResponse and HeaderResponseContainer.
keywords: footer scripts scripts at bottom before </body> move JavaScript page speed render blocking header response decorator bucket
body: Move scripts to the end of the body when you want the browser to render the page before it downloads and runs the JavaScript. Components keep calling renderHead; a header response decorator sorts their items into the head and into a container at the bottom of the page.

page: Put JavaScript at the end of the body
title: Defer scripts instead
text: If you only want scripts not to block rendering, adding defer to the script tags in the head has the same effect without a container: JavaScriptHeaderItem.forRe
body: If you only want scripts not to block rendering, adding defer to the script tags in the head has the same effect without a container: JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(…).setDefer(true). To defer every script of the application, Wicket has JavaScriptDeferHeaderResponse, which it marks as experimental. The decorators are listed in Header items.

page: Put JavaScript at the end of the body
title: Keep one script in the head
text: Some scripts must run before the body renders, for example one that sets a theme class on the document to prevent a flash of the wrong colours. Wrap its item in
apis: FilteredHeaderItem Override IHeaderResponse JavaScriptHeaderItem ThemeJs FilteringHeaderResponse HeaderResponseContainer
body: Some scripts must run before the body renders, for example one that sets a theme class on the document to prevent a flash of the wrong colours. Wrap its item in a FilteredHeaderItem with the name of the head bucket: @Override public void renderHead(IHeaderResponse response) { super.renderHead(response); response.render(new FilteredHeaderItem( JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(ThemeJs.get()), FilteringHeaderResponse.DEFAULT_HEADER_FILTER_NAME)); } A FilteredHeaderItem goes into the bucket it names, whatever the filters say, and its dependencies follow it. The same works the other way: wrap an item with your own bucket name and render that bucket with another HeaderResponseContainer anywhere in the page.

page: Put JavaScript at the end of the body
title: Render the bucket in the page
text: Add a HeaderResponseContainer with the bucket name to every page, as the last element of the body. A base page does it once for all pages: BasePage.java public
body: Add a HeaderResponseContainer with the bucket name to every page, as the last element of the body. A base page does it once for all pages: BasePage.java public abstract class BasePage extends WebPage { public BasePage() { add(new HeaderResponseContainer("footerScripts", "footer-scripts")); } } BasePage.html <!DOCTYPE html> <html xmlns:wicket="http://wicket.apache.org"> <head> <meta charset="utf-8"/> <title>Example</title> </head> <body> <wicket:child/> <wicket:container wicket:id="footerScripts"/> </body> </html> The first argument is the component id, the second the bucket name. The container renders only the script tags, not its own tag. A page that renders script items without the container loses those scripts, so make sure every page extends the base page. During an Ajax request Wicket sends header items with the Ajax response as usual, so components updated with Ajax keep working.

page: Put JavaScript at the end of the body
title: Send script items to a footer bucket
text: Register a JavaScriptFilteredIntoFooterHeaderResponse in init(). The second argument names the bucket for the scripts: WicketApplication.java @Override protecte
body: Register a JavaScriptFilteredIntoFooterHeaderResponse in init(). The second argument names the bucket for the scripts: WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); getHeaderResponseDecorators().add( response -> new JavaScriptFilteredIntoFooterHeaderResponse(response, "footer-scripts")); } From now on, every JavaScriptHeaderItem, OnDomReadyHeaderItem, OnLoadHeaderItem and OnEventHeaderItem goes into the footer-scripts bucket. Stylesheets, meta tags and the markup of the page’s own <head> stay in the head. add places the decorator inside the resource aggregation, so dependencies, bundles and ordering still apply before the items are sorted into buckets, and Wicket still adds the Content Security Policy nonce to every script.

page: Inspect and change settings with JMX
title: Inspect and change settings with JMX
text: Add wicket-jmx to see a running application's settings and session counts in JConsole, clear the markup cache, and change some settings without a restart.
keywords: Java Management Extensions MBean JConsole VisualVM monitoring clearMarkupCache clearLocalizerCache hot fix markup live sessions management console
body: Use this when you want to look into a running Wicket application, or fix a typo in markup or a properties file in production without restarting it. Module wicket-jmx publishes the application’s settings as JMX MBeans, which any JMX client can read and change.

page: Inspect and change settings with JMX
title: Add wicket-jmx
text: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-jmx</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> </dependency> There is nothing to con
body: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-jmx</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> </dependency> There is nothing to configure. The module has an initializer that registers the MBeans with the platform MBean server when the application starts. To register them with another MBean server, set one of these system properties: Property Selects wicket.mbean.server.agentid The MBean server with this agent id. wicket.mbean.server.class The first MBean server of this class.

page: Inspect and change settings with JMX
title: Change a setting at runtime
text: Attributes with a setter can be changed from JConsole. For example: MBean Attribute Example value ApplicationSettings DefaultMaximumUploadSize 20MB DebugSetting
apis: ApplicationSettings DefaultMaximumUploadSize DebugSettings AjaxDebugModeEnabled MarkupSettings StripComments RequestCycleSettings Timeout ResourceSettings ThrowExceptionOnMissingResource
body: Attributes with a setter can be changed from JConsole. For example: MBean Attribute Example value ApplicationSettings DefaultMaximumUploadSize 20MB DebugSettings AjaxDebugModeEnabled true MarkupSettings StripComments true RequestCycleSettings Timeout PT1M (an ISO-8601 duration) ResourceSettings ThrowExceptionOnMissingResource false The change lasts until the application restarts; put permanent settings in init().

page: Inspect and change settings with JMX
title: Connect with JConsole
text: Start jconsole, which comes with the JDK, and connect to the process of your servlet container. For a server on another machine, start that JVM with the standar
apis: Application ApplicationSettings DebugSettings MarkupSettings PageSettings RequestCycleSettings ResourceSettings SecuritySettings SessionSettings StoreSettings RequestLogger
body: Start jconsole, which comes with the JDK, and connect to the process of your servlet container. For a server on another machine, start that JVM with the standard com.sun.management.jmxremote options and connect remotely. Open the MBeans tab. The Wicket MBeans are in the domain org.apache.wicket.app.<name>, where the name is the name of the Wicket filter, as returned by Application.getName(). MBean Shows type=Application Application class, home page class, configuration type, Wicket version, size of the markup cache. type=Application,name=ApplicationSettings Error pages, unexpected exception display, default maximum upload size. type=Application,name=DebugSettings Ajax debug mode, component use check, component path attribute, development utilities. type=Application,name=MarkupSettings Automatic linking, whitespace compression, comment and Wicket tag stripping, markup encoding. type=Application,name=PageSettings Whether pages are versioned by default. type=Application,name=RequestCycleSettings Response buffering, request timeout, character encoding, exception retry count. type=Application,name=ResourceSettings Localizer, resource finders, string resource loaders, poll frequency, missing resource behavior. type=Application,name=SecuritySettings Authorization strategy, crypt factory, unauthorized instantiation listener. type=Application,name=SessionSettings Page factory and session store. type=Application,name=StoreSettings Maximum page store size per session, file store folder, asynchronous storing. type=RequestLogger Created, live and peak sessions, current and peak active requests.

page: Inspect and change settings with JMX
title: Publish a markup or text fix without a restart
text: In deployment mode Wicket caches markup and localized texts and does not look at the files again. After you replace an HTML or properties file in the deployed a
body: In deployment mode Wicket caches markup and localized texts and does not look at the files again. After you replace an HTML or properties file in the deployed application, run these operations on the type=Application MBean: Operation Effect clearMarkupCache Wicket reads the markup files again when it next needs them. clearLocalizerCache Wicket looks up localized texts again.

page: Inspect and change settings with JMX
title: See session and request counts
text: The RequestLogger MBean reads its numbers from Wicket’s request logger, which is off by default. Turn it on in init(): getRequestLoggerSettings().setRequestLogg
body: The RequestLogger MBean reads its numbers from Wicket’s request logger, which is off by default. Turn it on in init(): getRequestLoggerSettings().setRequestLoggerEnabled(true); Its restart operation restarts the request logger and stop turns it off. Anyone who can connect to the JMX port can change these settings. Do not open it to untrusted networks.

title: Inject with JSR-330 annotations
text: Use the standard @Inject and @Named annotations instead of @SpringBean, with the Spring, Guice and CDI integrations.
keywords: Jakarta Dependency Injection jakarta.inject Inject Named Qualifier javax.inject Guice portable annotations
body: Use this when you want components that do not depend on one container’s annotations. The Jakarta Dependency Injection annotations (jakarta.inject.Inject, jakarta.inject.Named, formerly JSR-330) work with every injection module of Wicket. They come with wicket-ioc, which wicket-spring and wicket-guice depend on, so you need no extra dependency. Only the jakarta.inject package works. Fields annotated with the old javax.inject.Inject are not injected.

title: Inject other objects
text: With Spring and Guice, objects that Wicket does not create are injected by calling Injector.get().inject(this) in their constructor, whichever annotation they u
body: With Spring and Guice, objects that Wicket does not create are injected by calling Injector.get().inject(this) in their constructor, whichever annotation they use. With CDI, use NonContextual.of(this).inject(this).

title: With CDI
text: @Inject is CDI’s own annotation, so nothing changes; see Inject CDI beans. Qualifiers work as defined by CDI.
body: @Inject is CDI’s own annotation, so nothing changes; see Inject CDI beans. Qualifiers work as defined by CDI.

title: With Guice
text: Module wicket-guice injects fields annotated with @jakarta.inject.Inject or @com.google.inject.Inject. Register the injector with your Guice modules in init():
apis: Inject Override GuiceComponentInjector ServicesModule Named Qualifier BindingAnnotation
body: Module wicket-guice injects fields annotated with @jakarta.inject.Inject or @com.google.inject.Inject. Register the injector with your Guice modules in init(): @Override protected void init() { super.init(); getComponentInstantiationListeners().add(new GuiceComponentInjector(this, new ServicesModule())); } A qualifier on the field, such as @Named("archive") or your own annotation marked @jakarta.inject.Qualifier or @BindingAnnotation, selects the binding. Only one qualifier per field is allowed. Optional injection needs Guice’s own annotation, @com.google.inject.Inject(optional = true). Like the Spring integration, wicket-guice injects serializable proxies, so the same rules apply: inject interfaces or non-final classes, and add Objenesis for classes without a constructor without arguments. See Keep injected fields serializable.

title: With Spring
text: Register SpringComponentInjector as described in Inject Spring beans. It injects fields annotated with @Inject as well as @SpringBean: public class ProductPage
apis: SpringComponentInjector Inject SpringBean ProductPage WebPage ProductService Named IllegalStateException
body: Register SpringComponentInjector as described in Inject Spring beans. It injects fields annotated with @Inject as well as @SpringBean: public class ProductPage extends WebPage { @Inject private ProductService products; @Inject @Named("archiveProductService") private ProductService archive; } @Named selects a bean by name, like @SpringBean(name = ...). A field with @Inject is always required: when no bean matches, Wicket throws an IllegalStateException. For an optional dependency, use @SpringBean(required = false).

title: Run on Apache Karaf
text: Install Wicket in Apache Karaf or another OSGi container with the Karaf feature that every Wicket release publishes.
keywords: OSGi bundle Karaf feature features.xml feature:install feature:repo-add wicket-core feature Karaf assembly Pax Web
body: Use this when you deploy Wicket applications as bundles in Apache Karaf. Every Wicket jar is an OSGi bundle, and each release publishes a Karaf feature file that installs Wicket and its dependencies in one step. Wicket uses the jakarta.servlet API, so the Karaf runtime needs an HTTP service that supports Jakarta Servlet.

title: Include Wicket in a Karaf assembly
text: To build a custom Karaf distribution with Wicket in it, reference the feature file as a Maven dependency of the assembly project: <dependency> <groupId>org.apac
body: To build a custom Karaf distribution with Wicket in it, reference the feature file as a Maven dependency of the assembly project: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> <type>xml</type> <classifier>features</classifier> </dependency> The Karaf documentation on provisioning describes how features and assemblies work.

title: Install the Wicket feature
text: Add the feature repository of your Wicket version, with that version in place of <version>: karaf@root()> feature:repo-add mvn:org.apache.wicket/wicket/<version
body: Add the feature repository of your Wicket version, with that version in place of <version>: karaf@root()> feature:repo-add mvn:org.apache.wicket/wicket/<version>/xml/features Check that the feature is available: karaf@root()> feature:list | grep -i wicket The list shows a feature named wicket-core. Install it: karaf@root()> feature:install wicket-core

title: What the feature contains
text: feature:info wicket-core lists the bundles the feature installs: Bundle   wicket-util, wicket-request, wicket-core The core of Wicket. wicket-extensions, wicket
body: feature:info wicket-core lists the bundles the feature installs: Bundle   wicket-util, wicket-request, wicket-core The core of Wicket. wicket-extensions, wicket-auth-roles, wicket-devutils, wicket-jmx, wicket-objectsizeof-agent Optional Wicket modules. openjson, commons-io, commons-fileupload2-jakarta, commons-collections4, jdk-serializable-functional Libraries Wicket depends on. The feature also provides the OSGi capability wicket;provider:=apache-wicket, which your own features can require. Modules outside this list, such as wicket-spring, wicket-cdi, wicket-native-websocket and wicket-bean-validation, are bundles too, but you install them and their dependencies yourself, for example in a feature of your own.

title: Keep a page stateless
text: Build a page that Wicket does not store in the session, find the component that makes it stateful, and guard it with a test.
keywords: stateless no session isPageStateless setStatelessHint getStatelessHint isStateless is not stateless because of component public pages crawler jsessionid
apis: Page StatelessChecker StatelessComponent StatelessLink StatelessForm BookmarkablePageLink
body: Keep a page stateless when it is public, visited by many anonymous users or meant to be bookmarked, such as a home page, a product page or a login page. A stateless page needs no session. Stateful and stateless pages explains the trade-off.

title: Fail fast with StatelessChecker
text: wicket-devutils has an annotation and a checker that throws an exception when a page or component marked as stateless is not. Register the checker in developmen
apis: Override StatelessChecker StatelessComponent ProductPage WebPage StatelessCheckFailureException
body: wicket-devutils has an annotation and a checker that throws an exception when a page or component marked as stateless is not. Register the checker in development mode: WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); if (usesDevelopmentConfig()) { getComponentPostOnBeforeRenderListeners().add(new StatelessChecker()); } } and annotate the page: @StatelessComponent public class ProductPage extends WebPage { // ... } When ProductPage renders with a stateful component, StatelessChecker throws a StatelessCheckFailureException that names the component. The annotation has no effect without the checker, and is inherited by subclasses; @StatelessComponent(enabled = false) turns it off for a subclass that is allowed to be stateful.

title: Find the component that makes the page stateful
text: Page.isPageStateless() tells you whether the page is stateless. To find the culprit, visit the components and log those that are not: @Override protected void o
body: Page.isPageStateless() tells you whether the page is stateless. To find the culprit, visit the components and log those that are not: @Override protected void onBeforeRender() { super.onBeforeRender(); if (getApplication().usesDevelopmentConfig() && !isPageStateless()) { visitChildren((component, visit) -> { if (!component.isStateless()) { log.warn("Stateful component: {}", component.getPageRelativePath()); } }); } } With debug logging on for org.apache.wicket.Page, Wicket logs the same thing itself: “Page ‘…’ is not stateless because of component with path ‘…’”.

title: Make the page bookmarkable
text: Wicket must be able to create the page itself, for every request. Give it a public constructor without arguments, or one that takes only PageParameters, and rea
apis: PageParameters ProductPage WebPage IModel Product LoadableDetachableModel Label BookmarkablePageLink
body: Wicket must be able to create the page itself, for every request. Give it a public constructor without arguments, or one that takes only PageParameters, and read everything else from the parameters: public class ProductPage extends WebPage { public ProductPage(PageParameters parameters) { long id = parameters.get("id").toLong(); IModel<Product> product = LoadableDetachableModel.of(() -> productService.find(id)); add(new Label("name", product.map(Product::getName))); } } Link to it by class, with BookmarkablePageLink or setResponsePage(ProductPage.class, parameters), so Wicket creates it from the URL. Pass parameters to a page shows how to build those URLs.

title: Test it
text: Assert the statelessness in a test, so a later change cannot break it unnoticed: @Test void productPageIsStateless() { tester.startPage(ProductPage.class, new P
body: Assert the statelessness in a test, so a later change cannot break it unnoticed: @Test void productPageIsStateless() { tester.startPage(ProductPage.class, new PageParameters().add("id", 42)); assertTrue(tester.getLastRenderedPage().isPageStateless()); } Test pages and components shows how to set up WicketTester.

title: Use stateless components
text: A page is stateless only when every visible, enabled component on it, and every behavior on those components, is stateless. These components are: Instead of Use
apis: Link BookmarkablePageLink StatelessLink Form StatelessForm ExternalLink
body: A page is stateless only when every visible, enabled component on it, and every behavior on those components, is stateless. These components are: Instead of Use Link BookmarkablePageLink to go to a page, StatelessLink to run code on click Form StatelessForm, see Build a stateless form Ajax behaviors and links their stateless variants, see Use Ajax on stateless pages any link to another site ExternalLink, which has no callback Labels, images, containers and other components without a callback are stateless already. A stateful component that is hidden or disabled does not make the page stateful. Calling getPageReference() on a page makes it stateful, and so does setStatelessHint(false).

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Read and write data with lambda models
text: Use lambdas, method references and the default methods of IModel to show computed values and bind components to properties without strings.
keywords: method reference map flatMap filter orElse orElseGet combineWith isPresent functional interface read-only model UnsupportedOperationException type-safe
body: Use lambda models when a component shows a value computed from other data, or reads and writes one property of an object that another model holds. They are checked by the compiler and survive a rename, unlike property expressions. The examples use a personModel of type IModel<Person>, for instance a detachable model that loads the person by id.

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Bind a field of the page
text: For a value that belongs to the page or panel, use LambdaModel.of(getter, setter) with method references on this: SearchPage.java public class SearchPage extend
apis: LambdaModel SearchPage WebPage String Form Void Override ResultsPage TextField
body: For a value that belongs to the page or panel, use LambdaModel.of(getter, setter) with method references on this: SearchPage.java public class SearchPage extends WebPage { private String query; public SearchPage() { Form<Void> form = new Form<>("form") { @Override protected void onSubmit() { setResponsePage(new ResultsPage(query)); } }; form.add(new TextField<>("query", LambdaModel.of(this::getQuery, this::setQuery))); add(form); } public String getQuery() { return query; } public void setQuery(String query) { this.query = query; } }

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Combine two models
text: combineWith computes a value from the objects of two models. It returns null when either object is null: IModel<String> first = personModel.map(Person::getFirst
body: combineWith computes a value from the objects of two models. It returns null when either object is null: IModel<String> first = personModel.map(Person::getFirstName); IModel<String> last = personModel.map(Person::getLastName); add(new Label("name", first.combineWith(last, (f, l) -> f + " " + l)));

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Derive a value from another model
text: map turns a model into a model of something computed from its object: add(new Label("fullName", personModel.map(Person::getFullName))); add(new Label("city", pe
body: map turns a model into a model of something computed from its object: add(new Label("fullName", personModel.map(Person::getFullName))); add(new Label("city", personModel.map(Person::getAddress).map(Address::getCity))); map returns null instead of calling the function when the object is null, so a chain of map calls never throws a NullPointerException halfway. The resulting model is read-only. Detaching it detaches personModel.

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Fall back to a default
text: orElse returns a fixed value when the object is null; orElseGet calls a supplier instead: add(new Label("nickname", personModel.map(Person::getNickname).orElse(
body: orElse returns a fixed value when the object is null; orElseGet calls a supplier instead: add(new Label("nickname", personModel.map(Person::getNickname).orElse("(none)"))); add(new Label("since", personModel.map(Person::getJoined).orElseGet(LocalDate::now)));

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Keep or test an object
text: filter keeps the object only when a predicate holds, and returns null otherwise. isPresent gives a Boolean model that is true when the object is not null. as ke
apis: Boolean IModel Order Link Override Customer
body: filter keeps the object only when a predicate holds, and returns null otherwise. isPresent gives a Boolean model that is true when the object is not null. as keeps the object only when it is an instance of a class: IModel<Order> openOrder = orderModel.filter(Order::isOpen); add(new Link<>("cancel", openOrder) { @Override public void onClick() { orderService.cancel(getModelObject()); } @Override protected void onConfigure() { super.onConfigure(); setVisible(openOrder.isPresent().getObject()); } }); IModel<Customer> customer = partyModel.as(Customer.class);

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Keep what the lambda captures small
text: The lambdas you pass to these methods are serializable types (SerializableSupplier, SerializableFunction and so on), because they are stored with the page. Ever
body: The lambdas you pass to these methods are serializable types (SerializableSupplier, SerializableFunction and so on), because they are stored with the page. Everything a lambda captures is stored with it. Capture models, ids and this. The page or panel is serialized anyway. Do not capture entities or large objects. LambdaModel.of(person::getName, person::setName) stores person in the page, with the problems described in Why new Model<>(entity) goes wrong. Use the LambdaModel.of(personModel, ...) form instead. Do not capture services or connections, which are rarely serializable. Reach them through an injected field of the component, as described in Inject Spring beans. Model classes lists every default method of IModel.

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Read and write a property
text: LambdaModel.of(target, getter, setter) gives a model that reads and writes one property of the object in target: IModel<String> email = LambdaModel.of(personMod
body: LambdaModel.of(target, getter, setter) gives a model that reads and writes one property of the object in target: IModel<String> email = LambdaModel.of(personModel, Person::getEmail, Person::setEmail); form.add(new EmailTextField("email", email)); When the form is submitted, the field calls setObject(), which calls setEmail on the person the target model holds at that moment. When the target holds null, getObject() returns null and setObject() does nothing. The model detaches its target. flatMap does the same for a mapper that returns a model, which is useful when the object already offers models for its parts: IModel<String> name = personModel.flatMap(p -> LambdaModel.of(p::getName, p::setName));

page: Read and write data with lambda models
title: Show a computed value
text: IModel has a single abstract method, getObject(), so any lambda that returns a value is a model: add(new Label("now", () -> LocalTime.now())); Wicket calls the
body: IModel has a single abstract method, getObject(), so any lambda that returns a value is a model: add(new Label("now", () -> LocalTime.now())); Wicket calls the lambda every time the label renders. A model written this way is read-only: its setObject() throws UnsupportedOperationException. That is fine for labels, but a form component needs a model it can write to.

title: Show a list with ListView
text: Render markup for every element of a java.util.List, keep form input in the rows, and avoid the pitfalls of index-based items.
keywords: for each iterate table rows list of objects populateItem setReuseItems form in list validation lost feedback lost removeAll
body: Use a ListView to render a fragment of markup for each element of a java.util.List, such as a row per person in a table. For large or paged data use a DataView instead; a ListView always works with the whole list.

title: Bind the row components by id
text: PropertyListView gives each item a CompoundPropertyModel, so components without a model bind to the property named by their id: add(new PropertyListView<>("pers
apis: PropertyListView CompoundPropertyModel Override ListItem Person Label
body: PropertyListView gives each item a CompoundPropertyModel, so components without a model bind to the property named by their id: add(new PropertyListView<>("persons", persons) { @Override protected void populateItem(ListItem<Person> item) { item.add(new Label("fullName")); item.add(new Label("email")); } }); Bind components to a JavaBean describes the property expressions.

title: Mind that items are identified by index
text: The model of a ListItem is a ListItemModel: it reads element number n from the list view’s model, not a particular object. When the list changes between two req
body: The model of a ListItem is a ListItemModel: it reads element number n from the list view’s model, not a particular object. When the list changes between two requests, item n refers to a different element than before. A link in row 3 that deletes “its” person deletes whatever is at index 3 when the click arrives. Two ways to avoid this: Override getListItemModel(listModel, index) and return a model that keeps the element’s id, such as a detachable model loaded by id. Use a RefreshingView or DataView, which build each item from a model you provide. Control how items are reused shows how.

title: Move and remove elements
text: ListView has factory methods for links that change the list: moveUpLink(id, item), moveDownLink(id, item) and removeLink(id, item). They change the list in the
body: ListView has factory methods for links that change the list: moveUpLink(id, item), moveDownLink(id, item) and removeLink(id, item). They change the list in the list view’s model, so that model must hold a modifiable list that lives with the page, such as a Model or ListModel.

title: Put form fields in the rows
text: By default a ListView throws its items away and creates new ones every time it renders. Inside a form that breaks validation: when a submit fails, the new field
apis: ListView Person Override ListItem TextField LambdaModel
body: By default a ListView throws its items away and creates new ones every time it renders. Inside a form that breaks validation: when a submit fails, the new fields have lost the user’s input, and the error messages belonged to the old fields, so they are not shown either. Tell the list view to keep its items: ListView<Person> rows = new ListView<>("persons", persons) { @Override protected void populateItem(ListItem<Person> item) { item.add(new TextField<>("name", LambdaModel.of(item.getModel(), Person::getName, Person::setName)).setRequired(true)); } }; rows.setReuseItems(true); form.add(rows); With setReuseItems(true) the list view creates an item only for an index it has no item for yet, and removes items whose index is past the end of the list. To rebuild all items after you change the list, for instance after adding or deleting an element, call removeAll() on the list view.

title: Render a row per element
text: Attach the ListView to the tag to repeat. Wicket calls populateItem once per element, with a ListItem whose model holds that element: PersonsPage.html <table> <
apis: ListView ListItem IModel List Person LoadableDetachableModel Override Label AttributeModifier
body:
Attach the ListView to the tag to repeat. Wicket calls populateItem once per element, with a ListItem whose model holds that element: PersonsPage.html
PersonsPage.java IModel> persons = LoadableDetachableModel.of(() -> personService.findAll()); add(new ListView<>("persons", persons) { @Override protected void populateItem(ListItem item) { item.add(new Label("name", item.getModel().map(Person::getFullName))); item.add(new Label("email", item.getModel().map(Person::getEmail))); } }); Add the components to item, not to the list view. The ListItem is what renders the , so behaviors and attributes for the row go on the item as well, for example item.add(AttributeModifier.append("class", "inactive")). The list view also accepts a plain List, which it wraps in a model. Pass a model, as above, when the list comes from a database, so the list is loaded per request and not stored with the page.

title: Repeat a fixed number of times
text: To repeat markup n times without a list, use Loop. Its populateItem(LoopItem) gets the iteration number from item.getIndex(): IModel<Integer> stars = productMod
apis: Loop LoopItem IModel Integer Product Override WebMarkupContainer
body: To repeat markup n times without a list, use Loop. Its populateItem(LoopItem) gets the iteration number from item.getIndex(): IModel<Integer> stars = productModel.map(Product::getRating); add(new Loop("stars", stars) { @Override protected void populateItem(LoopItem item) { item.add(new WebMarkupContainer("star")); } }); Loop rebuilds its items on every render.

page: Translate the options of a choice
title: Translate the options of a choice
text: Show translated options in a DropDownChoice, RadioChoice or other choice component, translate enum values, and change the "Choose One" text.
keywords: localizeDisplayValues translate dropdown translate select options enum translation Choose One null option nullValid placeholder option
apis: AbstractChoice EnumChoiceRenderer DropDownChoice RadioChoice CheckBoxMultipleChoice AbstractSingleSelectChoice ListChoice
body: Choice components, such as DropDownChoice, RadioChoice, ListChoice and CheckBoxMultipleChoice, show the display value of each choice as it is. To show it in the user’s language, look the display value up as a key, or render enum values through an EnumChoiceRenderer.

page: Translate the options of a choice
title: Change the text of the empty option
text: A DropDownChoice shows an extra option when it has no selection yet, by default “Choose One”. When setNullValid(true) makes no selection a valid choice, the ext
body: A DropDownChoice shows an extra option when it has no selection yet, by default “Choose One”. When setNullValid(true) makes no selection a valid choice, the extra option is always there and is empty by default. Both texts are looked up like other texts: Option Keys tried in turn Default no selection yet, null not valid <id>.null, null Choose One null is valid <id>.nullValid, nullValid empty color.null=Pick a color size.nullValid=No preference null=... without an id in the application bundle changes the text for every drop-down in the application. These keys work whether or not the display values are translated. The lookup of each key follows the usual order, described in Where Wicket looks for texts. The choice components themselves are listed in Form components.

page: Translate the options of a choice
title: Translate enum values
text: For an enum, use an EnumChoiceRenderer. It looks up the key <enum class simple name>.<constant name>: public enum Size { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE } add(new DropDown
apis: EnumChoiceRenderer Size DropDownChoice List Small Medium Large
body: For an enum, use an EnumChoiceRenderer. It looks up the key <enum class simple name>.<constant name>: public enum Size { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE } add(new DropDownChoice<>("size", sizeModel, List.of(Size.values()), new EnumChoiceRenderer<>(this))); Size.SMALL=Small Size.MEDIUM=Medium Size.LARGE=Large Pass a component to the constructor, usually the page or panel, so that its bundles are searched. Without one, the renderer only looks in application-wide bundles. Unlike localizeDisplayValues, a missing key is an error, so every constant needs a text. Override resourceKey(T) to use other keys.

body: Override localizeDisplayValues() to return true. body: To translate a page or panel, put its texts in properties files next to its class, one file per language, and refer to them by key from the markup or the Java code. How Wicket finds the right file is explained in How Wicket localizes.

Texts used on many pages go in the bundle of a base page, a package (wicket-package.properties) or the application class (WicketApplication.properties).

The next render uses the new locale for texts, markup files and number and date formats.

title: Save files with non-Latin characters as UTF-8
text: Wicket reads .properties files as ISO 8859-1, like java.util.Properties. When your editor saves UTF-8, as most do, characters such as ü come out garbled, and Ch
body: Wicket reads .properties files as ISO 8859-1, like java.util.Properties. When your editor saves UTF-8, as most do, characters such as ü come out garbled, and Chinese or Cyrillic text cannot be written in that encoding at all. In a .properties file you have to write them as Unicode escapes, such as ü. Name the file .utf8.properties instead, and Wicket reads it as UTF-8. This is the simplest choice for every language, German included: HomePage_zh.utf8.properties greeting=欢迎光临本网站！ Wicket also reads XML properties files, which declare their own encoding, with the extension .properties.xml: HomePage_ja.properties.xml <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <!DOCTYPE properties SYSTEM "http://java.sun.com/dtd/properties.dtd"> <properties> <entry key="greeting">ショップへようこそ！</entry> </properties> For each file name, Wicket uses the first of .properties, .utf8.properties and .properties.xml that exists. Keep one format per file name.

title: Show a text from Java
text: Use a ResourceModel for the model of a component. It looks up the text when the component renders, so it follows a change of language and works in the construct
body: Use a ResourceModel for the model of a component. It looks up the text when the component renders, so it follows a change of language and works in the constructor: add(new Label("greeting", new ResourceModel("greeting"))); Component#getString(key) returns the text right away. Call it during rendering, in onConfigure or inside a model lambda, not in the constructor: until the component is on a page, Wicket cannot search the bundles of its parents. add(new Label("greeting", () -> getString("greeting"))); To put values in a text, such as a name or a date, see Put model values into translated texts.

To translate attributes, add a wicket:message attribute with attribute:key pairs, separated by commas: The text is not escaped by default. body: You need this when some pages may only be seen by a user who has signed in. The wicket-auth-roles module gives you a session that knows whether the user is signed in, an application class that sends anonymous users to a sign-in page, and a ready-made sign-in form.

apis: UsernamePasswordPanel SignInPage WebPage Sign UsernamePasswordPage SignInPanel
body:
UsernamePasswordPanel contains a feedback panel and a stateless form with a username and a password field. On success it continues to the page the user originally asked for, or to the home page if there was none. On failure it shows the message with the resource key signInFailed. SignInPage.java public class SignInPage extends WebPage { public SignInPage() { add(new UsernamePasswordPanel("signIn")); } } SignInPage.html

Sign in

If the default layout is good enough, return UsernamePasswordPage.class from getSignInPageClass() and skip your own page. UsernamePasswordPanel and UsernamePasswordPage exist since Wicket 10.11.0. Wicket 10 also has SignInPanel and SignInPage, whose “remember me” option stores the username and password in a cookie. They are deprecated since 10.11.0.
