title: Pass parameters to a page
text: Put values in the URL of a page with PageParameters, read them in the page constructor and convert them to the types you need.
keywords: query string request parameter URL parameter named parameter indexed parameter fragment getPageParameters bookmarkable page
body: You need page parameters when the URL itself has to carry data: a link in an email that confirms a subscription, a product page that people bookmark, a search page that other sites link to. Inside your application, passing objects or models to a page constructor is usually simpler.

title: Add a fragment to the URL
text: Since Wicket 10.4, PageParameters supports the fragment of a URL, the part after #. PageParameters parameters = new PageParameters().add("id", 42); parameters.s
body: Since Wicket 10.4, PageParameters supports the fragment of a URL, the part after #. PageParameters parameters = new PageParameters().add("id", 42); parameters.setFragment("reviews"); setResponsePage(ProductPage.class, parameters); // ...?id=42#reviews Browsers do not send the fragment to the server, so you can set it on outgoing URLs but not read it from an incoming request.

title: Build a full URL for an email
text: A confirmation link in an email needs the protocol and host as well. mapUrlFor builds the URL of a page with its parameters, and the URL renderer of the request
body: A confirmation link in an email needs the protocol and host as well. mapUrlFor builds the URL of a page with its parameters, and the URL renderer of the request cycle makes it absolute: RequestCycle cycle = RequestCycle.get(); Url url = cycle.mapUrlFor(ConfirmPage.class, new PageParameters().add("token", token)); String link = cycle.getUrlRenderer().renderFullUrl(url);

title: Build the parameters
text: PageParameters holds name-value pairs, like a query string. add and set both return the PageParameters, so you can chain them. Values are stored as strings; Wic
body: PageParameters holds name-value pairs, like a query string. add and set both return the PageParameters, so you can chain them. Values are stored as strings; Wicket calls toString() on what you pass. PageParameters parameters = new PageParameters() .add("id", 42) .add("tab", "reviews"); set(name, value) replaces any value the name already has. add(name, value) appends another value, so add("tag", "red").add("tag", "blue") produces ?tag=red&tag=blue. remove(name) deletes a parameter.

title: Convert a parameter to a number, date or enum
text: get(name) never returns null. It returns a StringValue, which is empty when the parameter is missing, and which converts the text for you: Method Missing parame
apis: StringValue Class StringValueConversionException Tab AbortWithHttpErrorCodeException Long List
body: get(name) never returns null. It returns a StringValue, which is empty when the parameter is missing, and which converts the text for you: Method Missing parameter Text that does not convert toLong(), toInt(), toBoolean(), toEnum(Class) throws StringValueConversionException throws StringValueConversionException toLong(42), toInt(1), toEnum(Tab.INFO) returns the default returns the default toOptionalLong(), toOptionalInteger(), toOptionalString() returns null throws StringValueConversionException toString() returns null — isNull(), isEmpty() true — Parameters come from the user, who can edit the URL. Decide what a missing or broken value means. To answer with a 404, throw an AbortWithHttpErrorCodeException: Long id = parameters.get("id").toOptionalLong(); if (id == null) { throw new AbortWithHttpErrorCodeException(404); } getValues(name) returns all values of a parameter that occurs more than once, as a List<StringValue>.

title: Read the parameters in the page
text: Give the page a constructor that takes PageParameters and pass them to super. The page keeps them, so getPageParameters() returns them later, and Wicket uses th
apis: PageParameters ProductPage WebPage IModel Product LoadableDetachableModel Label
body: Give the page a constructor that takes PageParameters and pass them to super. The page keeps them, so getPageParameters() returns them later, and Wicket uses them when it builds the URL of the page. ProductPage.java public class ProductPage extends WebPage { public ProductPage(PageParameters parameters) { super(parameters); long id = parameters.get("id").toLong(); // products is your own data access service IModel<Product> product = LoadableDetachableModel.of(() -> products.find(id)); add(new Label("name", product.map(Product::getName))); } } A page with a PageParameters constructor, or with a constructor without arguments, is bookmarkable: Wicket can create it from the URL alone, without anything in the session.

title: Send the user to a page with parameters
text: Call setResponsePage with the page class and the parameters, for example in the onClick of a link or the onSubmit of a form: setResponsePage(ProductPage.class,
body: Call setResponsePage with the page class and the parameters, for example in the onClick of a link or the onSubmit of a form: setResponsePage(ProductPage.class, new PageParameters().add("id", product.getId())); To render a plain link to the page without a click handler, use a BookmarkablePageLink, described in Link to a page. Without a mount, the URL contains the class name: /wicket/bookmarkable/com.example.ProductPage?id=42&tab=reviews. Give pages readable URLs shows how to turn this into /products/42.

title: Use indexed parameters
text: Besides named parameters, PageParameters holds indexed parameters. Wicket renders them as path segments after the page path, before the query string: PageParame
body: Besides named parameters, PageParameters holds indexed parameters. Wicket renders them as path segments after the page path, before the query string: PageParameters parameters = new PageParameters() .set(0, "2026") .set(1, "october") .add("sort", "date"); // /archive/2026/october?sort=date when ArchivePage is mounted at /archive Read them with get(0), get(1), and so on. A mount path with placeholders such as /archive/${year}/${month} gives the same URL with named parameters, which are easier to read in code.

title: How pages are stored
text: How Wicket finds the page for a request, and the chain of stores that keeps stateful pages in the request, the session and on disk.
keywords: page store page cache session size disk filestore serialization back button PageExpiredException data file page manager
apis: IPageManager IPageStore IPageProvider IPageFactory RequestPageStore CachingPageStore InSessionPageStore SerializingPageStore AsynchronousPageStore CryptingPageStore DiskPageStore DefaultPageManagerProvider ISerializer
body: A stateful page has to outlive the request that created it, and earlier versions of it have to stay available for the back button. Wicket keeps them in a chain of page stores, each handling one concern: holding pages during the request, caching the last one in the session, serializing, writing in the background, encrypting, and writing to disk.

title: Encrypted pages
text: CryptingPageStore encrypts the bytes of every page before they reach the disk, with a random key per session that is kept in the session. Anyone who can read th
body: CryptingPageStore encrypts the bytes of every page before they reach the disk, with a random key per session that is kept in the session. Anyone who can read the store without the session sees only ciphertext. The key does not protect against someone who controls the session itself. Wicket deserializes whatever it reads back from the store. Treat the store as private storage either way: on a disk only the application can read, or in a database only the application can write to. The cipher comes from StoreSettings.setCrypter. The default DefaultCrypter (AES-256-CBC) is not authenticated; GCMSIVCrypter is the authenticated option. Configure the page store shows how to change the size, the folder, encryption and the stores in the chain.

title: Finding the page for a request
text: For each request that targets a page, Wicket asks an IPageProvider for the instance. The provider uses an IPageSource, which takes one of two routes: The URL ha
body: For each request that targets a page, Wicket asks an IPageProvider for the instance. The provider uses an IPageSource, which takes one of two routes: The URL has a page id, such as ?3: the IPageManager looks the page up in the stores. The URL has no page id, or the page is gone: the IPageFactory creates a new instance from the page class and its PageParameters. The IPageManager is the session’s entry point to the stores. It records every page that the request touches, which can be more than one when a handler calls setResponsePage(), and at the end of the request passes the stateful ones to the stores. Stateless pages are never stored.

title: The default chain
text: DefaultPageManagerProvider builds this chain, from the request to the disk: Store Role RequestPageStore holds the pages used in this request; adds them to the n
apis: DefaultPageManagerProvider RequestPageStore CachingPageStore InSessionPageStore SerializingPageStore SerializedPage AsynchronousPageStore CryptingPageStore DiskPageStore
body: DefaultPageManagerProvider builds this chain, from the request to the disk: Store Role RequestPageStore holds the pages used in this request; adds them to the next store when the request is detached CachingPageStore with an InSessionPageStore keeps the last page used, as a live object, in the HTTP session SerializingPageStore turns pages into SerializedPages: page id, page class and bytes AsynchronousPageStore hands the bytes to a background thread, so the request does not wait for the disk; on by default CryptingPageStore encrypts the bytes with a key kept in the session; off by default DiskPageStore writes the bytes to a file per session The three levels a page can be found on look like this: Reading goes the same way. A page used again in the same request comes from the request store. A click on the page the user just saw finds it in the session cache, without deserializing. Only the back button, or a second browser tab on another page, reaches the disk, and those pages are deserialized from bytes.

title: The disk store
text: DiskPageStore keeps one file named data per session, in a folder named after the application followed by -filestore. That folder is created in the folder from S
body: DiskPageStore keeps one file named data per session, in a folder named after the application followed by -filestore. That folder is created in the folder from StoreSettings.getFileStoreFolder(), by default the servlet container’s temporary directory. The file has a maximum size per session, 10 MB by default; when it is full, new pages overwrite the oldest ones. Pages that have been overwritten are gone, and a request for them ends in a PageExpiredException or, for bookmarkable pages, a new instance. When the HTTP session ends, the store removes the session’s pages. The disk store keeps the pages of a session in one file, with the most recent ones winning. Several browser tabs with Ajax timers can push each other’s pages out. FilePageStore, which writes a file per page, avoids that.

title: The session cache and clustering
text: The session holds only the last page used, as a live object. When the servlet container serializes the session, to replicate it to another node or to save it on
body: The session holds only the last page used, as a live object. When the servlet container serializes the session, to replicate it to another node or to save it on shutdown, the cached page is left out. The next request finds it in the persistent store instead. In a cluster, that store must be reachable from every node: a shared disk, a database or a distributed cache. The WicketStuff project has stores for distributed caches and databases.

title: Why the pages are serialized
text: The back button needs the earlier state of a page, not the current one. Keeping a live object is not enough, because the next request changes that same object.
body: The back button needs the earlier state of a page, not the current one. Keeping a live object is not enough, because the next request changes that same object. Serializing after each request freezes a copy. A chain needs at least one store that makes such copies, or the back button shows the current state. Serialization is also what turns a page into bytes for the disk, or for a database or cache in other stores. Wicket uses the ISerializer from FrameworkSettings.getSerializer(), by default JavaSerializer with standard Java serialization. This is why everything a page references must be serializable, and why detachable models matter: their data is dropped before this step.

title: Page through data
text: Load one page of rows at a time with an IDataProvider, show them in a DataView or DataTable, and let users move between pages.
keywords: pagination paging pager page size items per page offset limit large result set sortable table sort column
apis: IDataProvider DataView PagingNavigator AjaxPagingNavigator ListDataProvider SortableDataProvider DefaultDataTable AjaxFallbackDefaultDataTable LambdaColumn
body: Use a data provider and a pageable repeater when a list is too long to show at once, such as the result of a database query. The repeater asks the provider for the rows of the current page only, and a navigator lets the user move between pages.

title: Add a navigator
text: PagingNavigator renders links to the first, previous, numbered, next and last pages of any pageable component: add(new PagingNavigator("navigator", rows)); Each
body:
PagingNavigator renders links to the first, previous, numbered, next and last pages of any pageable component: add(new PagingNavigator("navigator", rows)); Each click is a normal request that renders the whole page again. To replace only the table, use AjaxPagingNavigator and wrap the view in a container that writes its markup id. The navigator updates the nearest parent of the view that has setOutputMarkupId(true): WebMarkupContainer table = new WebMarkupContainer("table"); table.setOutputMarkupId(true); table.add(rows); add(table); add(new AjaxPagingNavigator("navigator", rows)); ...
Both navigators are stateful: they keep the current page in the view.

title: Let DataTable build the table
text: DataTable in wicket-extensions generates the whole <table> from a list of columns. DefaultDataTable adds a header row with sortable headers, a navigation toolba
apis: DataTable DefaultDataTable ISortableDataProvider SortableDataProvider PersonSortableProvider Person String SpringBean PersonService Injector SortOrder Override Iterator SortParam IModel PersonModel List IColumn LambdaColumn Model Name Email AjaxFallbackDefaultDataTable PageableListView ListView PagingNavigator
body:
DataTable in wicket-extensions generates the whole from a list of columns. DefaultDataTable adds a header row with sortable headers, a navigation toolbar and a “no records” row. Sorting needs an ISortableDataProvider; extend SortableDataProvider and read the requested order from getSort(): PersonSortableProvider.java public class PersonSortableProvider extends SortableDataProvider { @SpringBean private PersonService personService; public PersonSortableProvider() { Injector.get().inject(this); setSort("name", SortOrder.ASCENDING); } @Override public Iterator iterator(long first, long count) { SortParam sort = getSort(); return personService.find(first, count, sort.getProperty(), sort.isAscending()).iterator(); } @Override public long size() { return personService.count(); } @Override public IModel model(Person person) { return new PersonModel(person); } } PersonsPage.java List> columns = List.of( new LambdaColumn(Model.of("Name"), "name", Person::getFullName), new LambdaColumn(Model.of("Email"), Person::getEmail)); add(new DefaultDataTable<>("table", columns, new PersonSortableProvider(), 20));
A column with a sort property, "name" here, gets a clickable header. AjaxFallbackDefaultDataTable takes the same arguments and sorts and pages with Ajax. Repeaters lists the toolbars and column types. PageableListView is a ListView with a page size, and works with PagingNavigator too, but it always holds the complete list.

title: Write a data provider
text: An IDataProvider answers three questions: how many rows there are, which rows are on a page, and which model wraps a row: PersonDataProvider.java public class P

body: An IDataProvider answers three questions: how many rows there are, which rows are on a page, and which model wraps a row: PersonDataProvider.java public class PersonDataProvider implements IDataProvider<Person> { @SpringBean private PersonService personService; public PersonDataProvider() { Injector.get().inject(this); } @Override public Iterator<? extends Person> iterator(long first, long count) { return personService.find(first, count).iterator(); } @Override public long size() { return personService.count(); } @Override public IModel<Person> model(Person person) { return new PersonModel(person); } } iterator(first, count) maps directly to an offset and a limit in a query. model should return a detachable model that keeps only the id, so the rows are not stored with the page. The provider is stored with the page itself, so it reaches the service through an injected field (Inject Spring beans). For a list that is already in memory, ListDataProvider does all three: new ListDataProvider<>(list).

title: Bind components to a JavaBean
text: Read and write bean properties with PropertyModel, and let form fields find their property by id with CompoundPropertyModel.
keywords: property expression OGNL model inheritance bind nested property list index map key form fields Property could not be resolved for class
apis: PropertyModel CompoundPropertyModel IComponentInheritedModel IModel Person Serializable String Address List Map
body: Use property models when you bind many components to properties of one object, most often the fields of a form. They name the property with a string, a property expression. For a single property, lambda models do the same with compile-time checks. The examples bind to this bean, held in a personModel of type IModel<Person>: Person.java public class Person implements Serializable { private String name; private String email; private Address address; private Person spouse; private List<Person> children; private Map<String, String> phones; // getters and setters }

title: Bind a form with CompoundPropertyModel
text: Give the form a CompoundPropertyModel and leave the fields without a model. Each field then binds to the property named by its id: EditPersonPage.java Form<Pers
apis: CompoundPropertyModel Form Person Override TextField EmailTextField Label Save IComponentInheritedModel
body:
Give the form a CompoundPropertyModel and leave the fields without a model. Each field then binds to the property named by its id: EditPersonPage.java Form form = new Form<>("form", new CompoundPropertyModel<>(personModel)) { @Override protected void onSubmit() { personService.save(getModelObject()); } }; form.add(new TextField<>("name")); form.add(new EmailTextField("email")); form.add(new TextField<>("address.city")); form.add(new Label("spouse.name")); add(form); EditPersonPage.html
This works through model inheritance: a component created without a model asks its parents for an IComponentInheritedModel, and CompoundPropertyModel answers with a property model that uses the component’s id as the expression. The fields do not have to be direct children of the form: Wicket walks up the parents until it finds an inheritable model, so containers in between do not get in the way. The compound model can wrap a model, as above, or an object with CompoundPropertyModel.of(person). Wrap a model when the object comes from a database, so that it is loaded per request.

title: Bind one component with PropertyModel
text: PropertyModel reads and writes one property of an object or of a model’s object: add(new Label("name", new PropertyModel<>(personModel, "name"))); add(new Label
body: PropertyModel reads and writes one property of an object or of a model’s object: add(new Label("name", new PropertyModel<>(personModel, "name"))); add(new Label("spouseName", PropertyModel.of(personModel, "spouse.name"))); When the first argument is a model, the property model reads the property of that model’s current object, and detaches that model when it is detached itself. Pass a model rather than the bean, so the bean is not stored with the page. PropertyModel uses the getter and setter when they exist and falls back to the field, private fields included. Reading is null-safe: when a step in the path is null, getObject() returns null.

title: Give a field its own model inside the form
text: A component that has a model of its own does not inherit. Pass a model to the field and it ignores the form’s compound model: form.add(new TextField<>("name"));
apis: TextField LambdaModel Person CheckBox Model ComponentPropertyModel
body: A component that has a model of its own does not inherit. Pass a model to the field and it ignores the form’s compound model: form.add(new TextField<>("name")); // inherits "name" form.add(new TextField<>("nickname", LambdaModel.of(personModel, Person::getNickname, Person::setNickname))); // its own model form.add(new CheckBox("subscribe", Model.of(false))); // not a Person property Model classes describes the other property-based models, such as ComponentPropertyModel.

title: Use an id that differs from the property
text: When the id cannot be the property name, for example because two components show the same property, bind explicitly with bind: CompoundPropertyModel<Person> mod
body: When the id cannot be the property name, for example because two components show the same property, bind explicitly with bind: CompoundPropertyModel<Person> model = new CompoundPropertyModel<>(personModel); Form<Person> form = new Form<>("form", model); form.add(new TextField<String>("partner", model.bind("spouse.name"))); bind returns a property model on the same object, for any component that needs one, inside or outside the form.

body: Expression Resolves to name getName() and setName(), or the field name address.city getAddress().getCity(); on write, an Address is created when it is null and has a default constructor children.0.name or children[0].name the name of the first element of a list or array phones.home or phones[home] the value for key home in a map fullName() the result of calling the method fullName() A property that does not exist fails when the model is first used, with a WicketRuntimeException such as “Property could not be resolved for class: … expression: …”. The compiler does not check the string, and renaming a property in your IDE does not update it.

page: Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy
title: Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy
text: Queue components on a page or panel and let Wicket put each one in the right container by following the nesting in the markup.
keywords: component queueing queue dequeue add component hierarchy nesting markup hierarchy wrap in div Detach called on component while it had a non-empty queue
body: Use component queueing when the nesting of your markup changes often, or when you are tired of mirroring every <div wicket:id> in Java. With add, the Java hierarchy must match the markup exactly: wrapping two fields in a new container means moving their add calls into it. With queue, you hand the components to a page or panel and Wicket places them by reading the markup.

page: Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy
title: Keep sensitive components inside their container
text: Wicket places a queued component only inside the container you queued it on, or deeper. Use this to make sure markup changes cannot move a component out of a pr
body: Wicket places a queued component only inside the container you queued it on, or deeper. Use this to make sure markup changes cannot move a component out of a protected area: WebMarkupContainer payment = new WebMarkupContainer("payment") { @Override protected void onConfigure() { super.onConfigure(); setVisible(isViewingOwnProfile()); } }; queue(payment); payment.queue(new Label("cardNumber", cardNumberModel)); If someone moves the cardNumber tag outside the payment element, rendering fails instead of showing the number to everyone.

page: Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy
title: Know when components are placed
text: Wicket places queued components as soon as the container you queued them on is part of a page, because it needs the page to find the markup. On a page, and in a
body: Wicket places queued components as soon as the container you queued them on is part of a page, because it needs the page to find the markup. On a page, and in a panel’s onInitialize, that is right away: the components are placed before queue returns. In a panel’s constructor the panel has no page yet, so its queued components are placed when the panel is added to a page and initialized. Until then getParent() returns null, and methods that depend on the hierarchy, such as isVisibleInHierarchy(), do not give useful answers. A component that finds no matching tag stays in the queue. Wicket reports this at the end of the request with Detach called on component with id '...' while it had a non-empty queue.

page: Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy
title: Know where queueing stops
text: Pages, panels, borders, fragments and FormComponentPanels each have their own markup. Wicket does not place components across these boundaries: a component queu
body: Pages, panels, borders, fragments and FormComponentPanels each have their own markup. Wicket does not place components across these boundaries: a component queued on a page is never placed inside a panel on that page, even if the panel’s markup has a tag with the same id. Queue components on the panel, typically in the panel’s own onInitialize. In a repeater, queue on the item: protected void populateItem(ListItem<Order> item) { item.queue(new Label("number", item.getModel().map(Order::getNumber))); }

page: Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy
title: Queue components with the same id under different parents
text: Ids only need to be unique within one parent. When the same id appears twice in a file, queue each component on the container it belongs to, so Wicket knows whi
body:
Ids only need to be unique within one parent. When the same id appears twice in a file, queue each component on the container it belongs to, so Wicket knows which tag is meant:
queue(new Form("customer")); queue(new TextField<>("name", customerNameModel)); WebMarkupContainer partner = new WebMarkupContainer("partner"); queue(partner); partner.queue(new TextField<>("name", partnerNameModel));

page: Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy
title: Queue instead of add
text: Call queue on the page or panel for every component, containers included, in any order: CustomerPage.html <form wicket:id="customer"> <div wicket:id="nameRow" c
apis: Save Form Void WebMarkupContainer TextField LambdaModel EmailTextField
body:
Call queue on the page or panel for every component, containers included, in any order: CustomerPage.html
CustomerPage.java queue(new Form("customer")); queue(new WebMarkupContainer("nameRow")); queue(new TextField<>("first", LambdaModel.of(customer::getFirstName, customer::setFirstName))); queue(new TextField<>("last", LambdaModel.of(customer::getLastName, customer::setLastName))); queue(new EmailTextField("email", LambdaModel.of(customer::getEmail, customer::setEmail))); Wicket adds nameRow and email to the form and first and last to nameRow. If the designer later removes the nameRow element, the fields end up directly in the form; remove the queue call for nameRow and nothing else changes. You can mix queue and add. A container you created with add can still receive queued children.

page: Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy
title: Use queueing with wicket:enclosure
text: With add, a <wicket:enclosure> is not the parent of the components inside it, so fields in a hidden enclosure are still validated. With queue, Wicket places the
body: With add, a <wicket:enclosure> is not the parent of the components inside it, so fields in a hidden enclosure are still validated. With queue, Wicket places the components inside the enclosure, and hiding it skips them. See Hide surrounding markup with wicket:enclosure.

title: Redirects after a request
text: Why Wicket answers a form submit or link click with a redirect, how the three render strategies differ, and what that means for stateless pages and clusters.
keywords: REDIRECT_TO_BUFFER ONE_PASS_RENDER REDIRECT_TO_RENDER redirect after post post-redirect-get PRG double submit 302 refresh resubmits form lost in redirection sticky sessions cluster page id in URL
apis: RequestCycleSettings RenderStrategy RedirectPolicy BufferedResponseMapper WebPageRenderer Link
body: When a user submits a Wicket form or clicks a Link, the browser usually receives a redirect, followed by a second request that fetches the page. This is the redirect-after-post pattern, also known as post-redirect-get, and Wicket applies it to link clicks as well as form posts. It is why a stateful page has a number in its URL, and why the browser’s reload button shows the page again instead of submitting the form a second time.

title: How REDIRECT_TO_BUFFER works
text: With the default strategy, the first request runs the action, for example the onSubmit of a form, and renders the resulting page completely. Instead of sending
body: With the default strategy, the first request runs the action, for example the onSubmit of a form, and renders the resulting page completely. Instead of sending the HTML, Wicket stores it in a buffer and answers with a redirect to the URL of the page, such as /order?3. The browser follows the redirect. The BufferedResponseMapper recognizes the URL, finds the stored response for this session and URL, and sends it. No component code runs in the second request. The page is rendered once, in the same request cycle as the action, so models that the action loaded are still attached and feedback messages from validation are rendered with the page. The browser ends up on a URL that shows the page, and reload asks for that URL. If the buffer is gone by then, Wicket renders the page instance again from the page store. The buffers live in the WebApplication object, keyed by session id and URL. They are removed when fetched, and at most 1000 of them are kept for at most a minute.

title: Redirects in a cluster
text: The buffer of REDIRECT_TO_BUFFER is held in the memory of the server that rendered the page. It is not part of the session and is not replicated. When a load ba
body: The buffer of REDIRECT_TO_BUFFER is held in the memory of the server that rendered the page. It is not part of the session and is not replicated. When a load balancer sends the POST to one node and the redirected GET to another, the second node has no buffer. It handles the GET as a new request for the page, and whatever the first render showed only once is lost. The typical symptom is a form that, now and then, comes back without its validation errors. The same can happen when a node fails between the two requests. The fix is sticky sessions: the load balancer sends all requests of a session to the same node, and session replication only serves failover. This keeps the default strategy and its protection against double submits. Switching to ONE_PASS_RENDER also removes the problem, because there is no second request. It brings back the double-submit problem and the action URLs in the address bar, so it trades one problem for another. It suits clusters that cannot use sticky sessions, and applications whose pages are mostly stateless or driven by Ajax, where few full-page form posts happen. How the request cycle resolves handlers and mappers around these redirects is described in What happens during a request.

title: The problem a redirect solves
text: A form submit is a POST to a URL that means “do this”. If the server answers that POST with the page, the browser’s address bar and history hold the POST. Reloa
body: A form submit is a POST to a URL that means “do this”. If the server answers that POST with the page, the browser’s address bar and history hold the POST. Reload, or going back and forward, sends the POST again: the order is placed twice, the row is deleted twice, or the browser asks the user whether to resend data they never knew they sent. A redirect separates the action from the result. The server performs the action, then tells the browser to fetch the result from another URL with a GET. The address bar and history now hold that GET, and repeating it only shows the result again. Wicket goes one step further than most frameworks: a click on a Link also calls code on the server, so it is answered with a redirect too.

title: The three render strategies
text: RequestCycleSettings has three render strategies. The strategy decides how the two parts of a request, the action and the rendering of the page, map onto HTTP r
body: RequestCycleSettings has three render strategies. The strategy decides how the two parts of a request, the action and the rendering of the page, map onto HTTP requests. Strategy Requests Double submit on reload Notes REDIRECT_TO_BUFFER (default) action and rendering in the first, a redirect, the second request returns the stored result prevented the rendered page is kept in memory until the second request fetches it REDIRECT_TO_RENDER action in the first, a redirect, rendering in the second prevented models may be loaded and detached twice; two request cycles for one action ONE_PASS_RENDER action and rendering in one request, no redirect not prevented fewest requests; the address bar keeps the action URL You change the strategy in the init() method of your application: getRequestCycleSettings().setRenderStrategy(RequestCycleSettings.RenderStrategy.ONE_PASS_RENDER);

title: When Wicket does not redirect
text: The renderer compares the URL of the request with the URL of the page it is about to render. Besides the strategy, these cases decide what happens: When the two
apis: OrderPage RenderPageRequestHandler RequestCycle Class PageParameters RedirectPolicy
body: The renderer compares the URL of the request with the URL of the page it is about to render. Besides the strategy, these cases decide what happens: When the two URLs are equal and the page instance already exists, Wicket renders directly. A reload of /order?3 does not redirect again. When the page is stateless after rendering, Wicket writes it directly, also after a submit of a stateless form. Call setResponsePage with a page class in onSubmit when you want the redirect. Ajax requests never render a full page into the response. When an Ajax handler calls setResponsePage, Wicket sends the browser to the new page with a redirect. setResponsePage(OrderPage.class) and setResponsePage(OrderPage.class, parameters) always redirect, also with ONE_PASS_RENDER, so the browser ends up on the bookmarkable URL of the new page. setResponsePage(page) with an instance redirects only when needed. The last two are redirect policies, ALWAYS_REDIRECT and AUTO_REDIRECT, of the RenderPageRequestHandler that setResponsePage schedules. RequestCycle#setResponsePage(Class, PageParameters, RedirectPolicy) lets you pass NEVER_REDIRECT to render the page into the current response.

title: Why a stateful page gets an id in its URL
text: A request for /order creates a new instance of the page. If the page is stateful, its URL has to identify this instance, so that a later click on one of its lin
body: A request for /order creates a new instance of the page. If the page is stateful, its URL has to identify this instance, so that a later click on one of its links reaches the same object. Wicket renders the page, finds that its URL is now /order?3, stores the response and redirects to /order?3. A stateless page has nothing to find again. Wicket renders it directly into the response, without a buffer and without a redirect, and the URL stays /order. This is one reason to keep pages stateless where you can; Stateful and stateless pages explains the difference.

page: Control how items are reused with RefreshingView
title: Control how items are reused with RefreshingView
text: Build repeater items from models you supply, and keep an item's components across renders as long as its model stays in the list.
keywords: item reuse keep state in rows getItemModels equals hashCode setItemReuseStrategy form in repeater editable rows
apis: RefreshingView Item IItemReuseStrategy ReuseIfModelsEqualStrategy DefaultItemReuseStrategy ModelIteratorAdapter
body: Use a RefreshingView when you want to decide which model each item gets, and whether an item survives a re-render. Unlike a ListView, it does not tie an item to an index: you hand it a model per element, and with the right strategy it keeps the item for as long as that model is in the list. That keeps the user’s input and other state in the right row even when rows are added, removed or reordered.

page: Control how items are reused with RefreshingView
title: Keep items whose model is still in the list
text: By default a RefreshingView uses DefaultItemReuseStrategy: on each render it throws all items away and creates new ones. Switch to ReuseIfModelsEqualStrategy to
body: By default a RefreshingView uses DefaultItemReuseStrategy: on each render it throws all items away and creates new ones. Switch to ReuseIfModelsEqualStrategy to keep an item when a model equal to its model comes back from getItemModels(): RefreshingView<Person> persons = new RefreshingView<>("persons") { ... }; persons.setItemReuseStrategy(ReuseIfModelsEqualStrategy.getInstance()); Items whose model is no longer returned are removed. New models get new items, and populateItem is called only for those. Kept items stay in the order of the new models.

page: Control how items are reused with RefreshingView
title: Make the models comparable
text: The strategy compares the models, not the objects in them, so the model class needs equals and hashCode. Compare on what identifies the object, usually the id,
apis: PersonModel LoadableDetachableModel Person Override Object Long
body: The strategy compares the models, not the objects in them, so the model class needs equals and hashCode. Compare on what identifies the object, usually the id, so the comparison does not have to load anything: PersonModel.java public class PersonModel extends LoadableDetachableModel<Person> { private final long id; // constructor and load() as usual @Override public boolean equals(Object other) { return other instanceof PersonModel that && this.id == that.id; } @Override public int hashCode() { return Long.hashCode(id); } } Without these methods every model is different from every other, and the strategy behaves like the default one.

page: Control how items are reused with RefreshingView
title: Put form fields in the rows
text: With ReuseIfModelsEqualStrategy, form components in the items keep their input and error messages after a failed submit, because the same components render agai
apis: ReuseIfModelsEqualStrategy ListView DataView GridView DataTable IDataProvider
body: With ReuseIfModelsEqualStrategy, form components in the items keep their input and error messages after a failed submit, because the same components render again. This is what setReuseItems(true) does for a ListView, but tied to the element instead of the index. DataView, GridView and DataTable are refreshing views too and accept the same strategy, through setItemReuseStrategy on the view or on the DataTable. The models then come from IDataProvider.model(T), so that is where equal models have to be created.

page: Control how items are reused with RefreshingView
title: Supply a model per item
text: Implement getItemModels() to return an iterator of models, and populateItem(Item) to fill each item: PersonsPage.java add(new RefreshingView<Person>("persons")
apis: Item RefreshingView Person Override Iterator IModel ModelIteratorAdapter PersonModel Label
body:
Implement getItemModels() to return an iterator of models, and populateItem(Item) to fill each item: PersonsPage.java add(new RefreshingView("persons") { @Override protected Iterator> getItemModels() { return new ModelIteratorAdapter<>(personService.findAll()) { @Override protected IModel model(Person person) { return new PersonModel(person); } }; } @Override protected void populateItem(Item item) { item.add(new Label("name", item.getModel().map(Person::getFullName))); } }); PersonsPage.html
Wicket calls getItemModels() every time the view renders. ModelIteratorAdapter turns an iterable of objects into an iterator of models, using the model method you implement. PersonModel is a detachable model that keeps the person’s id.

page: Control how items are reused with RefreshingView
title: Write your own strategy
text: Implement IItemReuseStrategy for other rules. Its one method, getItems(factory, newModels, existingItems), returns the items to render: existing items it keeps,
body: Implement IItemReuseStrategy for other rules. Its one method, getItems(factory, newModels, existingItems), returns the items to render: existing items it keeps, and new ones made with factory.newItem(index, model). The view calls populateItem for the items the factory creates.

title: Render a component without its tag
text: Leave out a component's own HTML tag and render only its content, and know what stops working when you do.
keywords: setRenderBodyOnly strip tag remove span no wrapper element wicket:container A partial update is not possible for a component that has renderBodyOnly enabled
body: Use this when a component’s tag is only there to give Wicket a place to attach the component, and the element itself would be in the way: a <span> around plain text, or a wrapper that breaks your CSS or the HTML content model.

page: Render a component without its tag
title: Drop the tag in Java

Call setRenderBodyOnly(true). Wicket renders what the component puts inside its tag, but not the tag. HomePage.html

Hello, Jane
body:
Call setRenderBodyOnly(true). Wicket renders what the component puts inside its tag, but not the tag. HomePage.html

HomePage.java add(new Label("name", () -> user.getFirstName()).setRenderBodyOnly(true)); Output:

page: Render a component without its tag
title: Drop the tag in the markup
text: When the choice belongs to the markup, attach the component to a <wicket:container> tag instead. It needs no Java change and makes the intent visible to whoever
body:
When the choice belongs to the markup, attach the component to a tag instead. It needs no Java change and makes the intent visible to whoever edits the HTML:

Hello, Jane!

In deployment mode Wicket removes the tag. In development mode it stays in the output, which is harmless in the browser.

page: Render a component without its tag
title: Know what stops working without the tag
text: The tag carries everything Wicket writes about the component itself. Without it: Feature Effect Ajax updates Adding the component to an AjaxRequestTarget fails
body: The tag carries everything Wicket writes about the component itself. Without it: Feature Effect Ajax updates Adding the component to an AjaxRequestTarget fails with A partial update is not possible for a component that has renderBodyOnly enabled. Repaint a parent instead. Markup id Nothing to put the id on. Wicket logs Markup id set on a component that renders its body only. Placeholder tag setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag(true) has no effect, and Wicket logs a warning. Attribute modifiers Behaviors that change attributes have nothing to change. Ajax behaviors Event handlers have no element to listen on. To make the warnings fail fast during development, set getExceptionSettings().setNotRenderableErrorStrategy(NotRenderableErrorStrategy.THROW_EXCEPTION) in your application’s init(). Components that need any of these keep their tag. If the tag is in the way only for styling, change the tag instead: a <span> inside a paragraph is valid HTML and invisible without CSS.

title: Repeat markup with RepeatingView
text: Render a tag once for every child you add in code, for menus, button bars and other short lists you build in the constructor.
keywords: loop repeat for each dynamic number of components newChildId menu tabs
body: Use RepeatingView when you build a small, fixed set of items in code: a menu, a row of buttons, a set of badges. You add one child per item, and each child renders with the repeater’s tag. For items that come from a list or a database, use ListView or a data view, which build the children for you.

title: Change the items later
text: RepeatingView keeps its children until you change them. It does not rebuild them when it renders, so the items stay as you added them for the life of the page.
body: RepeatingView keeps its children until you change them. It does not rebuild them when it renders, so the items stay as you added them for the life of the page. To change the list, call removeAll(), remove(component) or add(component), for example in an event handler. When the items depend on data that changes between requests, rebuilding them yourself gets tedious. A ListView or RefreshingView rebuilds its items on every render by default; see Repeaters for how each repeater treats its items.

title: Repeat a fragment with components inside
text: When the repeated markup contains components, make each child a WebMarkupContainer and add the inner components to it: BasePage.html <nav> <a wicket:id="menu">
apis: WebMarkupContainer BasePage RepeatingView Home HomePage Orders OrdersPage Settings SettingsPage String Class Page BookmarkablePageLink Void Label MarkupContainer Panel Fragment
body:
When the repeated markup contains components, make each child a WebMarkupContainer and add the inner components to it: BasePage.html
BasePage.java public BasePage() { RepeatingView menu = new RepeatingView("menu"); addMenuItem(menu, "Home", HomePage.class); addMenuItem(menu, "Orders", OrdersPage.class); addMenuItem(menu, "Settings", SettingsPage.class); add(menu); } private static void addMenuItem(RepeatingView menu, String label, Class page) { BookmarkablePageLink link = new BookmarkablePageLink<>(menu.newChildId(), page); link.add(new Label("label", label)); menu.add(link); } Here the child is a link, which is itself a container. Any MarkupContainer can serve as the child, including a Panel or a Fragment when the items need different markup.

title: Repeat a single tag
text:
Attach the repeater to the tag to repeat, and add children with ids from newChildId(): HomePage.html
HomePage.java Repea
body:
Attach the repeater to the tag to repeat, and add children with ids from newChildId(): HomePage.html
HomePage.java RepeatingView colors = new RepeatingView("colors"); colors.add(new Label(colors.newChildId(), "green")); colors.add(new Label(colors.newChildId(), "blue")); colors.add(new Label(colors.newChildId(), "red")); add(colors); Output:
  • green
  • blue
  • red
The repeater itself writes no tag. Each child renders with the repeater’s markup,

title: What happens during a request
text: How Wicket turns an HTTP request into a request handler, runs it, and cleans up afterwards, and why it is built that way.
keywords: request lifecycle request handling servlet filter thread local detach page store listener invocation redirect after post
body: A Wicket application is a servlet filter. Every request that reaches WicketFilter gets its own RequestCycle, and that object carries the request from the first byte to the last cleanup. Most of the time you do not see it, because pages, links and forms hide it. It becomes visible when you need the raw request, want to run code around every request, or try to understand why a component behaves differently in the second request than in the first. The classes and hooks named here are listed in Request processing.

title: Components see two requests in one
text: For a stateful page, a click is handled on the page instance that rendered the link, taken from the page store. That gives a request its typical order: first th
body: For a stateful page, a click is handled on the page instance that rendered the link, taken from the page store. That gives a request its typical order: first the listener runs on the components as they were left by the previous render; then the page, or the part of it that an Ajax request updates, goes through onConfigure(), onBeforeRender() and rendering again. Code in onClick() changes state; code in onConfigure() reads that state and decides how the page looks. Component lifecycle lists the hooks in order.

title: Detach: forgetting what is not needed
text: When the last handler has run, the request cycle detaches. Every handler detaches what it used; for a page that means calling detach() on the page and every com
body: When the last handler has run, the request cycle detaches. Every handler detaches what it used; for a page that means calling detach() on the page and every component in it, which detaches their models. After that the session detaches and the page manager stores the pages the request touched. Detaching exists because a stateful page outlives the request. Between requests, Wicket keeps the page in the session and serializes it to disk, so the page must not hold the database entities, open connections or large result lists it used while rendering. A detachable model drops its object in detach() and loads it again when the next request asks for it. How pages are stored describes what happens to the page after this point. Detaching happens even when the request failed. The steps that end and detach a request run in finally blocks, so a database session opened in onBeginRequest() can be closed in onEndRequest() or onDetach() without leaking.

title: Exceptions become handlers too
text: An exception thrown while a handler runs is not passed to the servlet container. The request cycle turns it into another handler. First every IRequestCycleListe
body: An exception thrown while a handler runs is not passed to the servlet container. The request cycle turns it into another handler. First every IRequestCycleListener gets the chance to return one in onException(); if none does, the application’s exception mapper decides, for example by rendering the page-expired page or the internal error page. Treating an error as just another response keeps the error page inside Wicket, with the same session, localization and layout as the rest of the application. Handle exceptions and error pages shows how to plug into this.

title: From URL to request handler
text: The first thing the request cycle does is decide what the request is for. It does not look at the URL itself. It asks a request mapper, an IRequestMapper, to tu
body: The first thing the request cycle does is decide what the request is for. It does not look at the URL itself. It asks a request mapper, an IRequestMapper, to turn the request into a request handler, an IRequestHandler. The application’s root mapper is a list of mappers; each one reports how well it matches the request, and the best match produces the handler. A request handler is the unit of work: render this page, call this link’s onClick(), serve this CSS file, answer this Ajax call, redirect to that URL. Separating “what does the URL mean” from “what to do about it” is the core of the design. Because mappers work in both directions, the same mapper that reads /products/42 also writes it when a link to that page renders. Changing your URL scheme means changing mappers; your pages do not notice. See Request mappers and Give pages readable URLs. If no mapper recognizes the request, Wicket hands it back to the filter chain, so the container can serve static files or other servlets.

title: Handlers run one after another
text: Many requests consist of more than one handler. A click on a link first runs a ListenerRequestHandler, which finds the link on the stored page and calls onClick
body: Many requests consist of more than one handler. A click on a link first runs a ListenerRequestHandler, which finds the link on the stored page and calls onClick(). If onClick() calls setResponsePage(), the request cycle schedules a RenderPageRequestHandler to run next. If it does not, the listener handler schedules a render of the current page itself. The request cycle keeps executing the scheduled handler until none is left. This is why setResponsePage() does not render anything when you call it. It only records what should happen after the current handler finishes, and the last call wins. It is also why exceptions such as RestartResponseException work as flow control: they abandon the current handler and put another one in its place, from wherever in the call stack they are thrown. Whether the browser gets the page directly or is first redirected to it depends on the render strategy; Redirects after a request explains why Wicket redirects after a form post by default.

title: Listeners instead of filters
text: You could wrap a Wicket application in servlet filters to time requests or manage transactions. A request cycle listener does the same from inside Wicket, and k
body: You could wrap a Wicket application in servlet filters to time requests or manage transactions. A request cycle listener does the same from inside Wicket, and knows more: which handler was resolved, which page is about to render, which URL is being generated, and which exception happened. Wicket itself uses listeners for features such as protection against cross-site request forgery and the cross-origin isolation headers. A listener is shared by all requests and runs concurrently, so it keeps per-request data in the request cycle’s metadata, not in its own fields.

title: One object per request, on the current thread
text: A servlet container serves each request on one thread. Wicket binds the application, the session and the request cycle to that thread while it works, which is w
apis: RequestCycle Session Application CompletableFuture Request Response WicketTester
body: A servlet container serves each request on one thread. Wicket binds the application, the session and the request cycle to that thread while it works, which is why RequestCycle.get(), Session.get() and Application.get() work anywhere in your code without passing objects around. The same convenience is also the limit: code that runs in another thread, such as a scheduled job or a CompletableFuture, has no request cycle and no session unless you bind them yourself. The request cycle owns the Request and Response of the request. They are Wicket’s own abstractions, not the servlet classes. Wicket’s request processing does not depend on the servlet API, which is what lets the same machinery run inside WicketTester without a container and serve WebSocket messages. When you do need the servlet objects, getContainerRequest() and getContainerResponse() give them to you.

body: A behavior that implements IRequestListener makes its page stateful, because the URL points to one component instance on one page instance. title: How Wicket picks a mapper
text: The application has one root mapper. By default it is a SystemMapper, a CompoundRequestMapper that holds the built-in mappers and every mount. For an incoming r

body: The application has one root mapper. By default it is a SystemMapper, a CompoundRequestMapper that holds the built-in mappers and every mount. For an incoming request, a CompoundRequestMapper asks all its mappers for their score and calls mapRequest on them from the highest score down. When two mappers have the same score, the one added last goes first. To generate a URL, it calls mapHandler on its mappers from the last added to the first, and uses the first URL it gets. Mounts are added after the built-in mappers, so they win. Mapper Score MountedMapper, PackageMapper 0 when the URL does not start with the mount path; otherwise it grows with the length of the mount path, where fixed segments weigh more than placeholders and optional placeholders do not count ResourceMapper as MountedMapper, minus 1, so that pages win over resources on the same path BookmarkableMapper, PageInstanceMapper, BufferedResponseMapper Integer.MAX_VALUE when the URL is theirs, otherwise 0 HomePageMapper Integer.MIN_VALUE + 1, the last resort

body: Mount paths of mountPage, mountPackage, mountResource and the mapper constructors are made of segments separated by /. A leading / is optional. Segment Meaning Example name fixed text that must match /products ${name} required named parameter; the URL must have this segment /products/${id} #{name} optional named parameter; the segment is left out when the parameter is missing /products/${id}/#{tab} Rule   A placeholder is a whole segment /item-${id} is fixed text, not a placeholder Values of placeholders become named page parameters, read with parameters.get("id") Named parameters without a placeholder are encoded by the parameter encoder; by default in the query string Segments after the mount path become indexed parameters: /products/42 on a mount at /products gives get(0) = 42 Matching order left to right; required parameters are matched before optional ones, optional ones eagerly from the left Reserved segments a mount path must not start with a segment of the mapper context, wicket by default Missing required parameter mapHandler returns null: no URL for this mount, the next mapper is tried mountPage("/blog/${year}/#{month}/#{slug}", BlogPage.class); mountResource("/export/${format}", new ExportResourceReference());

title: Exceptions that change the flow
text: Throw these from a constructor, a listener or a lifecycle hook to stop the current handler and run another: Exception Effect RestartResponseException Renders th
body: Throw these from a constructor, a listener or a lifecycle hook to stop the current handler and run another: Exception Effect RestartResponseException Renders the given page instead. RestartResponseAtInterceptPageException Renders the given page and remembers the current URL, so continueToOriginalDestination() can return to it, for example after a login. NonResettingRestartException Like RestartResponseException, but keeps the headers already set on the response, such as cookies. RedirectToUrlException Redirects to a URL. AbortWithHttpErrorCodeException Sends an HTTP error status, such as 404.

title: IRequestCycleListener
text: All methods are default methods; implement the ones you need. Register a listener in Application.init() with getRequestCycleListeners().add(listener). One insta
apis: Application RequestCycle IRequestHandler Url Exception RequestTimer IRequestCycleListener Override System RequestCycleListenerCollection
body: All methods are default methods; implement the ones you need. Register a listener in Application.init() with getRequestCycleListeners().add(listener). One instance serves all requests at the same time, so it must be thread-safe. Method Called onBeginRequest(RequestCycle) When the cycle starts, before the handler is resolved. onRequestHandlerResolved(RequestCycle, IRequestHandler) Before a handler is executed. Called for each handler in the request. onRequestHandlerScheduled(RequestCycle, IRequestHandler) When a handler is scheduled to run after the current one. onRequestHandlerExecuted(RequestCycle, IRequestHandler) After a handler has run without an exception. onUrlMapped(RequestCycle, IRequestHandler, Url) After Wicket generates a URL for a handler. The listener may change the Url, for example to add a query parameter. onException(RequestCycle, Exception) When processing throws. Return a handler to take over, or null to leave the exception to the next listener and the exception mapper. onExceptionRequestHandlerResolved(RequestCycle, IRequestHandler, Exception) When the handler for an exception is chosen. onEndRequest(RequestCycle) When the request is finished, also after an exception. onDetach(RequestCycle) After the handlers are detached. public class RequestTimer implements IRequestCycleListener { @Override public void onEndRequest(RequestCycle cycle) { long millis = System.currentTimeMillis() - cycle.getStartTime(); log.info("{} took {} ms", cycle.getRequest().getUrl(), millis); } } getRequestCycleListeners() returns a RequestCycleListenerCollection, which is itself an IRequestCycleListener, so you can group listeners.

body: Object Class Lifetime Get it with Application WebApplication One per Wicket filter, for the life of the web application. Application.get(), Component.getApplication() Session WebSession or your subclass One per user, created by Application.newSession(). Session.get(), Component.getSession() Request cycle RequestCycle One per request. RequestCycle.get(), Component.getRequestCycle() Request ServletWebRequest (a WebRequest, a Request) One per request. RequestCycle.get().getRequest(), Component.getRequest() Response ServletWebResponse (a WebResponse, a Response) One per request; can be swapped during rendering. RequestCycle.get().getResponse(), Component.getResponse() The static get() methods read a thread-local value that Wicket sets while it serves the request. Outside a request, for example in a background thread, RequestCycle.get() returns null and Application.get() throws a WicketRuntimeException. Application.exists() and Session.exists() tell you whether one is bound to the thread.

title: Request mappers
text: IRequestMapper turns a request into a handler with mapRequest(Request) and a handler into a URL with mapHandler(IRequestHandler). getCompatibilityScore(Request)
body: IRequestMapper turns a request into a handler with mapRequest(Request) and a handler into a URL with mapHandler(IRequestHandler). getCompatibilityScore(Request) says how well the mapper fits a request; when several mappers can map it, the one with the highest score wins. The root mapper of an application is a SystemMapper that holds the built-in mappers and the ones you add with mount() and mountPage(). The mappers are listed in Request mappers.

title: RequestCycle methods
text: Method Description get() The request cycle bound to the current thread. getRequest(), getResponse(), getOriginalResponse() The request, the current response, an
apis: Response Component CharSequence Url IRequestHandler Class Optional AjaxRequestTarget Override MyRequestCycle RequestCycle RequestCycleContext
body: Method Description get() The request cycle bound to the current thread. getRequest(), getResponse(), getOriginalResponse() The request, the current response, and the response before any swap. setResponse(Response) Replaces the response, returns the old one. Components use this to render into a buffer. setResponsePage(...) Schedules a page to render after the current handler, by class, class and parameters, or instance. Component.setResponsePage() delegates here. urlFor(...) The URL of a page class, a resource reference or a request handler, as a CharSequence. mapUrlFor(...) The same, as a Url object. scheduleRequestHandlerAfterCurrent(IRequestHandler) Runs a handler after the current one. replaceAllRequestHandlers(IRequestHandler) Stops the current handler and runs this one instead. getActiveRequestHandler(), getRequestHandlerScheduledAfterCurrent() The handler running now and the one that runs next. find(Class) The active or scheduled handler of a type, as an Optional. find(AjaxRequestTarget.class) tells whether this is an Ajax request. setMetaData(key, value), getMetaData(key) Data that lives for this request only. getStartTime() When the cycle started, in milliseconds. getListeners() The listeners of this cycle. Override onBeginRequest(), onEndRequest() and onDetach() in a subclass to run code at those moments. Install the subclass with a provider, because createRequestCycle() is final: @Override protected void init() { super.init(); setRequestCycleProvider(MyRequestCycle::new); } public class MyRequestCycle extends RequestCycle { public MyRequestCycle(RequestCycleContext context) { super(context); } @Override protected void onBeginRequest() { super.onBeginRequest(); // ... } }

Response encodeURL(CharSequence) Adds the session id to a URL when cookies are off. WebResponse setHeader(), addHeader(), setContentType(), setStatus() Sets headers and status. title: Steps of a request
text: WicketFilter receives every request mapped to it and asks the application for a request cycle. RequestCycle.processRequestAndDetach() then runs these steps: Ste
apis: WicketFilter RequestCycle Application IRequestCycleProvider IRequestCycleListener IRequestHandler IExceptionMapper
body: WicketFilter receives every request mapped to it and asks the application for a request cycle. RequestCycle.processRequestAndDetach() then runs these steps: Step What happens Hooks called 1. Create Application.createRequestCycle(request, response) builds the cycle with the IRequestCycleProvider set by setRequestCycleProvider().   2. Begin The cycle binds itself to the thread. IRequestCycleListener.onBeginRequest(), then RequestCycle.onBeginRequest() 3. Resolve The root request mapper (Application.getRootRequestMapper()) maps the request to an IRequestHandler. If no mapper matches, the filter passes the request on to the rest of the filter chain, so the container can serve it.   4. Execute The handler’s respond() runs. If it schedules another handler, that one runs next, until none is left. onRequestHandlerResolved() before and onRequestHandlerExecuted() after each handler; onRequestHandlerScheduled() when one is scheduled 5. Handle an exception When a step throws, the listeners can return a handler; otherwise the IExceptionMapper from getExceptionMapperProvider() maps the exception to one. Wicket retries up to getRequestCycleSettings().getExceptionRetryCount() times (default 10) if handling fails again. onException(), then onExceptionRequestHandlerResolved() 6. End Runs also after an exception. IRequestCycleListener.onEndRequest(), then RequestCycle.onEndRequest() 7. Detach Every executed handler is detached; a page handler detaches the page and its components. Then the session detaches and the request logger records the request. RequestCycle.onDetach(), IRequestCycleListener.onDetach()

title: Combine resources into one bundle
text: Serve several package stylesheets or scripts as one file with ResourceBundles, and replace a resource throughout the application with addResourceReplacement.
keywords: bundle concatenate merge files fewer requests addJavaScriptBundle addCssBundle addResourceReplacement replace jQuery CDN replacement override library CSS
body: Bundle files that most pages load together, so the browser makes one request instead of several. You register the bundle once in the application; components keep rendering the individual files.

title: Defer a bundled script
text: addJavaScriptBundle has a variant with a defer flag that renders the bundle’s <script> with the defer attribute: getResourceBundles().addJavaScriptBundle(Wicket
body: addJavaScriptBundle has a variant with a defer flag that renders the bundle’s <script> with the defer attribute: getResourceBundles().addJavaScriptBundle(WicketApplication.class, "app.js", true, ChartCoreJs.get(), ChartJs.get(), DashboardJs.get()); A bundle is a trade-off: a page that needs one of its files downloads all of them. Put files in a bundle that appear together on most pages, and leave rarely used ones out.

title: Register a bundle
text: Call addJavaScriptBundle or addCssBundle in init(), with a scope class, a file name for the bundle and the references it consists of: WicketApplication.java @Ov
apis: Override WicketApplication ChartCoreJs ChartJs DashboardJs ChartCss DashboardCss JavaScriptResourceReference CssResourceReference IllegalArgumentException
body: Call addJavaScriptBundle or addCssBundle in init(), with a scope class, a file name for the bundle and the references it consists of: WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); getResourceBundles().addJavaScriptBundle(WicketApplication.class, "app.js", ChartCoreJs.get(), ChartJs.get(), DashboardJs.get()); getResourceBundles().addCssBundle(WicketApplication.class, "app.css", ChartCss.get(), DashboardCss.get()); } When a component renders any of these references, Wicket renders the bundle instead. The page gets one <script> for app.js with the three files concatenated in the order you listed them, and later requests for the other members are already satisfied. Follow these rules: Members must be package resources: JavaScriptResourceReference for a JavaScript bundle, CssResourceReference for a CSS bundle. List the files in the order they must run. Dependencies on references outside the bundle are kept, and Wicket renders those before the bundle. A reference can be part of one bundle only. Adding it to a second bundle throws an IllegalArgumentException. The name is the file name in the URL; give a JavaScript bundle a .js name and a CSS bundle a .css name.

title: Replace a resource throughout the application
text: WebApplication#addResourceReplacement makes Wicket render a different resource wherever the original is rendered, including in components you cannot change. Use
apis: WebApplication Override DatePickerCss CssResourceReference WicketApplication ChartCoreJs UrlResourceReference Url JavaScriptResourceReference
body: WebApplication#addResourceReplacement makes Wicket render a different resource wherever the original is rendered, including in components you cannot change. Use it to serve a library from a CDN or to swap a component’s stylesheet for your own: WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); addResourceReplacement(DatePickerCss.get(), new CssResourceReference(WicketApplication.class, "datepicker-theme.css")); addResourceReplacement(ChartCoreJs.get(), new UrlResourceReference(Url.parse("https://cdn.example.com/chart-core/4.4.0/chart-core.min.js"))); } The first argument is a CssResourceReference or a JavaScriptResourceReference; the replacement can be any reference. A replaced CSS item keeps its media attribute, and a replaced script keeps defer, async and the nonce. A replacement is a bundle with one member, so the original cannot also be part of a bundle. To replace jQuery, set the jQuery reference instead: getJavaScriptLibrarySettings().setJQueryReference(…), see Declare dependencies between resources.

title: Declare dependencies between resources
text: Make a script or stylesheet pull in the libraries it needs by overriding getDependencies, so Wicket always renders them first and only once.
keywords: getDependencies depends on jQuery load order script order jQuery plugin CDN library before plugin CircularDependencyException
apis: ResourceReference HeaderItem JQueryPluginResourceReference JavaScriptLibrarySettings UrlResourceReference JQueryResourceReference
body: Declare a dependency when a script or stylesheet only works after another one is loaded, such as a jQuery plugin or a theme on top of a base stylesheet. Every component that renders the file then gets the library too, in the right order, without knowing about it.

title: Declare what a reference depends on
text: Subclass the reference and override getDependencies(). Return header items for what must come first, and keep what the superclass returns: ChartJs.java public c
apis: ChartJs JavaScriptResourceReference Override List HeaderItem JavaScriptHeaderItem ChartCoreJs CssHeaderItem ChartCss IHeaderResponse CircularDependencyException
body: Subclass the reference and override getDependencies(). Return header items for what must come first, and keep what the superclass returns: ChartJs.java public class ChartJs extends JavaScriptResourceReference { private static final ChartJs INSTANCE = new ChartJs(); public static ChartJs get() { return INSTANCE; } private ChartJs() { super(ChartJs.class, "chart.js"); } @Override public List<HeaderItem> getDependencies() { List<HeaderItem> dependencies = super.getDependencies(); dependencies.add(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(ChartCoreJs.get())); dependencies.add(CssHeaderItem.forReference(ChartCss.get())); return dependencies; } } A component now renders only the reference it uses: @Override public void renderHead(IHeaderResponse response) { super.renderHead(response); response.render(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(ChartJs.get())); } Wicket renders ChartCoreJs and ChartCss before chart.js, and renders each file once even when several components on the page, or other references, depend on it. Dependencies can have dependencies of their own, and a script can depend on a stylesheet or the other way round. A cycle makes Wicket throw a CircularDependencyException while it renders the page.

title: Depend on a library from a CDN
text: UrlResourceReference points to a file on another server. It can declare dependencies like any other reference, and other references can depend on it: public cla
apis: UrlResourceReference JQueryUiJs Url Override List HeaderItem JavaScriptHeaderItem Application CrossOrigin
body: UrlResourceReference points to a file on another server. It can declare dependencies like any other reference, and other references can depend on it: public class JQueryUiJs extends UrlResourceReference { private static final JQueryUiJs INSTANCE = new JQueryUiJs(); public static JQueryUiJs get() { return INSTANCE; } private JQueryUiJs() { super(Url.parse("https://code.jquery.com/ui/1.14.1/jquery-ui.min.js")); } @Override public List<HeaderItem> getDependencies() { List<HeaderItem> dependencies = super.getDependencies(); dependencies.add(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference( Application.get().getJavaScriptLibrarySettings().getJQueryReference())); return dependencies; } } The default Content Security Policy allows the script because Wicket gives it a nonce, but stylesheets, fonts and images that the library loads from that server need the host in the matching directive, see Configure the Content Security Policy. For subresource integrity, render the item with setIntegrity(…) and setCrossOrigin(CrossOrigin.ANONYMOUS), or set both on the reference.

title: Depend on jQuery
text: For a jQuery plugin, extend JQueryPluginResourceReference. It depends on the jQuery that the application is configured with: public class DatePickerJs extends J
apis: JQueryPluginResourceReference DatePickerJs Wicket Event Ajax JavaScriptHeaderItem Application
body: For a jQuery plugin, extend JQueryPluginResourceReference. It depends on the jQuery that the application is configured with: public class DatePickerJs extends JQueryPluginResourceReference { private static final DatePickerJs INSTANCE = new DatePickerJs(); public static DatePickerJs get() { return INSTANCE; } private DatePickerJs() { super(DatePickerJs.class, "datepicker.js"); } } The jQuery version comes from getJavaScriptLibrarySettings().getJQueryReference(). Point that setting at another reference to use your own copy of jQuery everywhere, including in Wicket’s own components. By default that is jQuery 3. To depend on Wicket’s own Ajax and event functions, such as Wicket.Event or Wicket.Ajax, add JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(getJavaScriptLibrarySettings().getWicketAjaxReference()) to the dependencies; get the settings with Application.get(). That reference follows the application’s choice of library.

apis: HeaderItem OnDomReadyHeaderItem Chart Override List JavaScriptHeaderItem ChartJs

Override it when the dependency belongs to one inline script rather than to a file: response.render(new OnDomReadyHeaderItem("Chart.draw('" + getMarkupId() + "');") { @Override public List<HeaderItem> getDependencies() { List<HeaderItem> dependencies = super.getDependencies(); dependencies.add(JavaScriptHeaderItem.forReference(ChartJs.get())); return dependencies; } }); Wicket renders the dependencies first and the ready script after all files, as described in Control the order of header items.
