title: Customize where resources are loaded from
text: Make Wicket find markup, properties and package files in a folder of the web application or the file system by adding resource finders.
keywords: markup folder separate markup html outside classpath resource finder getResourceFinders sourceFolder markup reload templates folder theme folder resource locator
apis: ResourceSettings IResourceFinder WebApplicationPath Path ClassPathResourceFinder IResourceStreamLocator ResourceStreamLocator CachingResourceStreamLocator
body: Add a resource finder when markup files, properties files or package resources should live somewhere other than next to the classes, for example in a folder that designers edit or that a theme replaces.

page: Customize where resources are loaded from
title: Add a folder in the web application
text: Create a WebApplicationPath for the folder and add it to the list in init(). The folder must repeat the package structure: src/main/webapp/ markup/ com/example/
body: Create a WebApplicationPath for the folder and add it to the list in init(). The folder must repeat the package structure: src/main/webapp/ markup/ com/example/ HomePage.html HomePage.properties WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); getResourceSettings().getResourceFinders() .add(0, new WebApplicationPath(getServletContext(), "markup")); } Adding at index 0 makes the folder win over a file with the same name on the classpath, so a folder can override the markup of a component. Use add(finder) instead to search the folder only when the classpath has no match. WebApplicationPath never loads files under WEB-INF. Everything Wicket looks up by class and name goes through these finders: markup, properties files and package resources such as CSS and images. The package resource guard still decides which package files found in a folder are served, see Control which package resources are served.

page: Customize where resources are loaded from
title: Add a folder on the file system
text: Path searches a folder on disk. The folder must exist when the application starts: getResourceSettings().getResourceFinders() .add(0, new Path("/srv/example/tem
body: Path searches a folder on disk. The folder must exist when the application starts: getResourceSettings().getResourceFinders() .add(0, new Path("/srv/example/templates")); During development, a Path at index 0 that points at your source folder makes edits to markup show up without a rebuild: in development mode Wicket checks loaded markup files for changes every second and reloads them. if (usesDevelopmentConfig()) { getResourceSettings().getResourceFinders() .add(0, new Path("/home/me/projects/example/src/main/java")); } The sourceFolder init parameter of the Wicket filter also adds a Path in development mode, but at the end of the list, so it only finds files that are not on the classpath.

page: Customize where resources are loaded from
title: Where Wicket looks by default
text: Wicket looks up a file such as com/example/HomePage.html with a list of resource finders, in order, and takes the first match: the classpath, ClassPathResourceF
body: Wicket looks up a file such as com/example/HomePage.html with a list of resource finders, in order, and takes the first match: the classpath, ClassPathResourceFinder(""); the root of the web application, WebApplicationPath(servletContext, ""); META-INF/resources/ on the classpath, ClassPathResourceFinder("META-INF/resources/"). In a Maven project, files under src/main/resources end up on the classpath, so src/main/resources/com/example/HomePage.html is found by the first finder without configuration.

page: Customize where resources are loaded from
title: Write your own finder
text: IResourceFinder has one method, find(Class<?> clazz, String pathname), which returns an IResourceStream or null. Implement it to load files from a database or a
apis: IResourceFinder Class String IResourceStream IResourceStreamLocator CachingResourceStreamLocator
body: IResourceFinder has one method, find(Class<?> clazz, String pathname), which returns an IResourceStream or null. Implement it to load files from a database or a remote store, and add it to the list like the finders above. To replace the lookup as a whole, including the way locale, style and variation are combined into file names, set an IResourceStreamLocator with getResourceSettings().setResourceStreamLocator(…). Wrap your locator in a CachingResourceStreamLocator, as Wicket does with its own, or every lookup goes to your source again. Where Wicket looks for texts shows how locale and style become part of the names that the finders receive.

page: Put model values into translated texts
title: Put model values into translated texts
text: Show translated texts through ResourceModel and StringResourceModel, fill in property values and MessageFormat parameters, and choose the key from the data.
keywords: localized model translated label message parameters MessageFormat placeholder in translation plural property expression dynamic key default text
body: Use these models when a label, a link text or an attribute must show a translated text, possibly with values from your data in it. Both look up the text when the component renders, through the same search as <wicket:message>, so they follow a change of language. Where the texts live is covered in Translate component texts.

page: Put model values into translated texts
title: Choose the key from the data
text: The key may contain property expressions too. This picks one text per status of the order: add(new Label("status", new StringResourceModel("order.status.${statu
body: The key may contain property expressions too. This picks one text per status of the order: add(new Label("status", new StringResourceModel("order.status.${status}", this, orderModel))); order.status.ACCEPTED=Your payment for order ${number} was accepted. order.status.SHIPPED=Order ${number} is on its way. order.status.DELIVERED=Order ${number} was delivered.

page: Put model values into translated texts
title: Insert properties of an object
text: StringResourceModel takes a model of an object as well. ${...} expressions in the text are property expressions on that object, as in a PropertyModel: Order.jav
apis: StringResourceModel PropertyModel Order Serializable String LocalDate Status Label
body: StringResourceModel takes a model of an object as well. ${...} expressions in the text are property expressions on that object, as in a PropertyModel: Order.java public class Order implements Serializable { private String number; private LocalDate orderDate; private Status status; // getters and setters } OrderPanel.properties order.summary=Order ${number} of ${orderDate} OrderPanel.java add(new Label("summary", new StringResourceModel("order.summary", this, orderModel))); Values are converted to text with the converters of the component and its locale, so ${orderDate} shows as a date in the user’s format. The second argument is the component whose bundles are searched. Pass null, or use the constructor without it, to use the component the model is assigned to.

page: Put model values into translated texts
title: Pass parameters with MessageFormat
text: setParameters passes values for {0}, {1} and so on, formatted by java.text.MessageFormat in the locale of the component. A parameter that is a model is replaced
apis: MessageFormat IModel Integer Label StringResourceModel Order Don
body: setParameters passes values for {0}, {1} and so on, formatted by java.text.MessageFormat in the locale of the component. A parameter that is a model is replaced by its object each time the text is rendered. Here delayModel is an IModel<Integer> with the number of days: add(new Label("delay", new StringResourceModel("order.delay", this) .setParameters(orderModel.map(Order::getNumber), delayModel))); order.delay=Order {0} is delayed by {1,choice,1#one day|1<{1,number,integer} days}. The choice format picks a text by number, which handles singular and plural. You do not need to double single quotes in these texts: Wicket escapes quotes outside {...} before it calls MessageFormat, so Don't worry stays as it is. Property expressions and parameters can be combined. Wicket applies the parameters first, then the ${...} expressions on the model object.

title: Restrict access by role
text: Allow pages, components, actions and resources only for users with a given role, with annotations on classes and packages or in code.
keywords: authorization permissions RBAC access denied package-info admin page hide for role UnauthorizedInstantiationException setAccessDeniedPage
apis: AuthorizeInstantiation AuthorizeInstantiations AuthorizeAction AuthorizeActions AuthorizeResource AnnotationsRoleAuthorizationStrategy MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy RoleAuthorizationStrategy Roles IAuthorizationStrategy AuthenticatedWebApplication
body: You need this when some users may see or do more than others. The setup from Log users in is assumed: an AuthenticatedWebApplication and a session whose getRoles() returns the roles of the current user. Roles are plain strings; Roles.USER and Roles.ADMIN are predefined. AuthenticatedWebApplication installs a RoleAuthorizationStrategy, which combines an annotation-based and a metadata-based strategy. Both have to grant access. A class without any restriction is open to everyone.

title: Give users their roles
text: AppSession.java @Override public Roles getRoles() { if (!isSignedIn()) { return new Roles(); } Roles roles = new Roles(Roles.USER); if (user.isAdministrator())
body: AppSession.java @Override public Roles getRoles() { if (!isSignedIn()) { return new Roles(); } Roles roles = new Roles(Roles.USER); if (user.isAdministrator()) { roles.add(Roles.ADMIN); } return roles; }

title: Grant access in code instead of with annotations
text: MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy keeps the rules in application and component metadata. Set them up in init(): WicketApplication.java @Override protected void
body: MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy keeps the rules in application and component metadata. Set them up in init(): WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy.authorize(AdminPage.class, Roles.ADMIN); } Roles are given as a comma-separated string, such as "ADMIN,AUDITOR". This strategy looks up the exact class: it has no package rules and nothing is inherited from superclasses.

title: Hide or disable a component for a role
text: @AuthorizeAction restricts an action on every instance of a class. Wicket checks two actions: RENDER decides whether the component is rendered, ENABLE whether t
apis: AuthorizeAction Action Roles DeleteLink Link Void AuthorizeActions MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy Component
body: @AuthorizeAction restricts an action on every instance of a class. Wicket checks two actions: RENDER decides whether the component is rendered, ENABLE whether the user can use it. DeleteLink.java @AuthorizeAction(action = Action.RENDER, roles = Roles.ADMIN) public class DeleteLink extends Link<Void> { // ... } deny lists roles that are refused even when they also hold an accepted role. Use @AuthorizeActions(actions = {...}) for more than one action on the same class. To restrict a single instance instead of a class, use the metadata strategy: MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy.authorize(deleteLink, Component.RENDER, Roles.ADMIN);

title: Restrict a page to a role
text: AdminPage.java @AuthorizeInstantiation(Roles.ADMIN) public class AdminPage extends WebPage { } The user needs at least one of the listed roles. An anonymous use
apis: AuthorizeInstantiation Roles AdminPage WebPage AuthorizeInstantiations UnauthorizedInstantiationException
body: AdminPage.java @AuthorizeInstantiation(Roles.ADMIN) public class AdminPage extends WebPage { } The user needs at least one of the listed roles. An anonymous user is sent to the sign-in page; a signed-in user without the role gets the access-denied page. Several @AuthorizeInstantiation rules that must all hold go in @AuthorizeInstantiations(ruleset = {...}). The annotation works on any component, not only on pages. Instantiating a restricted panel throws UnauthorizedInstantiationException.

title: Restrict a resource
text: @AuthorizeResource works on IResource classes and their packages: @AuthorizeResource(Roles.ADMIN) public class ExportResource extends AbstractResource { // ...
apis: AuthorizeResource IResource Roles ExportResource AbstractResource IUnauthorizedResourceRequestListener
body: @AuthorizeResource works on IResource classes and their packages: @AuthorizeResource(Roles.ADMIN) public class ExportResource extends AbstractResource { // ... } A refused request is passed to the IUnauthorizedResourceRequestListener in the security settings, which responds with 403 Forbidden by default.

title: Restrict a whole package
text: Put the annotation in the package-info.java of the package. The annotations come before the package line, the imports after it. com/example/admin/package-info.j
apis: AuthorizeInstantiation AuthorizeAction AuthorizeActions AuthorizeInstantiations AuthorizeResource AdminHelpPage WebPage Inherited SecuredPage ReportPage
body: Put the annotation in the package-info.java of the package. The annotations come before the package line, the imports after it. com/example/admin/package-info.java @AuthorizeInstantiation("ADMIN") package com.example.admin; import org.apache.wicket.authroles.authorization.strategies.role.annotations.AuthorizeInstantiation; Wicket resolves @AuthorizeInstantiation for a class like this: An annotation on a class replaces the annotation on its package. It is not added to it. Annotations at the same level are combined with AND: each one has to grant access. A package annotation applies to that package only. Annotating com.example does not restrict com.example.admin. The package-info.java file must be compiled, shipped and loaded by the same class loader as the classes in the package. The other role annotations do not follow these rules. @AuthorizeAction on a package is ignored, @AuthorizeActions and @AuthorizeInstantiations cannot be placed on a package, @AuthorizeInstantiations on a class does not replace the package rule, and @AuthorizeResource on a class and on its package must both grant access. Exempt one class from its package An annotation without roles allows everyone. Because it still replaces the package annotation, it opens up a single class: com/example/admin/AdminHelpPage.java @AuthorizeInstantiation() public class AdminHelpPage extends WebPage { } Watch out for annotated superclasses The role annotations are @Inherited. An annotation on a superclass counts as an annotation on the subclass, wherever the superclass lives, and so it replaces the annotation of the subclass’s own package: // com/example/base/SecuredPage.java @AuthorizeInstantiation("USER") public class SecuredPage extends WebPage { } // com/example/admin/ReportPage.java, in the ADMIN package above public class ReportPage extends SecuredPage { } ReportPage requires USER, not ADMIN. Moving a page into a restricted package has no effect when one of its superclasses is annotated. Annotate such a page explicitly.

title: Show your own access-denied page
text: getApplicationSettings().setAccessDeniedPage(AccessDeniedPage.class); The page must be bookmarkable. To react differently when a signed-in user is refused a pag
body: getApplicationSettings().setAccessDeniedPage(AccessDeniedPage.class); The page must be bookmarkable. To react differently when a signed-in user is refused a page, override onUnauthorizedPage(Component) in your AuthenticatedWebApplication; it throws UnauthorizedInstantiationException by default.

title: Write your own authorization strategy
text: When roles do not fit, implement IAuthorizationStrategy. It has three checks: isInstantiationAuthorized(Class), isActionAuthorized(Component, Action) and isReso
apis: IAuthorizationStrategy Class Component Action IResource PageParameters CompoundAuthorizationStrategy AllowAllAuthorizationStrategy SimplePageAuthorizationStrategy
body: When roles do not fit, implement IAuthorizationStrategy. It has three checks: isInstantiationAuthorized(Class), isActionAuthorized(Component, Action) and isResourceAuthorized(IResource, PageParameters). Register it with getSecuritySettings().setAuthorizationStrategy(...), and combine it with others in a CompoundAuthorizationStrategy. IAuthorizationStrategy.AllowAllAuthorizationStrategy allows everything and is a convenient base class. For the common case of “pages below this base class need a signed-in user” without wicket-auth-roles, extend SimplePageAuthorizationStrategy and implement isAuthorized().

title: Security headers and external checks
text: The response headers that scanners such as Mozilla Observatory check, which of them Wicket sends by default, and the Wicket API or hook that sets each one.
keywords: Mozilla Observatory security scan HSTS Strict-Transport-Security X-Content-Type-Options nosniff X-Frame-Options clickjacking frame-ancestors Referrer-Policy Permissions-Policy X-XSS-Protection response headers
body: Scanners such as Mozilla Observatory grade a site by the security headers in its responses. Wicket sends some of them itself; the others you add in your application, in the container or in a reverse proxy in front of it.

title: Add headers to every page
text: Override setHeaders in your base page. Call super.setHeaders to keep the caching headers. BasePage.java @Override protected void setHeaders(WebResponse response
apis: Override WebResponse Content Type Options Referrer Policy
body: Override setHeaders in your base page. Call super.setHeaders to keep the caching headers. BasePage.java @Override protected void setHeaders(WebResponse response) { super.setHeaders(response); response.setHeader("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff"); response.setHeader("Referrer-Policy", "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"); }

title: Add headers to every response
text: A request cycle listener also reaches resources, Ajax responses and redirects. Set the headers both when the handler is resolved and after it has run, the way W
apis: SecurityHeadersListener IRequestCycleListener Override RequestCycle IRequestHandler WebResponse Strict Transport Security Content Type Options Policy
body: A request cycle listener also reaches resources, Ajax responses and redirects. Set the headers both when the handler is resolved and after it has run, the way Wicket’s own COOP and COEP listeners do, so they survive a redirect to a buffered response: SecurityHeadersListener.java public class SecurityHeadersListener implements IRequestCycleListener { @Override public void onRequestHandlerResolved(RequestCycle cycle, IRequestHandler handler) { setHeaders(cycle); } @Override public void onRequestHandlerExecuted(RequestCycle cycle, IRequestHandler handler) { setHeaders(cycle); } private void setHeaders(RequestCycle cycle) { if (cycle.getResponse() instanceof WebResponse response && response.isHeaderSupported()) { response.setHeader("Strict-Transport-Security", "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"); response.setHeader("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff"); } } } WicketApplication.java getRequestCycleListeners().add(new SecurityHeadersListener()); Do not set Content-Security-Policy or the cross-origin policies this way: Wicket already sends them, and a second value either replaces Wicket’s policy or is combined with it by the browser.

title: Headers and who sets them
text: Header Sent by Wicket by default Set with Content-Security-Policy Yes, a strict policy with nonces, on every WebPage getCspSettings(), see Configure the Content
apis: Content Security Policy WebPage Cross Origin Opener Embedder Report Only Vary ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener Cache Control Pragma Expires WebResponse Strict Transport Type Options Frame Referrer Permissions Protection
body: Header Sent by Wicket by default Set with Content-Security-Policy Yes, a strict policy with nonces, on every WebPage getCspSettings(), see Configure the Content Security Policy Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy Yes, same-origin, on every response getSecuritySettings().setCrossOriginOpenerPolicyConfiguration(...), see Isolate the page with COOP and COEP Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy As Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy-Report-Only: require-corp, on every response getSecuritySettings().setCrossOriginEmbedderPolicyConfiguration(...) Vary: sec-fetch-dest, sec-fetch-site, sec-fetch-mode Only with ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener registered See Protect against cross-site request forgery Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, Pragma: no-cache, Expires Yes, on every WebPage Override WebPage#setHeaders(WebResponse) Strict-Transport-Security No Your own code, the container or the proxy X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff No Your own code, the container or the proxy X-Frame-Options No Your own code, or the frame-ancestors directive of the CSP Referrer-Policy No Your own code, the container or the proxy Permissions-Policy No Your own code, the container or the proxy X-XSS-Protection controlled a filter that current browsers no longer have. Leave it out; the Content Security Policy replaces it.

title: Require HTTPS in web.xml
text: The servlet container can redirect every plain HTTP request to HTTPS: web.xml <security-constraint> <web-resource-collection> <web-resource-name>Entire applicat
body: The servlet container can redirect every plain HTTP request to HTTPS: web.xml <security-constraint> <web-resource-collection> <web-resource-name>Entire application</web-resource-name> <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern> </web-resource-collection> <user-data-constraint> <transport-guarantee>CONFIDENTIAL</transport-guarantee> </user-data-constraint> </security-constraint> Require HTTPS covers HTTPS in Wicket itself. After adding headers, check that the application still works: Strict-Transport-Security with includeSubDomains affects every subdomain for as long as max-age says, and a strict frame-ancestors breaks pages that are meant to be embedded.

title: Stop other sites from framing your pages
text: The CSP directive frame-ancestors is the current replacement for X-Frame-Options: getCspSettings().blocking().add(CSPDirective.FRAME_ANCESTORS, CSPDirectiveSrcV
body: The CSP directive frame-ancestors is the current replacement for X-Frame-Options: getCspSettings().blocking().add(CSPDirective.FRAME_ANCESTORS, CSPDirectiveSrcValue.SELF);

title: How Wicket keeps applications secure
text: What Wicket defends against by default (escaping, a strict CSP, stateful URLs and encryption) and what it leaves to your application and your deployment.
keywords: security model XSS cross-site scripting CSRF escapeModelStrings nonce unsafe-inline trust boundary Host header page store deserialization threat model
body: Wicket’s security comes mostly from how it is built rather than from features you switch on. Pages are Java objects kept on the server, URLs point at those objects, and markup is produced by components that know what they write. That design closes some doors by default. It leaves others to you: who may do what, how users sign in, and what the servlet container and proxy in front of the application let through.

title: Authorization belongs in a strategy
text: Because a URL can be guessed, replayed or leaked, the question whether a user may see a page or press a button has to be answered on the server for every reques
body: Because a URL can be guessed, replayed or leaked, the question whether a user may see a page or press a button has to be answered on the server for every request. Wicket asks the IAuthorizationStrategy before it creates a component and before it renders or enables one. A restricted page therefore stays restricted whether the request came from a link, a bookmark or a hand-made URL. Restrict access by role shows the annotation-based strategy. Signing in is part of the same picture: AuthenticatedWebSession.signIn gives the session a new id when the user signs in, so a session id planted before the sign-in cannot be used afterwards.

title: Content Security Policy
text: Escaping prevents injection; the Content Security Policy limits the damage if an injection gets through anyway. Wicket sends a strict policy with every page: sc
body: Escaping prevents injection; the Content Security Policy limits the damage if an injection gets through anyway. Wicket sends a strict policy with every page: scripts and stylesheets run only when they carry a nonce that is new for every response, and inline scripts, inline styles and event attributes are refused. There is no 'unsafe-inline', so a <script> that an attacker manages to place in the page does not run. That policy is only usable because Wicket itself writes no inline JavaScript. Since Wicket 6, Ajax components do not write onclick attributes; they register their handlers from a script, and every script Wicket contributes is a header item that gets the nonce. 'strict-dynamic' then lets those scripts load what they need. The cost lands on application code that still writes onclick attributes or style attributes, which has to move them into header items and stylesheets. Configure the Content Security Policy shows how.

title: Cross-site request forgery
text: A forged request comes from a page on another site, but the browser sends your session cookie with it, so the server sees a signed-in user. The defence is to re
body: A forged request comes from a page on another site, but the browser sends your session cookie with it, so the server sees a signed-in user. The defence is to require something in the request that the other site cannot know or cannot produce. On a stateful page, Wicket’s URLs already ask for more than a cookie. The URL of a link or a form names a page instance that lives in the user’s session, and the number of times that page has been rendered. If the instance does not exist, or has been rendered again since, Wicket renders the page and does not run the listener. The page id and render count are small counters, though, so they make a forgery unlikely to land, not impossible. CryptoMapper closes that gap. It encrypts every URL with a key that is unique to the session, so the URL itself becomes a secret token that another site cannot construct. Stateless pages have no instance to name: the URL of a stateless form is the same for every user and easy to predict, so neither of these defences applies. What does apply everywhere is checking where a request comes from. Browsers add Sec-Fetch-Site to every request, and other documents cannot forge or remove it. ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener reads it and refuses a listener invocation that comes from another origin, while still letting other sites link to your pages. It is not registered by default. Protect against cross-site request forgery shows how to add it.

title: Encrypted URLs
text: An encrypted URL hides which pages and components exist and makes listener URLs unguessable per session. It is not access control. A URL can leak through a log,
body: An encrypted URL hides which pages and components exist and makes listener URLs unguessable per session. It is not access control. A URL can leak through a log, a browser history or a Referer header, and whoever has it can replay it within the session. Encrypted URLs are deterministic by design: the same URL must encrypt to the same text so that a regenerated URL matches the requested one and resources stay cacheable. Equal URLs are therefore recognisable as equal, and anyone holding the key can confirm a guess. With the default per-session key that stays within one user’s session. By default, URLs are encrypted with PBEWithMD5AndDES and stored pages with AES-CBC, neither of which is authenticated.

title: Escaping by default
text: Cross-site scripting needs a way to get attacker-controlled text into a page as markup. In Wicket, text from a model reaches the page through a component, and e
body: Cross-site scripting needs a way to get attacker-controlled text into a page as markup. In Wicket, text from a model reaches the page through a component, and every component escapes what it renders from its model: escapeModelStrings is on by default, so <, >, &, " and ' become entities. A Label showing a user’s name cannot inject a script, whatever the name contains. Attribute values that Wicket writes into a tag are escaped as well. On the other side of that line are the inputs the developer writes. Markup files are templates, rendered as markup. Message bundles are trusted too: <wicket:message> renders its text as markup, so a bundle can contain formatting. Turning off escaping with setEscapeModelStrings(false) moves model data to that side: the application then says the value is markup and takes responsibility for it. Two gaps remain. ${name} in a message first resolves to a child component, whose output is escaped by that component; only when there is no such child is the value read from the model and written as it is. And HTML escaping is the wrong escaping for a JavaScript context, a <style> element, an unquoted attribute or a URL whose scheme is the payload. A value you put into a script, for example through a TextTemplate, needs JavaScript encoding, which you have to apply yourself.

title: What the deployment has to provide
text: Wicket takes its own identity, the scheme, host and port it is served on, from the servlet container. It does not check the Host header. Every absolute URL, eve
body: Wicket takes its own identity, the scheme, host and port it is served on, from the servlet container. It does not check the Host header. Every absolute URL, every redirect to HTTPS, and the fallback Origin check of the resource isolation listener rely on it. The container or proxy has to reject unexpected host names; Require HTTPS lists what to configure. X-Forwarded-* headers are ignored unless you install the wrapper that reads them. Pages and sessions are serialized to the page store, and Java deserialization of untrusted bytes is dangerous. Wicket treats the page store and the session store as trusted, private storage. Encrypting the page store keeps stored pages confidential, but the key lives in the session, so it protects against someone who can read or write the store, not against someone who holds the session. Development mode adds debugging aids and detailed error pages. It is not hardened and must not run in production; see Switch between development and deployment mode. The SECURITY.md file in the Wicket source lists these trust boundaries in full, along with how to report a vulnerability.

title: Select several values
text: Let the user select several values from a list with ListMultipleChoice, or move them between two lists with Palette.
keywords: multi-select multiple selection select multiple list box transfer list dual list shuttle palette
body: You need this when the user picks any number of values from a list that is too long for checkboxes. For a short list, checkboxes are easier to use.

title: Move values between two lists
text: A Palette from wicket-extensions shows the available choices on the left and the selected ones on the right, with buttons to move them across. Users find it eas
apis: Palette Person LambdaModel Team LambdaChoiceRenderer DefaultTheme Everyone In
body:
A Palette from wicket-extensions shows the available choices on the left and the selected ones on the right, with buttons to move them across. Users find it easier than Ctrl-clicking, and the selection stays visible. Palette palette = new Palette<>("members", LambdaModel.of(team, Team::getMembers, Team::setMembers), people, new LambdaChoiceRenderer<>(Person::getFullName, Person::getId), 10, // visible rows true); // show buttons to change the order palette.add(new DefaultTheme()); form.add(palette);
The choice renderer of a Palette must return a real id, not the position in the list. With ordering turned on, the user can move selected values up and down, and the model gets them in that order. A constructor with one more boolean adds buttons to move all choices at once. DefaultTheme adds a stylesheet that places the two lists side by side. Without it, you style the CSS classes of the palette yourself: palette-choices, palette-buttons, palette-selected and palette-header. Change the headers with the keys palette.available and palette.selected in your properties file: palette.available=Everyone palette.selected=In this team

title: Select several values from a list
text: A ListMultipleChoice renders a <select multiple>. The user holds Ctrl (or Command on a Mac) to select more than one option. Its model holds the collection of se
apis: ListMultipleChoice IModel List Person LoadableDetachableModel LambdaModel Team LambdaChoiceRenderer ListChoice DropDownChoice
body: A ListMultipleChoice renders a <select multiple>. The user holds Ctrl (or Command on a Mac) to select more than one option. Its model holds the collection of selected choices. TeamPage.java IModel<List<Person>> people = LoadableDetachableModel.of(personService::findAll); ListMultipleChoice<Person> members = new ListMultipleChoice<>("members", LambdaModel.of(team, Team::getMembers, Team::setMembers), people, new LambdaChoiceRenderer<>(Person::getFullName, Person::getId)); members.setMaxRows(8); form.add(members); TeamPage.html <select wicket:id="members"></select> Wicket adds the multiple attribute, and a size attribute from setMaxRows() unless the markup has one. Give the renderer an id, so that the selection survives a change in the list. A ListChoice looks the same but lets the user pick only one value. It works like a DropDownChoice that shows several rows.

title: Write the options yourself
text: When you need control over each <option>, for example to add <optgroup> elements to a multiple select, use Select with SelectOptions from wicket-extensions. For
apis: Select SelectOptions ListMultipleChoice Developers List Person LambdaModel Team IOptionRenderer Override String IModel Model
body: When you need control over each <option>, for example to add <optgroup> elements to a multiple select, use Select with SelectOptions from wicket-extensions. For several values, the model object of the Select must be a collection; Wicket clears it and adds the selected values. Each option is a component, so this uses more memory than a ListMultipleChoice. <select wicket:id="members" multiple> <optgroup label="Developers"> <wicket:container wicket:id="developers"> <option wicket:id="option">name</option> </wicket:container> </optgroup> </select> Select<List<Person>> select = new Select<>("members", LambdaModel.of(team, Team::getMembers, Team::setMembers)); form.add(select); select.add(new SelectOptions<>("developers", developers, new IOptionRenderer<Person>() { @Override public String getDisplayValue(Person person) { return person.getFullName(); } @Override public IModel<Person> getModel(Person person) { return Model.of(person); } }));

title: Send events between components
text: Let a component notify others on the page without holding references to them, with send(), onEvent() and a payload class.
keywords: event bus publish subscribe observer notify onEvent payload inter-component communication decouple components Ajax update other panel
body: Use events when an action in one component must update components it does not know about, for example when adding a product in one panel must refresh the cart summary in another. The sender sends a payload object; every component that cares checks for that payload in onEvent().

title: Change how events are delivered
text: Wicket calls onEvent() through an IEventDispatcher. To deliver events another way, for example to methods marked with an annotation, add your own dispatcher in
body: Wicket calls onEvent() through an IEventDispatcher. To deliver events another way, for example to methods marked with an annotation, add your own dispatcher in init() with getFrameworkSettings().add(dispatcher).

title: Choose how the event travels
text: The second argument of send() decides which sinks receive the event, starting at the sink you pass: Broadcast Receivers, in order BREADTH The sink, then its chi
body: The second argument of send() decides which sinks receive the event, starting at the sink you pass: Broadcast Receivers, in order BREADTH The sink, then its children, then their children, and so on. Sent to the application, it reaches the application, the session, the request cycle, the page and all its components. DEPTH The children first, deepest first, then the sink. Sent to the application, it reaches the components, the page, the request cycle, the session and the application last. BUBBLE The sink, then its parents up to the page, then the request cycle, the session and the application. EXACT Only the sink. Use BUBBLE to notify the containers around a component, for example to tell the panel that holds a form that the form was saved: send(this, Broadcast.BUBBLE, new Saved(target)); Components, the page, the session, the request cycle and the application can all receive events: they implement IEventSink. Only components can send them.

title: Define a payload
text: The payload is any object. Give each kind of event its own type, so receivers can recognize it: public record CartChanged(AjaxRequestTarget target, Product prod
body: The payload is any object. Give each kind of event its own type, so receivers can recognize it: public record CartChanged(AjaxRequestTarget target, Product product) {} Carrying the AjaxRequestTarget in the payload lets receivers add themselves to the Ajax response.

title: React to every Ajax request
text: Wicket itself sends an event during every Ajax request: before it writes the response, it broadcasts the AjaxRequestTarget with BREADTH from the application to
body: Wicket itself sends an event during every Ajax request: before it writes the response, it broadcasts the AjaxRequestTarget with BREADTH from the application to the whole page. A component that must refresh after any Ajax request can listen for it: @Override public void onEvent(IEvent<?> event) { super.onEvent(event); if (event.getPayload() instanceof AjaxRequestTarget target) { target.add(this); } } Put this in a subclass of FeedbackPanel, for example, and it stays up to date without every Ajax handler adding it. Use it sparingly: the check runs for every component on every Ajax request of the page.

title: Receive the event
text: Override onEvent() and check the payload type: public class CartSummaryPanel extends Panel { public CartSummaryPanel(String id, IModel<Cart> cart) { super(id, c
apis: CartSummaryPanel Panel String IModel Cart Label Override IEvent CartChanged Component
body: Override onEvent() and check the payload type: public class CartSummaryPanel extends Panel { public CartSummaryPanel(String id, IModel<Cart> cart) { super(id, cart); setOutputMarkupId(true); add(new Label("count", cart.map(Cart::size))); } @Override public void onEvent(IEvent<?> event) { super.onEvent(event); if (event.getPayload() instanceof CartChanged changed) { changed.target().add(this); } } } Behaviors receive events too, in onEvent(Component component, IEvent<?> event), right after the component they belong to.

title: Send the event
text: Every component can send an event with send(sink, broadcast, payload). To reach every component on the page, send it to the page with Broadcast.BREADTH: add(new
apis: Broadcast AjaxLink Void Override AjaxRequestTarget CartChanged
body: Every component can send an event with send(sink, broadcast, payload). To reach every component on the page, send it to the page with Broadcast.BREADTH: add(new AjaxLink<Void>("addToCart") { @Override public void onClick(AjaxRequestTarget target) { cart.add(product); send(getPage(), Broadcast.BREADTH, new CartChanged(target, product)); } }); send() delivers the event right away, before it returns.

title: Stop an event
text: IEvent lets a receiver control the rest of the delivery: Method Effect stop() No further sink receives the event. dontBroadcastDeeper() With BREADTH, the childr
body: IEvent lets a receiver control the rest of the delivery: Method Effect stop() No further sink receives the event. dontBroadcastDeeper() With BREADTH, the children of the current component do not receive it. getSource() The component that sent the event. getType() The Broadcast used. getPayload() The payload.

page: Share a resource across the application
title: Share a resource across the application
text: Register a resource once under an application-wide key with getSharedResources and refer to it from any component with SharedResourceReference.
keywords: shared resource global resource application scope register resource getSharedResources resource key wicket/resource/org.apache.wicket.Application
body: Register a shared resource when one resource instance should serve the whole application under a fixed key, and components that link to it should not need a reference to the instance. If you want a readable URL instead, mount it: Give a resource a URL.

page: Share a resource across the application
title: Keep the resource safe for concurrent use
text: There is one instance for all users and all requests, and requests run in parallel. Do not keep request or user data in fields of the resource; read what you ne
body: There is one instance for all users and all requests, and requests run in parallel. Do not keep request or user data in fields of the resource; read what you need from the request, the session or a service while it responds. Package resources are shared resources too, without registration: Wicket finds them by their class and file name. Register only resources that you create in code.

page: Share a resource across the application
title: Refer to it by name
text: Anywhere in the application, a SharedResourceReference with the same name finds the registered resource: add(new ResourceLink<Void>("export", new SharedResource
body: Anywhere in the application, a SharedResourceReference with the same name finds the registered resource: add(new ResourceLink<Void>("export", new SharedResourceReference("ordersCsv"))); The link renders a URL with the scope and the name: ./wicket/resource/org.apache.wicket.Application/ordersCsv The scope of resources added by name alone is Application. A name that is not registered gives a 404 response when the URL is requested, so register shared resources before the first request, in init(). To get the URL as text, use RequestCycle.get().urlFor(new SharedResourceReference("ordersCsv"), null).

page: Share a resource across the application
title: Register the resource
text: Add the resource to the shared resources in init(), under a name: WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); getSharedResources().ad
body: Add the resource to the shared resources in init(), under a name: WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); getSharedResources().add("ordersCsv", new OrdersCsvResource()); } OrdersCsvResource is the resource from Generate a resource in code.

page: Share a resource across the application
title: Scope a shared resource to a class
text: Pass a class to keep names apart, for example in a library that registers resources from an IInitializer: getSharedResources().add(ReportsModule.class, "summary
body: Pass a class to keep names apart, for example in a library that registers resources from an IInitializer: getSharedResources().add(ReportsModule.class, "summary", null, null, null, new SummaryResource()); new SharedResourceReference(ReportsModule.class, "summary") The three null arguments are the locale, style and variation, which are part of the key. Configure a module with an initializer shows where a library runs such code.

page: Show, hide or disable a component
title: Show, hide or disable a component
text: Hide a component or make it read-only depending on the state of your application, and decide that state once per request in onConfigure.
keywords: visibility setVisible isVisible setEnabled isEnabled disabled hidden conditional rendering onConfigure isVisibleInHierarchy setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag
body: Use this when part of a page should only appear, or only be usable, under some condition: a link for administrators, a warning when a list is empty, a field that cannot be changed after an order is placed.

page: Show, hide or disable a component
title: Decide visibility on every request with onConfigure
text: Override onConfigure and set the visibility there. Wicket calls onConfigure once per request, before it renders the component, so the condition is always curren
body: Override onConfigure and set the visibility there. Wicket calls onConfigure once per request, before it renders the component, so the condition is always current. add(new Label("warning", "Your trial ends tomorrow.") { @Override protected void onConfigure() { super.onConfigure(); setVisible(account.isTrialEndingSoon()); } }); Always call super.onConfigure(); Wicket checks that you do. Prefer this to overriding isVisible(). Wicket calls isVisible() many times while it processes a request, so any work in it, such as a database query, runs many times. An overridden isVisible() can also return different answers within one request, which makes isVisibleInHierarchy() unreliable.

page: Show, hide or disable a component
title: Disable a component
text: Call setEnabled(false), in onConfigure when the condition can change: add(new TextField<>("customerNumber", customerNumberModel) { @Override protected void onCo
body: Call setEnabled(false), in onConfigure when the condition can change: add(new TextField<>("customerNumber", customerNumberModel) { @Override protected void onConfigure() { super.onConfigure(); setEnabled(!order.isPlaced()); } }); A disabled component is still rendered, but: form components get the disabled attribute, and Wicket ignores their input; links lose their href, and buttons get the disabled attribute; Wicket refuses requests to the component’s listeners, so its Ajax behaviors do nothing, even when someone calls their URL by hand. Disabling a container disables everything inside it. isEnabledInHierarchy() tells you whether a component and all its parents are enabled.

page: Show, hide or disable a component
title: Hide a component
text: Call setVisible(false). An invisible component renders nothing, not even its tag, and neither do its children. Label warning = new Label("warning", "Your trial
body: Call setVisible(false). An invisible component renders nothing, not even its tag, and neither do its children. Label warning = new Label("warning", "Your trial ends tomorrow."); warning.setVisible(account.isTrialEndingSoon()); add(warning); This decides the visibility once, when the page is built. If the page stays on screen and the condition changes, the component keeps its old state.

page: Show, hide or disable a component
title: Hide a group of components at once
text: Hiding a container hides all of its children. Put the components in a WebMarkupContainer and set the visibility on the container. See Group components with WebM
body: Hiding a container hides all of its children. Put the components in a WebMarkupContainer and set the visibility on the container. See Group components with WebMarkupContainer. To hide the text around a single component together with it, without a container in Java, use wicket:enclosure.

page: Show, hide or disable a component
title: Show a hidden component with Ajax
text: An invisible component leaves no tag in the page, so an Ajax response has nowhere to put it when it becomes visible. Call setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag(true) on
body: An invisible component leaves no tag in the page, so an Ajax response has nowhere to put it when it becomes visible. Call setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag(true) on it: Wicket then renders an empty, hidden placeholder tag with the component’s markup id in its place. Label details = new Label("details", detailsModel); details.setVisible(false); details.setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag(true); add(details); add(new AjaxLink<Void>("toggle") { @Override public void onClick(AjaxRequestTarget target) { details.setVisible(!details.isVisible()); target.add(details); } }); See Update components with Ajax for more on repainting components.

title: Inject Spring beans
text: Inject beans from a Spring application context into pages, components, behaviors and other objects with @SpringBean.
keywords: dependency injection Spring Framework ApplicationContext AnnotationConfigApplicationContext ContextLoaderListener Spring Boot autowire Autowired service repository proxy NotSerializableException Objenesis
body: Use this when your services live in a Spring application context and your pages need them. Spring does not create Wicket components, so @Autowired has no effect in them. Module wicket-spring fills fields annotated with @SpringBean instead, as each component is constructed. Wicket 10 works with Spring 6.

title: Add the dependencies
text: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-spring</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupI
body: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-spring</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework</groupId> <artifactId>spring-web</artifactId> <version>${spring.version}</version> </dependency> wicket-spring brings spring-context along; spring-web you add yourself.

title: Inject a bean
text: Annotate a field with @SpringBean. It is filled when the component’s constructor runs, before the code of your subclass, so you can use it in the constructor: P
apis: SpringBean ProductPage WebPage ProductService PageParameters Label Primary IllegalStateException AuditLog Inject Named
body: Annotate a field with @SpringBean. It is filled when the component’s constructor runs, before the code of your subclass, so you can use it in the constructor: ProductPage.java public class ProductPage extends WebPage { @SpringBean private ProductService products; public ProductPage(PageParameters parameters) { super(parameters); long id = parameters.get("id").toLong(); add(new Label("name", () -> products.find(id).getName())); } } By default Wicket looks for the single bean of the field’s type, generics included. When the context has more than one, it picks the one marked @Primary, then the one whose bean name equals the field name; otherwise it throws an IllegalStateException that lists the candidates. Name the bean to choose one yourself, and mark a dependency as optional to get null instead of an exception when no bean exists: @SpringBean(name = "archiveProductService") private ProductService archive; @SpringBean(required = false) private AuditLog auditLog; wicket-spring also understands @jakarta.inject.Inject with @Named; see Inject with JSR-330 annotations.

title: Inject into objects that are not components
text: Models, validators and other helpers are not created by Wicket, so nothing injects them. Call the injector yourself in their constructor: public class ProductMo
apis: ProductModel LoadableDetachableModel Product SpringBean ProductService Injector Override
body: Models, validators and other helpers are not created by Wicket, so nothing injects them. Call the injector yourself in their constructor: public class ProductModel extends LoadableDetachableModel<Product> { @SpringBean private ProductService products; private final long id; public ProductModel(long id) { this.id = id; Injector.get().inject(this); } @Override protected Product load() { return products.find(id); } }

title: Keep injected fields serializable
text: Wicket serializes pages between requests, and services are rarely serializable. So @SpringBean does not put the bean itself in the field but a small proxy that
body: Wicket serializes pages between requests, and services are rarely serializable. So @SpringBean does not put the bean itself in the field but a small proxy that serializes to a reference and looks the bean up again after deserialization. Do not make injected fields transient: the proxy already takes care of it, and a transient field is null after the page comes back from the page store. The proxy has limits: Injecting an interface type always works. For a class, Wicket generates a subclass, so the class cannot be final, and it needs a constructor without arguments unless you add Objenesis to your dependencies. String, primitive wrappers and enums are injected directly, without a proxy. Pass false as the third constructor argument of SpringComponentInjector to inject the beans without proxies. Then the components must not be serialized with them.

title: Let Spring create the application
text: To define the WebApplication itself as a Spring bean, so it can have its own dependencies injected by Spring, let the Wicket filter take it from the Spring cont
body: To define the WebApplication itself as a Spring bean, so it can have its own dependencies injected by Spring, let the Wicket filter take it from the Spring context: <filter> <filter-name>wicket</filter-name> <filter-class>org.apache.wicket.protocol.http.WicketFilter</filter-class> <init-param> <param-name>applicationFactoryClassName</param-name> <param-value>org.apache.wicket.spring.SpringWebApplicationFactory</param-value> </init-param> </filter> The factory takes the single WebApplication bean from the context created by ContextLoaderListener; with more than one, name it in the applicationBean init parameter. With a contextConfigLocation init parameter, the factory creates a separate context for the application as a child of that one. AnnotationConfigSpringWebApplicationFactory does the same, but reads contextConfigLocation as @Configuration classes instead of XML files. To test pages that use Spring beans, see Test with Spring.

title: Register the injector
text: Add a SpringComponentInjector to the component instantiation listeners in init(). The simplest setup creates the Spring context there: WicketApplication.java @O
apis: SpringComponentInjector Override AnnotationConfigApplicationContext AppConfig ContextLoaderListener SpringBean Behavior
body: Add a SpringComponentInjector to the component instantiation listeners in init(). The simplest setup creates the Spring context there: WicketApplication.java @Override protected void init() { super.init(); var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class); getComponentInstantiationListeners().add(new SpringComponentInjector(this, context)); } If something else already creates the Spring context for the web application, such as Spring’s ContextLoaderListener in web.xml or Spring Boot, leave out the context. The injector then finds it in the servlet context: getComponentInstantiationListeners().add(new SpringComponentInjector(this)); The injector also injects behaviors, so @SpringBean works in a Behavior as well.

title: Stateful and stateless pages
text: Why Wicket keeps pages between requests, how page versions serve the back button, and what a stateless page gives up and gains.
keywords: state session page id page version versioning back button page expired bookmarkable scalability memory serialization isPageStateless setVersioned
body: Most web frameworks create a fresh page for every request and throw it away after the response. Wicket can do that too, but by default it keeps the page. A stateful page is a Java object that survives between requests: the user clicks a link on it, and Wicket calls onClick() on the very Link object that rendered that link, in the same page, with the same fields and models. A stateless page is created for a request and forgotten afterwards, like a page in most other frameworks.

title: Choosing
text: Make pages stateless that are public, visited by many people who do not log in, or meant to be bookmarked and shared: the home page, product pages, search resul
body: Make pages stateless that are public, visited by many people who do not log in, or meant to be bookmarked and shared: the home page, product pages, search results, the login page. Their state fits in the URL, and a session per visitor would be waste. Let pages be stateful when they behave like an application: multi-step forms, editors, pages with Ajax interaction, anything behind a login. That is where the programming model pays off, and the user has a session anyway.

title: How Wicket decides
text: You do not declare a page stateful or stateless; Wicket works it out before rendering. Page.isPageStateless() returns true when: the page class is bookmarkable,
body: You do not declare a page stateful or stateless; Wicket works it out before rendering. Page.isPageStateless() returns true when: the page class is bookmarkable, the page’s stateless hint is not switched off, and every visible and enabled component on the page, and every behavior on those components, reports that it is stateless. One Link, Form or Ajax behavior anywhere on the page makes the whole page stateful. A hidden or disabled one does not count, since it renders no callback. Because a single component can change the outcome, pages tend to turn stateful by accident; Keep a page stateless shows how to check. A session exists for stateless requests too, but it is temporary: Wicket creates it for the request and drops it at the end, unless something binds it. Keep data in the session describes when that happens.

title: Page ids and versions
text: Every stateful page instance gets a page id from the session, the number after the ? in its URL. When a request changes a stateful page, for example by replacin
body: Every stateful page instance gets a page id from the session, the number after the ? in its URL. When a request changes a stateful page, for example by replacing a component, adding one, or changing a model through setDefaultModelObject(), Wicket gives the page a new id before rendering it. The previous state stays in the store under the old id. That is what makes the back button work. The browser goes back to the URL with the old id, and Wicket renders the page as it was then, not as it is now. A click on that old page acts on the old version. Without versions, the back button would show a page whose components no longer match what the server holds. Versioning can be switched off per page with setVersioned(false), or for all pages with PageSettings.setVersionPagesByDefault(false). The page then keeps one id for its whole life, and the back button shows the current state. getPageReference() returns a PageReference that can fetch the page instance later, for example to return to the calling page after an edit. Asking for a reference makes the page stateful.

title: What a stateless page gives up
text: A stateless page needs no session and can be cached and shared like any other URL. In exchange, nothing survives the response. Wicket has to be able to create t
body: A stateless page needs no session and can be cached and shared like any other URL. In exchange, nothing survives the response. Wicket has to be able to create the page again for every request, from its class and its PageParameters, so the page must be bookmarkable: a public constructor without arguments or with a single PageParameters argument. Anything the page needs must come from the URL, a cookie, the session or the database. The components that normally keep state have stateless versions with the same limitation. A StatelessLink or StatelessForm makes Wicket create a new page instance when it is clicked or submitted, run the handler on the new instance, and render that. Ajax behaviors can be stateless too, as described in Use Ajax on stateless pages.

title: What keeping pages costs
text: A stateful page lives in the user’s HTTP session and in the page store. Wicket creates the session the first time it has to store a page. From then on: Every ob
body: A stateful page lives in the user’s HTTP session and in the page store. Wicket creates the session the first time it has to store a page. From then on: Every object reachable from the page is serialized after each request. Components, models and their objects must be serializable, and large objects make every request slower. Models and component data explains how detachable models keep pages small. Memory and disk grow with the number of users and the pages they open. Every version goes to disk, up to a size limit per session, and the last page used also stays in the session. How pages are stored describes the layers. A page can disappear: the session expires, or the store drops old versions when the limit is reached. A request for it then ends in a PageExpiredException and the page-expired error page. For a bookmarkable page, Wicket creates a new instance from the URL instead (PageSettings.setRecreateBookmarkablePagesAfterExpiry, on by default), but the old instance’s state is gone and a click on a component of it is not executed. In a cluster, the session must reach the node that handles the next request, through sticky sessions or session replication. Every visitor of a stateful page gets a session, including search engine crawlers.

title: Why Wicket keeps pages
text: Keeping the page is what lets you program a web page like a desktop screen. A component can hold state in its fields and models, and an event handler can change
body: Keeping the page is what lets you program a web page like a desktop screen. A component can hold state in its fields and models, and an event handler can change the component tree, and none of that has to be written into URLs or hidden fields. A Link needs no parameters to know which row it belongs to: it is a Java object in that row. The URLs show this. A stateful page renders links like ./orders?3-1.-table-rows-2-delete: page instance 3, render count 1, then the path of the component to call. The request goes back to that instance and that component. A stateless page renders links that carry everything needed to build the page again, such as ./orders?status=open.

title: Use Ajax on stateless pages
text: Make Ajax components and behaviors stateless with getStatelessHint, so a page such as a login page keeps working without a stored page instance.
keywords: stateless getStatelessHint setStatelessHint page expired login page static markup id session-less
body: Use this when a page has to stay stateless, for example a login page or a public landing page, and still uses Ajax. By default an Ajax component or behavior makes its page stateful, because its callback URL points to a page instance that Wicket must keep. A stateless Ajax callback recreates the page from its URL instead. Stateful and stateless pages explains the difference.

title: Give the updated components fixed markup ids
text: On a stateless page, every Ajax request builds a new page instance from the URL and its parameters. The markup ids that setOutputMarkupId(true) generates come f
body: On a stateless page, every Ajax request builds a new page instance from the URL and its parameters. The markup ids that setOutputMarkupId(true) generates come from a counter in the session, so the new instance can give a component another id than the one in the browser, and the update would not find its element. Give every component that you add to the target an id that does not change. Write it in the markup: or set it in Java with setMarkupId("counter") together with setOutputMarkupId(true), as in the first example. The id must be unique on the page.

title: Keep the state in the URL
text: A stateless callback never sees the fields of the previous page instance: the instance is new. Keep what the page needs in its page parameters, as in the counte
body: A stateless callback never sees the fields of the previous page instance: the instance is new. Keep what the page needs in its page parameters, as in the counter example above, or in the session; see Keep data in the session. To check that the page really stays stateless, see Keep a page stateless.

title: Make an Ajax behavior stateless
text: For a behavior, override getStatelessHint(Component): select.add(new AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior("change") { @Override protected void onUpdate(AjaxRequest
body: For a behavior, override getStatelessHint(Component): select.add(new AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior("change") { @Override protected void onUpdate(AjaxRequestTarget target) { selected.setDefaultModelObject("Selected: " + select.getModelObject()); target.add(selected); } @Override public boolean getStatelessHint(Component component) { return true; } });

title: Make an Ajax component stateless
text: Override getStatelessHint() and return true. AjaxLink, AjaxFallbackLink, AjaxButton, AjaxSubmitLink and AjaxFallbackButton pass this hint on to their Ajax behav
apis: AjaxLink AjaxFallbackLink AjaxButton AjaxSubmitLink AjaxFallbackButton Label Void Override Optional AjaxRequestTarget StatelessForm
body: Override getStatelessHint() and return true. AjaxLink, AjaxFallbackLink, AjaxButton, AjaxSubmitLink and AjaxFallbackButton pass this hint on to their Ajax behavior: Label counterLabel = new Label("counterLabel", () -> getPageParameters().get("counter").toInt(0)); counterLabel.setMarkupId("counter").setOutputMarkupId(true); add(counterLabel); add(new AjaxFallbackLink<Void>("increment") { @Override public void onClick(Optional<AjaxRequestTarget> target) { int counter = getPage().getPageParameters().get("counter").toInt(0); getPage().getPageParameters().set("counter", counter + 1); target.ifPresent(t -> t.add(counterLabel)); } @Override protected boolean getStatelessHint() { return true; } }); Forms on a stateless page have to be stateless too. Put the Ajax submit components in a StatelessForm; see Build a stateless form.

title: Build a stateless form
text: Use StatelessForm so a page with a form stays stateless, never expires and does not create a session until it must.
keywords: stateless page expired login form PageExpiredException session bookmarkable search form
body: You need this for forms on public pages, such as a login, search or contact form. A normal Form makes its page stateful: Wicket stores the page in the session, and a submit after the session has timed out ends in a “page expired” error. A StatelessForm keeps the page stateless, so a submit always works and a crawler that requests the page does not create sessions.

title: Keep everything on the page stateless
text: A StatelessForm only helps when the whole page is stateless. The page must be bookmarkable: it needs a constructor without arguments or one that takes PageParam
body: A StatelessForm only helps when the whole page is stateless. The page must be bookmarkable: it needs a constructor without arguments or one that takes PageParameters. Every other component on the page must be stateless too. Labels, fields and buttons are; a normal Link or an Ajax behavior makes the page stateful again. Use a StatelessLink or a BookmarkablePageLink for links. Keep a page stateless shows how to find the component that breaks it.

title: Pass page parameters along
text: The form posts back to the page with the page’s current parameters, so a search form on /search?category=books keeps category across the submit. Read the parame
body: The form posts back to the page with the page’s current parameters, so a search form on /search?category=books keeps category across the submit. Read the parameters in the constructor, as the page is built anew on each submit: public SearchPage(PageParameters parameters) { super(parameters); String category = parameters.get("category").toString("all"); // build the form for this category } To show the result on a bookmarkable URL, redirect with new parameters from onSubmit(): setResponsePage(SearchPage.class, new PageParameters().set("q", query));

title: Replace Form with StatelessForm
text: LoginPage.java public class LoginPage extends WebPage { private String username; private String password; public LoginPage(PageParameters parameters) { super(pa
apis: LoginPage WebPage String PageParameters StatelessForm Void Override AuthenticatedWebSession Unknown IModel LambdaModel TextField PasswordTextField FeedbackPanel Log
body: LoginPage.java public class LoginPage extends WebPage { private String username; private String password; public LoginPage(PageParameters parameters) { super(parameters); StatelessForm form = new StatelessForm<>("form") { @Override protected void onSubmit() { if (AuthenticatedWebSession.get().signIn(username, password)) { continueToOriginalDestination(); setResponsePage(getApplication().getHomePage()); } else { error("Unknown username or password"); } } }; add(form); IModel usernameModel = LambdaModel.of(() -> username, value -> username = value); IModel passwordModel = LambdaModel.of(() -> password, value -> password = value); form.add(new TextField<>("username", usernameModel).setRequired(true)); form.add(new PasswordTextField("password", passwordModel)); add(new FeedbackPanel("feedback")); } } LoginPage.html

title: Understand what the form gets on submit
text: When the form is submitted, Wicket does not find the page in the session. It creates a new instance of the page from its class and page parameters, and then pro
body: When the form is submitted, Wicket does not find the page in the session. It creates a new instance of the page from its class and page parameters, and then processes the form on that new instance. For your code this means: The models start out the way the constructor sets them up. Anything you changed on the earlier instance, such as a value set by an earlier submit or a choice list filtered at runtime, is gone. Only what the browser submits reaches the models. A DropDownChoice can only find the submitted option if the constructor builds the same list of choices again. Hidden state belongs in page parameters or in a HiddenField, not in fields of the page. A failed submit renders the new instance with the errors and the user’s input, as with a normal form.

title: Use links on stateless pages
text: Handle clicks on a stateless page with StatelessLink and keep the state the click needs in page parameters, because every click builds a new page.
keywords: stateless page stateless link onClick on stateless page page becomes stateful instance variable reset session not created
body: A plain Link makes its page stateful: its URL points to a component of a page instance that Wicket keeps in the page store. On a page that has to stay stateless, such as a landing page or a login page that must not create a session, use a StatelessLink for clicks that run code, and a BookmarkablePageLink for plain navigation. Why a page is stateful or stateless is explained in Stateful and stateless pages.

title: Check that the page stays stateless
text: A page that you expect to be stateless can turn stateful when someone adds a component later. Keep a page stateless shows how to find the component that makes a
body: A page that you expect to be stateless can turn stateful when someone adds a component later. Keep a page stateless shows how to find the component that makes a page stateful and how to test for it. For forms and Ajax on stateless pages, see Build a stateless form and Use Ajax on stateless pages.

title: Keep the state of a click in page parameters
text: The URL of a StatelessLink names the page class, the page parameters and the link. When the user clicks, Wicket creates a new instance of the page from those pa
apis: StatelessLink CounterPage WebPage PageParameters Void Override Label Clicked Click BookmarkablePageLink
body:
The URL of a StatelessLink names the page class, the page parameters and the link. When the user clicks, Wicket creates a new instance of the page from those parameters, calls onClick() on the link in that new instance, and renders the result. Nothing from the instance the user saw survives. Instance fields start from their initial values on every click: public class CounterPage extends WebPage { private int count; public CounterPage(PageParameters parameters) { super(parameters); add(new StatelessLink("increment") { @Override public void onClick() { count++; // always goes from 0 to 1 } }); } } Put the state that a click needs in the page parameters instead, and send the user to a page with new parameters: CounterPage.java public class CounterPage extends WebPage { public CounterPage(PageParameters parameters) { super(parameters); int count = parameters.get("count").toInt(0); add(new Label("count", count)); add(new StatelessLink("increment") { @Override public void onClick() { setResponsePage(CounterPage.class, new PageParameters().add("count", count + 1)); } }); } } CounterPage.html

Clicked 0 times.

Click The link URL carries the current page parameters, so the new instance that handles the click sees the same count as the page the user clicked on. When a click only navigates, a BookmarkablePageLink with the new parameters does the same with one request instead of a click request and a redirect: add(new BookmarkablePageLink("increment", CounterPage.class, new PageParameters().add("count", count + 1)));

title: Replace Link with StatelessLink
text: StatelessLink has the same onClick() as Link: add(new StatelessLink<Void>("logout") { @Override public void onClick() { getSession().invalidate(); setResponsePa
body: StatelessLink has the same onClick() as Link: add(new StatelessLink<Void>("logout") { @Override public void onClick() { getSession().invalidate(); setResponsePage(getApplication().getHomePage()); } }); The page must be bookmarkable, with a constructor without arguments or one that takes PageParameters, and all its other components must be stateless too. One stateful component anywhere on the page makes the whole page stateful.

title: Keep preview markup out of the output
text: Leave sample content in your HTML files so they look complete in a browser or design tool, and make sure Wicket never sends it.
keywords: wicket:remove mock markup sample data placeholder content designer static preview dummy content
body: Use this when the markup files are also your design: you or a designer open them directly in a browser and want them to show realistic content, while Wicket renders the real content at runtime. Wicket has three places where preview markup is safe.

page: Use more than one submit button
title: Add a Cancel button that skips validation
text: Turn off default form processing on the button. Wicket then skips validation and the model update, and only calls the button’s onSubmit() and onAfterSubmit(). T
body: Turn off default form processing on the button. Wicket then skips validation and the model update, and only calls the button’s onSubmit() and onAfterSubmit(). The form’s onSubmit() is not called. form.add(new Button("cancel") { @Override public void onSubmit() { setResponsePage(ArticlesPage.class); } }.setDefaultFormProcessing(false)); The user’s input is neither validated nor stored.

page: Use more than one submit button
title: Choose the button for the Enter key
text: When the user presses Enter in a text field, the browser acts as if the first submit button of the form was clicked. To make Enter act as another button, set it
body: When the user presses Enter in a text field, the browser acts as if the first submit button of the form was clicked. To make Enter act as another button, set it as the default button: form.setDefaultButton(publish); Wicket adds a small script to the form that clicks this button when Enter is pressed in an input field.

page: Use more than one submit button
title: Run different code per button
text: Add a Button per action and override its onSubmit(). The button’s onSubmit() runs after the form has been validated and the models are updated, before the form’
apis: Button Form Article Override ArticlesPage Save Publish
body: Add a Button per action and override its onSubmit(). The button’s onSubmit() runs after the form has been validated and the models are updated, before the form’s own onSubmit(). Use onAfterSubmit() for code that has to run after the form’s onSubmit(), such as navigating away. EditArticlePage.java Form<Article> form = new Form<>("form", articleModel) { @Override protected void onSubmit() { articleService.save(getModelObject()); } }; add(form); form.add(new Button("save")); Button publish = new Button("publish") { @Override public void onSubmit() { form.getModelObject().setPublished(true); } @Override public void onAfterSubmit() { setResponsePage(ArticlesPage.class); } }; form.add(publish); EditArticlePage.html <form wicket:id="form"> ... <button type="submit" wicket:id="save">Save</button> <button type="submit" wicket:id="publish">Publish</button> </form> A Button works on <button> and on <input type="submit">. Give it a model to set the text from Java: the model becomes the body of a <button> or the value of an <input>. If validation fails, the clicked button’s onError() is called first, then the form’s onError(). Neither onSubmit() runs.
