body: AjaxButton and AjaxSubmitLink do the same over Ajax and give you an AjaxRequestTarget in onSubmit and onError, so you can update the feedback panel without rendering the whole page. See Ajax components.

title: Test forms
text: Fill in fields, pick options, upload files and submit a form in a unit test with FormTester, then check the feedback messages and the model.
keywords: submit form setValue select selectMultiple setFile feedback messages assertErrorMessages assertInfoMessages validation test AjaxButton test newFormTester
body: You need this when you want to test a form the way a user fills it in: type values, choose options, press a button, and see the result. FormTester does that for one form on the page that WicketTester last rendered. Test pages and components covers setting up the tester.

title: Check the feedback messages
text: form.setValue("email", "not an address"); form.submit(); tester.assertErrorMessages("The value of 'email' is not a valid email address."); tester.assertModelVal
body: form.setValue("email", "not an address"); form.submit(); tester.assertErrorMessages("The value of 'email' is not a valid email address."); tester.assertModelValue("form:email", null); Method Checks assertErrorMessages(String...) Exactly these error messages, in any order assertInfoMessages(String...) Exactly these info messages assertNoErrorMessage(), assertNoInfoMessage() No such messages assertFeedback(path, String...) What a FeedbackPanel at that path renders assertComponentFeedbackMessage(component, key, model, filter) A message from a resource key for one component The tester keeps all messages until the next request, and the FormTester clears them before it submits.

title: Check the model after submitting
text: Read the model of a field with assertModelValue, or check the object behind the form directly: form.setValue("name", "Grace Hopper"); form.submit("save"); Perso
body: Read the model of a field with assertModelValue, or check the object behind the form directly: form.setValue("name", "Grace Hopper"); form.submit("save"); Person saved = (Person) tester.getComponentFromLastRenderedPage("form") .getDefaultModelObject(); assertEquals("Grace Hopper", saved.getName());

title: Fill in and submit a form
text: Ask the tester for a FormTester with the path of the form, set the values with the ids of the fields relative to the form, and submit: SignUpPageTest.java @Test
apis: FormTester Test SignUpPage Ada Lovelace WelcomePage
body: Ask the tester for a FormTester with the path of the form, set the values with the ids of the fields relative to the form, and submit: SignUpPageTest.java @Test void signsUp() { tester.startPage(SignUpPage.class); FormTester form = tester.newFormTester("form"); form.setValue("name", "Ada Lovelace"); form.setValue("email", "ada@example.com"); form.setValue("terms", true); form.submit(); tester.assertNoErrorMessage(); tester.assertRenderedPage(WelcomePage.class); } A new FormTester starts with the values the fields show, as a browser would send them. Text fields without a value are sent as empty strings; newFormTester("form", false) leaves them out of the request instead. Invisible and disabled fields are never sent. Each FormTester submits once. Create a new one for the next submit. FormTester sends the request directly, so the browser’s own checks of required and pattern attributes do not run. A test that submits an empty required field therefore reaches Wicket’s server-side validation, which is what you want to test.

title: Fire an Ajax event on a field
text: A field with an AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior only processes its value when the event fires. Set the value with a FormTester, then fire the event: FormTeste
apis: AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior FormTester ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener Sec Fetch Site
body: A field with an AjaxFormComponentUpdatingBehavior only processes its value when the event fires. Set the value with a FormTester, then fire the event: FormTester form = tester.newFormTester("form"); form.setValue("country", "NL"); tester.executeAjaxEvent("form:country", "change"); tester.assertComponentOnAjaxResponse("form:province"); If the application uses ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener, add the Sec-Fetch-Site header before each submit; see Test pages and components.

title: Press a specific button
text: submit() submits the form without naming a button, so no button’s onSubmit runs. To press a button, name it: form.submit("save"); For an AjaxButton or AjaxSubmi
body: submit() submits the form without naming a button, so no button’s onSubmit runs. To press a button, name it: form.submit("save"); For an AjaxButton or AjaxSubmitLink, submit("id") fires the Ajax event, so you can check the Ajax response afterwards: form.submit("saveAjax"); tester.assertComponentOnAjaxResponse("feedback"); A SubmitLink, inside or outside the form, is pressed with submitLink(path, pageRelative): with true the path starts at the page, with false at the form.

title: Set each kind of field

title: Test markup
text: Find tags in the rendered output with TagTester and check their attributes and content, render a component to a string, or compare a page with an expected file.
keywords: HTML assertions attribute CSS class rendered markup getTagByWicketId createTagByAttribute expected output golden file snapshot test executeTest
body: You need this when a test has to check the markup a page or component renders, not only which components it contains: a CSS class, an attribute, the text inside a tag. TagTester finds tags in a piece of markup and gives you their name, attributes and content. Test pages and components covers rendering the page first.

title: Check a tag
text: OrderPageTest.java @Test void showsTotalAsWarningWhenOverLimit() { tester.startPage(new OrderPage(Model.of(largeOrder))); TagTester total = tester.getTagByWicke
body: OrderPageTest.java @Test void showsTotalAsWarningWhenOverLimit() { tester.startPage(new OrderPage(Model.of(largeOrder))); TagTester total = tester.getTagByWicketId("total"); assertNotNull(total); assertEquals("span", total.getName()); assertTrue(total.getAttributeContains("class", "warning")); assertEquals("€ 12.500,00", total.getValue()); } Method Returns getName() The tag name hasAttribute(name) Whether the attribute is present getAttribute(name) The attribute value, or null getAttributeIs(name, value) Whether the value equals value getAttributeContains(name, part) Whether the value contains part getAttributeEndsWith(name, end) Whether the value ends with end getValue() Everything between the open and close tag getMarkup() The tag itself with everything inside it hasChildTag(name) Whether a tag with that name is nested inside getChild(name), getChild(attribute, value) The first nested tag that matches, as a TagTester

title: Check the whole response
text: For a quick check without finding a tag, assertContains and assertContainsNot match a regular expression against the last response: tester.assertContains("<h1>O
body:
For a quick check without finding a tag, assertContains and assertContainsNot match a regular expression against the last response: tester.assertContains("

Order 42

"); tester.assertContainsNot("class=\"error\""); tester.getLastResponseAsString() returns the markup if you want to search it yourself.

title: Compare a page with an expected file
text: executeTest renders a page and compares the output with a file next to the test class: tester.executeTest(OrderPageTest.class, OrderPage.class, "OrderPage_expec
body: executeTest renders a page and compares the output with a file next to the test class: tester.executeTest(OrderPageTest.class, OrderPage.class, "OrderPage_expected.html"); Run the tests once with -Dwicket.replace.expected.results=true to create or update the files, and review the changes before you commit them. executeTest also takes a page instance or a component, and executeListener and executeBehavior compare the response of a listener or an Ajax behavior. These comparisons are strict: any change in the markup, including attributes a new Wicket version adds, makes them fail.

title: Find a tag
text: The tester has shortcuts that search the last response: tester.startPage(OrderPage.class); TagTester total = tester.getTagByWicketId("total"); TagTester status
body: The tester has shortcuts that search the last response: tester.startPage(OrderPage.class); TagTester total = tester.getTagByWicketId("total"); TagTester status = tester.getTagById("order-status"); List<TagTester> rows = tester.getTagsByWicketId("row"); getTagByWicketId looks for the wicket:id attribute in the output. Wicket keeps that attribute in development mode, which is the default in tests, and strips it in deployment mode. TagTester itself searches any markup string: Method Returns TagTester.createTagByName(markup, "table") The first <table> tag TagTester.createTagByAttribute(markup, "class", "total") The first tag whose class is exactly total TagTester.createTagsByAttribute(markup, "class", "total", false) Every such tag; true stops after the first TagTester.createTags(markup, tag -> ..., false) Every tag the function accepts The methods return null or an empty list when nothing matches.

title: Render a component to a string
text: ComponentRenderer renders a page or a component outside a request and returns the markup. Use it for components whose output you test or use elsewhere, such as
apis: ComponentRenderer CharSequence InvoicePanel Model TagTester WicketTester
body: ComponentRenderer renders a page or a component outside a request and returns the markup. Use it for components whose output you test or use elsewhere, such as the body of an email: var renderer = new ComponentRenderer(); CharSequence html = renderer.renderComponent(() -> new InvoicePanel("invoice", Model.of(invoice))); TagTester amount = TagTester.createTagByAttribute(html.toString(), "class", "amount"); assertEquals("€ 99,00", amount.getValue()); A ComponentRenderer created without arguments uses its own mock application; new ComponentRenderer(application) uses yours. Call destroy() on it when you are done. Inside a running request, or in a test that already has a WicketTester, the static ComponentRenderer.renderComponent(component) renders a new component with the current application.

title: Test pages and components
text: Render pages and single components in a unit test, click links, fire Ajax events and check what they render, with WicketTester and JUnit.
keywords: unit test JUnit startPage assertRenderedPage clickLink executeAjaxEvent startComponentInPage assertLabel request header integration test
body: You need this when you want to check, without a browser or a server, that a page renders and reacts to the user as intended. WicketTester runs your application in memory: it renders pages, clicks links, submits forms and fires Ajax events, and remembers the last rendered page and response so you can check them. Test a page with WicketTester is a step-by-step introduction; WicketTester lists every method.

title: Add the dependencies
text: pom.xml <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-tester</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> <scope>test</scope> </depe
body: pom.xml <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-tester</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId> <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> The quickstart project already has both.

title: Check the response itself
text: getLastResponse() returns the MockHttpServletResponse of the last request, with its status, headers and content: tester.startResource(new ReportResource()); Moc
body: getLastResponse() returns the MockHttpServletResponse of the last request, with its status, headers and content: tester.startResource(new ReportResource()); MockHttpServletResponse response = tester.getLastResponse(); assertEquals(200, response.getStatus()); assertTrue(response.getDocument().startsWith("id,name")); startResource and startResourceReference request a resource. executeUrl("./orders/42") requests any URL, which is how you test mounted pages and request mappers.

title: Check what a component shows
text: Components are addressed by their path from the page: the ids of the containers, separated by colons. tester.assertLabel("greeting", "Hello, Ada"); tester.asser
body:
Components are addressed by their path from the page: the ids of the containers, separated by colons. tester.assertLabel("greeting", "Hello, Ada"); tester.assertComponent("form:name", TextField.class); tester.assertVisible("form:save"); tester.assertInvisible("adminPanel"); tester.assertDisabled("form:delete"); tester.assertModelValue("form:name", "Ada"); tester.assertContains("

Orders

"); assertContains matches a regular expression against the whole response. getComponentFromLastRenderedPage(path) gives you the component itself for anything the assert methods do not cover.

title: Click a link
text: tester.startPage(CounterPage.class); tester.assertLabel("count", "0"); tester.clickLink("increment"); tester.assertLabel("count", "1"); clickLink simulates a br
body: tester.startPage(CounterPage.class); tester.assertLabel("count", "0"); tester.clickLink("increment"); tester.assertLabel("count", "1"); clickLink simulates a browser with JavaScript. For an AjaxLink it fires the Ajax event; for an AjaxFallbackLink too. clickLink(path, false) simulates a browser without JavaScript: an AjaxFallbackLink then does a normal request, and an AjaxLink fails the test.

title: Render a page
text: Create a tester with your application, start a page and check that it rendered. Create a new tester for every test and destroy it afterwards, so tests do not sh
apis: HomePageTest WicketTester BeforeEach WicketApplication AfterEach Test HomePage PageParameters MockApplication
body: Create a tester with your application, start a page and check that it rendered. Create a new tester for every test and destroy it afterwards, so tests do not share an application or a session. HomePageTest.java class HomePageTest { private WicketTester tester; @BeforeEach void setUp() { tester = new WicketTester(new WicketApplication()); } @AfterEach void tearDown() { tester.destroy(); } @Test void rendersSuccessfully() { tester.startPage(HomePage.class); tester.assertRenderedPage(HomePage.class); } } startPage also takes PageParameters or a page instance. new WicketTester() without arguments uses a MockApplication, which is enough for components that do not depend on your application class.

title: Set request headers
text: addRequestHeader sets a header on the next request only: tester.addRequestHeader("Accept-Language", "nl-NL"); tester.startPage(HomePage.class); An application w
apis: Accept Language HomePage ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener Sec Fetch Site FetchMetadataResourceIsolationPolicy
body: addRequestHeader sets a header on the next request only: tester.addRequestHeader("Accept-Language", "nl-NL"); tester.startPage(HomePage.class); An application with ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener refuses listener requests that carry no Sec-Fetch-Site header. Add it before each click or submit: tester.addRequestHeader(FetchMetadataResourceIsolationPolicy.SEC_FETCH_SITE_HEADER, FetchMetadataResourceIsolationPolicy.SAME_ORIGIN); tester.clickLink("delete");

title: Test a component on its own
text: startComponentInPage renders a component in a generated page, attached to a <span> tag. That suits panels and labels: tester.startComponentInPage(new AddressPan
apis: AddressPanel Model Amsterdam TextField Link IMarkupFragment
body: startComponentInPage renders a component in a generated page, attached to a <span> tag. That suits panels and labels: tester.startComponentInPage(new AddressPanel("address", Model.of(address))); tester.assertLabel("address:city", "Amsterdam"); Paths may start with the id of the component you passed; the tester adds it when you leave it out. A component that needs a specific tag, such as a TextField or a Link, needs page markup of its own: pass it with startComponentInPage(component, markup) as an IMarkupFragment.

title: Test Ajax
text: Fire an event on a component that has an AjaxEventBehavior, then check that the right components were added to the Ajax response: tester.startPage(CounterPage.c
body: Fire an event on a component that has an AjaxEventBehavior, then check that the right components were added to the Ajax response: tester.startPage(CounterPage.class); tester.executeAjaxEvent("ajaxIncrement", "click"); tester.assertComponentOnAjaxResponse("count"); tester.assertLabel("count", "1"); executeBehavior(behavior) calls any AbstractAjaxBehavior directly, and executeAllTimerBehaviors(page) fires the timers on a page once.

title: Use files from the web application folder
text: When your application loads markup or resources from src/main/webapp, tell the tester where that folder is. There is no servlet container to ask: tester = new W
body: When your application loads markup or resources from src/main/webapp, tell the tester where that folder is. There is no servlet container to ask: tester = new WicketTester(new WicketApplication(), new File("src/main/webapp").getAbsolutePath()); Forms have their own helper, FormTester; see Test forms. Markup details are easier to check with TagTester, described in Test markup.

title: Test WebSocket behaviors
text: Send messages to a page's WebSocket behavior and check what it pushes back with WebSocketTester, without a servlet container.
keywords: unit test junit websocket test onOutMessage sendMessage broadcast wicket-native-websocket-tester
apis: WebSocketTester WicketTester PageIdKey IWebSocketPushMessage WebSocketBehavior WebSocketResource
body: Use this to test the WebSocketBehavior of a page, or a WebSocketResource, in a unit test. WebSocketTester opens an emulated connection on top of a WicketTester, sends messages as the browser would, and hands you every message the server sends back.

title: Add the test dependency
text: pom.xml <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-native-websocket-tester</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> <scope>te
body: pom.xml <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-native-websocket-tester</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> The class is org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.tester.WebSocketTester. It works with the WicketTester you already use; see Test pages and components.

title: Send a message and check the answer
text: Start the page, create a WebSocketTester for it, and override onOutMessage to collect what the server pushes: ChatPageTest.java class ChatPageTest { private Wic
apis: WebSocketTester ChatPageTest WicketTester BeforeEach WicketApplication AfterEach Test ChatPage List String ArrayList Override
body: Start the page, create a WebSocketTester for it, and override onOutMessage to collect what the server pushes: ChatPageTest.java class ChatPageTest { private WicketTester tester; @BeforeEach void setUp() { tester = new WicketTester(new WicketApplication()); } @AfterEach void tearDown() { tester.destroy(); } @Test void echoesMessageInUpperCase() { ChatPage page = tester.startPage(ChatPage.class); List<String> received = new ArrayList<>(); WebSocketTester webSocket = new WebSocketTester(tester, page) { @Override protected void onOutMessage(String message) { received.add(message); } }; webSocket.sendMessage("hello"); webSocket.destroy(); assertEquals(List.of("HELLO"), received); } } sendMessage calls the behavior’s onMessage in the test thread, so by the time it returns the answers are in. Binary messages work the same way with sendMessage(byte[], offset, length) and the matching onOutMessage(byte[], int, int). destroy() closes the connection, which calls the behavior’s onClose. When the behavior re-renders components with handler.add(...), the message you receive is the <ajax-response> XML. Check that it contains the markup you expect.

title: Test a push from the server
text: Push messages do not come from the browser. Broadcast one to the page’s connection, identified by the application, the session id and the page key: webSocket.br
body: Push messages do not come from the browser. Broadcast one to the page’s connection, identified by the application, the session id and the page key: webSocket.broadcast(tester.getApplication(), tester.getHttpSession().getId(), new PageIdKey(page.getPageId(), page.getClass().getName()), new JobProgress(50)); The PageIdKey takes the page class name as second argument, because the connection is registered with it. broadcastAll(application, message) reaches every connection. The page’s onEvent or the behavior’s onPush runs in the test thread, and its answer arrives in onOutMessage. WebSocketTester sets a same-thread executor for push messages, so nothing has to be awaited.

title: Test a WebSocketResource
text: For a shared WebSocketResource, pass its name instead of a page: WebSocketTester webSocket = new WebSocketTester(tester, "prices") { @Override protected void on
body: For a shared WebSocketResource, pass its name instead of a page: WebSocketTester webSocket = new WebSocketTester(tester, "prices") { @Override protected void onOutMessage(String message) { received.add(message); } }; The resource must be registered in the application’s init() as in production. Push updates over a WebSocket shows the behavior and resource side.

title: Test with Spring
text: Test pages that use @SpringBean with WicketTester, either with mock beans in an ApplicationContextMock or against a real Spring test context.
keywords: Spring integration test SpringJUnitConfig SpringExtension mock beans Mockito No WebApplicationContext found ContextLoaderListener Transactional rollback
body: You need this when your pages get their services through @SpringBean and you want to test them with WicketTester. The test has to give the SpringComponentInjector a Spring context: one filled with mock beans for a fast unit test, or a context from Spring’s test support for an integration test. Inject Spring beans covers the setup of the application itself. If the application creates its Spring context in init(), a test with new WicketTester(new WicketApplication()) already runs against that context and needs nothing from this page. The rest is for applications that let the servlet container or Spring Boot create the context. In a test there is no container, so new SpringComponentInjector(this) fails with “No WebApplicationContext found: no ContextLoaderListener registered?”.

title: Let tests replace the injector
text: Create the injector in a method of its own, so that a test can pass in a context: WicketApplication.java public class WicketApplication extends WebApplication {
apis: WicketApplication WebApplication Override SpringComponentInjector Spring Boot
body: Create the injector in a method of its own, so that a test can pass in a context: WicketApplication.java public class WicketApplication extends WebApplication { @Override protected void init() { super.init(); getComponentInstantiationListeners().add(newSpringComponentInjector()); } protected SpringComponentInjector newSpringComponentInjector() { // finds the context that the container or Spring Boot created return new SpringComponentInjector(this); } // getHomePage() and the rest of the application }

title: Roll back database changes
text: WicketTester handles each request on the thread of the test, so Spring’s test transactions cover what your pages do. Annotate the test method or class with @Tra
body: WicketTester handles each request on the thread of the test, so Spring’s test transactions cover what your pages do. Annotate the test method or class with @Transactional, with a transaction manager in the context, and Spring rolls back after each test: @Test @Transactional void savesOrder() { // ... } Pages that start their own transactions, through a service with @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) for instance, commit them as usual.

title: Test against a Spring test context
text: For an integration test, let Spring’s TestContext framework build the context from your configuration and give it to the injector. Add spring-test with test sco
apis: SpringJUnitConfig TestConfig OrderPageIT Autowired ApplicationContext WicketTester BeforeEach WicketApplication Override SpringComponentInjector AfterEach Test NewOrderPage FormTester Grace Hopper OrderSavedPage WebApplication
body: For an integration test, let Spring’s TestContext framework build the context from your configuration and give it to the injector. Add spring-test with test scope, in the version of your Spring Framework. Wicket 10 is built against Spring 6.2 and JUnit 5. OrderPageIT.java @SpringJUnitConfig(TestConfig.class) class OrderPageIT { @Autowired private ApplicationContext context; private WicketTester tester; @BeforeEach void setUp() { tester = new WicketTester(new WicketApplication() { @Override protected SpringComponentInjector newSpringComponentInjector() { return new SpringComponentInjector(this, context); } }); } @AfterEach void tearDown() { tester.destroy(); } @Test void savesOrder() { tester.startPage(NewOrderPage.class); FormTester form = tester.newFormTester("form"); form.setValue("customer", "Grace Hopper"); form.submit("save"); tester.assertRenderedPage(OrderSavedPage.class); } } TestConfig can be your production configuration or a configuration for tests, for example with an in-memory database. Spring keeps the context between tests, while each test gets a new Wicket application. Do not hand a WebApplication bean from the context to the tester: every tester initializes its application, and one Spring bean would be initialized again by every test.

title: Test with mock beans
text: ApplicationContextMock, part of wicket-spring, is a Spring context you fill with bean instances yourself. Each test gets its own beans and starts in millisecond
apis: ApplicationContextMock OrderPageTest WicketTester BeforeEach InMemoryOrderService List Order Ada Lovelace WicketApplication Override SpringComponentInjector AfterEach Test OrderPage PageParameters OrderService SpringBean
body: ApplicationContextMock, part of wicket-spring, is a Spring context you fill with bean instances yourself. Each test gets its own beans and starts in milliseconds: OrderPageTest.java class OrderPageTest { private final ApplicationContextMock context = new ApplicationContextMock(); private WicketTester tester; @BeforeEach void setUp() { context.putBean("orderService", new InMemoryOrderService(List.of( new Order(42, "Ada Lovelace")))); tester = new WicketTester(new WicketApplication() { @Override protected SpringComponentInjector newSpringComponentInjector() { return new SpringComponentInjector(this, context); } }); } @AfterEach void tearDown() { tester.destroy(); } @Test void showsOrder() { tester.startPage(OrderPage.class, new PageParameters().add("id", 42)); tester.assertLabel("customer", "Ada Lovelace"); } } putBean(bean) without a name uses the class name. A mock from Mockito works as well as a hand-written fake: context.putBean("orderService", mock(OrderService.class)). @SpringBean finds beans by type, or by name when the annotation has one.

title: Update components with Ajax
text: Re-render components, show hidden ones, refresh lists and run JavaScript in response to an Ajax request.
keywords: refresh repaint partial update setOutputMarkupId setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag appendJavaScript target.add was not found while trying to perform markup update
body: Use this when an Ajax callback has changed some state and the browser should show the result without reloading the page. Every Ajax callback receives an AjaxRequestTarget; what you add to it is rendered again and sent back. For what happens underneath, see How Wicket Ajax works.

title: Let a component refresh itself
text: When a component should be refreshed after every Ajax request on the page, for example a FeedbackPanel or a header with a shopping cart, let it add itself. Wick
apis: FeedbackPanel AjaxRequestTarget CartSummary Panel String Override IEvent RequestCycle Optional
body: When a component should be refreshed after every Ajax request on the page, for example a FeedbackPanel or a header with a shopping cart, let it add itself. Wicket sends the AjaxRequestTarget as an event to every component on the page before it responds: public class CartSummary extends Panel { public CartSummary(String id) { super(id); setOutputMarkupId(true); // ... } @Override public void onEvent(IEvent<?> event) { super.onEvent(event); if (event.getPayload() instanceof AjaxRequestTarget target) { target.add(this); } } } Code outside a callback, such as a service method that only has the component, can find the target of the current request with RequestCycle.get().find(AjaxRequestTarget.class), which returns an Optional that is empty for a normal request. Events between components are covered in Send events between components.

title: Re-render a component
text: Give the component a markup id when you create it, change its state in the callback and add it to the target: HomePage.java public class HomePage extends WebPag
apis: HomePage WebPage Label AjaxLink Void Override AjaxRequestTarget Clicked Click
body:
Give the component a markup id when you create it, change its state in the callback and add it to the target: HomePage.java public class HomePage extends WebPage { private int clicks; public HomePage() { Label counter = new Label("counter", () -> clicks); counter.setOutputMarkupId(true); add(counter); add(new AjaxLink("increment") { @Override public void onClick(AjaxRequestTarget target) { clicks++; target.add(counter); } }); } } HomePage.html

Clicked times.

Click me target.add takes any number of components. The markup id must be there from the first render: without setOutputMarkupId(true) the browser has no element to replace, and the browser console shows “Component with id … was not found while trying to perform markup update”. See Give a component a markup id for the ways to set one.

title: Refresh a list or table
text: Repeaters such as ListView, RepeatingView and DataView have no tag of their own, and target.add throws an IllegalArgumentException for them. Wrap the repeater i
apis: ListView RepeatingView DataView IllegalArgumentException WebMarkupContainer Override ListItem Todo Label
body:
Repeaters such as ListView, RepeatingView and DataView have no tag of their own, and target.add throws an IllegalArgumentException for them. Wrap the repeater in a container and add the container: TodoPage.html
TodoPage.java WebMarkupContainer items = new WebMarkupContainer("items"); items.setOutputMarkupId(true); add(items); items.add(new ListView<>("item", todos) { @Override protected void populateItem(ListItem item) { item.add(new Label("title", item.getModel().map(Todo::getTitle))); } }); // in the callback target.add(items); For tables with paging and sorting, the Ajax variants in Ajax components refresh themselves. A whole page can be added too, target.add(getPage()); Wicket then redirects the browser to the page instead of sending a partial update.

title: Run JavaScript after the update
text: appendJavaScript runs a script after the components are replaced, prependJavaScript before: target.add(counter); target.appendJavaScript("document.getElementByI
body: appendJavaScript runs a script after the components are replaced, prependJavaScript before: target.add(counter); target.appendJavaScript("document.getElementById('" + counter.getMarkupId() + "').scrollIntoView();"); Never put user input into the script without escaping it; Wicket sends the string as it is. To move the keyboard focus, use target.focusComponent(component), which needs the component’s markup id as well.

title: Show a component that was hidden
text: An invisible component renders nothing, so there is nothing to replace. Call setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag(true) to make it leave an empty, hidden tag with its
apis: Label Saved Override AjaxLink Void AjaxRequestTarget
body: An invisible component renders nothing, so there is nothing to replace. Call setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag(true) to make it leave an empty, hidden tag with its id: Label message = new Label("message", "Saved.") { @Override protected void onConfigure() { super.onConfigure(); setVisible(saved); } }; message.setOutputMarkupPlaceholderTag(true); add(message); add(new AjaxLink<Void>("save") { @Override public void onClick(AjaxRequestTarget target) { saved = true; target.add(message); } }); The placeholder tag implies a markup id. Use it on every component that you hide or show through Ajax, and on a container whose visibility depends on its children. Show, hide or disable a component covers onConfigure.

title: Upload files
text: Let users upload one or more files with FileUploadField, limit their size and number, and show upload progress.
keywords: file upload multipart input type file max size upload limit attachment multiple files progress bar
body: You need this when a form takes a file from the user, such as an avatar or a document. The browser sends the file along with the form as a multipart request; Wicket switches the form to multipart as soon as it contains a FileUploadField.

title: Limit the size of uploads
text: Set the limits on the form. A request that exceeds them fails before your onSubmit() runs, and the form reports an error message instead. form.setMaxSize(Bytes.
body: Set the limits on the form. A request that exceeds them fails before your onSubmit() runs, and the form reports an error message instead. form.setMaxSize(Bytes.megabytes(10)); // whole request form.setFileMaxSize(Bytes.megabytes(2)); // each file form.setFileCountMax(5); // number of files Set a default for every form in the application in init(): getApplicationSettings().setDefaultMaximumUploadSize(Bytes.megabytes(10)); The messages use the keys uploadTooLarge, uploadSingleFileTooLarge, uploadTooManyFiles and, for other upload errors, uploadFailed, with the variables ${maxSize}, ${fileMaxSize} and ${fileCountMax}. Override them in your properties files like any other message. Your servlet container may have its own limit on the request size as well.

title: React when the user picks a file
text: FilesSelectedBehavior sends the name, size and type of the selected files to the server over Ajax, before the form is submitted. Use it to warn about a file tha
body: FilesSelectedBehavior sends the name, size and type of the selected files to the server over Ajax, before the form is submitted. Use it to warn about a file that is too large: fileField.add(FilesSelectedBehavior.onSelected((target, files) -> { for (FileDescription file : files) { // check file.getFileSize(), file.getFileName(), file.getMimeType() } }));

title: Show upload progress
text: UploadProgressBar from wicket-extensions shows how far a large upload has come. Turn on progress tracking in the application and add the bar to the form: // in
body: UploadProgressBar from wicket-extensions shows how far a large upload has come. Turn on progress tracking in the application and add the bar to the form: // in WicketApplication.init() getApplicationSettings().setUploadProgressUpdatesEnabled(true); form.add(new UploadProgressBar("progress", form, fileField));

title: Upload a file
text: Add a FileUploadField to the form and bind it to <input type="file">. In onSubmit(), ask the field for the uploaded file. UploadPage.java FileUploadField fileFi
apis: FileUploadField Form Void Override FileUpload InputStream Uploaded IOException Upload FeedbackPanel File String
body:
Add a FileUploadField to the form and bind it to . In onSubmit(), ask the field for the uploaded file. UploadPage.java FileUploadField fileField = new FileUploadField("file"); fileField.setRequired(true); Form form = new Form<>("form") { @Override protected void onSubmit() { FileUpload upload = fileField.getFileUpload(); try (InputStream in = upload.getInputStream()) { documentService.store(upload.getClientFileName(), upload.getContentType(), in); success("Uploaded " + upload.getClientFileName()); } catch (IOException e) { error("Upload failed"); } } }; form.add(fileField); form.add(new FeedbackPanel("feedback")); add(form); UploadPage.html
getFileUpload() returns null when the user did not pick a file. A FileUpload gives you: Method Returns getClientFileName() the file name as the browser sent it getContentType() the content type as the browser sent it getSize() the size in bytes getInputStream() the content as a stream getBytes() the content as a byte array writeTo(File) writes the content to a file writeToTempFile() writes the content to a new temporary file and returns it getDigest(String), getMD5() a checksum of the content Handle the upload in the same request. At the end of the request Wicket closes the streams of the upload and sets the field’s model back to null, so do not keep the FileUpload for later. The client file name and content type come from the browser. Do not use them as a path on your server without checking them.

title: Upload several files at once
text: Add the multiple attribute to the input. The browser then lets the user pick several files, and getFileUploads() returns them all: <input type="file" multiple w
body: Add the multiple attribute to the input. The browser then lets the user pick several files, and getFileUploads() returns them all: <input type="file" multiple wicket:id="files"> for (FileUpload upload : filesField.getFileUploads()) { // store each file } MultiFileUploadField offers a list in which the user adds files one by one and can remove them before submitting. Its model holds the collection of uploads.

title: Wrap content with a Border
text: Write the markup that goes around content once, as a Border, and wrap any part of a page in it while the page keeps its own components.
keywords: wicket:border wicket:body wrapper frame box card decorator addToBorder layout around content
body: Use a border when the same markup goes around different content: a card with a title bar, a collapsible box, a form section with a heading. A panel replaces the content of its tag; a border keeps that content and puts its own markup around it.

title: Add components to the border or to the body
text: A border has two places for child components, and a separate method for each: Where the tag is Method In the border’s own markup file (title above) addToBorder,
body: A border has two places for child components, and a separate method for each: Where the tag is Method In the border’s own markup file (title above) addToBorder, removeFromBorder, replaceInBorder, queueToBorder In the content inside the border’s tag in the page (user above) add, remove, replace, queue add on a border goes to its body container, which you can also get with getBodyContainer(). If <wicket:body/> sits inside a component in the border’s markup, add the body container to that component yourself: WebMarkupContainer collapsible = new WebMarkupContainer("collapsible"); addToBorder(collapsible); collapsible.add(getBodyContainer());

title: Hide the content but keep the frame
text: The body container is a component, so you can hide only the content, for example for a collapsed box: getBodyContainer().setVisible(false);
body: The body container is a component, so you can hide only the content, for example for a collapsed box: getBodyContainer().setVisible(false);

title: Wrap a single component with BorderBehavior
text: When the content is one component and the frame needs no components of its own, a BorderBehavior is lighter. Subclass it, give it a markup file with <wicket:bor
body: When the content is one component and the frame needs no components of its own, a BorderBehavior is lighter. Subclass it, give it a markup file with <wicket:border> and <wicket:body/> like above, and add it to the component: public class FieldFrame extends BorderBehavior { } form.add(new TextField<>("email", emailModel).add(new FieldFrame())); The frame markup is written around the component’s tag. A BorderBehavior cannot hold components in its markup.

text: Attach the border to a tag in the page and write the content inside that tag. Components in that content are added to the border with add: AccountPage.html <sec
body:
Attach the border to a tag in the page and write the content inside that tag. Components in that content are added to the border with add: AccountPage.html

title: Hide surrounding markup with wicket:enclosure
text: Hide a caption, label or table row together with the component it describes, without a container component in Java.
keywords: wicket:enclosure hide label hide caption enclosure child attribute inline enclosure optional field empty value
body: Use this when a value comes with markup that describes it, such as a caption, a <dt> or a table row, and that markup should disappear when the value’s component is hidden. Without an enclosure you would need a WebMarkupContainer around both and keep its visibility in sync.

title: Choose the controlling component
text: With one component inside the enclosure, that component decides. With more, name the one that decides in the child attribute; otherwise Wicket stops with Use <w
body:
With one component inside the enclosure, that component decides. With more, name the one that decides in the child attribute; otherwise Wicket stops with Use to name the child component.
Phone
()
 When the controlling component sits inside a container, give its path with : between the ids:
Phone

title: Use enclosures around form components
text: An enclosure does not become the parent of the components inside it: in Java they stay children of the page or panel. When the enclosure is hidden because one f
body: An enclosure does not become the parent of the components inside it: in Java they stay children of the page or panel. When the enclosure is hidden because one field is invisible, the other fields in it are still part of the form. They are validated on submit, and a required field raises an error the user cannot see. Two ways around this: Add the components with queue() instead of add(). Wicket then builds the hierarchy from the markup, and the enclosure becomes the real parent of the fields. Hidden enclosure, skipped fields. See Add components without repeating the markup hierarchy. Replace the tag with an EnclosureContainer: a container you add yourself, attached to an ordinary tag or a <wicket:container>, that takes its visibility from one child. Add the fields to it. TextField<String> phone = new TextField<>("phone", phoneModel); EnclosureContainer phoneGroup = new EnclosureContainer("phoneGroup", phone); phoneGroup.add(phone, new TextField<>("phoneType", phoneTypeModel)); add(phoneGroup); <wicket:container wicket:id="phoneGroup"> <label>Phone <input wicket:id="phone"></label> <label>Type <input wicket:id="phoneType"></label> </wicket:container> EnclosureContainer renders without its own tag, so it cannot be repainted with Ajax; repaint its parent instead. For why enclosures behave this way, see How markup becomes components.

title: Use the enclosure as an attribute
text: When the markup to hide is a single element, put wicket:enclosure on that element instead of adding a tag around it. Leave the value empty to let the first comp
body:
When the markup to hide is a single element, put wicket:enclosure on that element instead of adding a tag around it. Leave the value empty to let the first component inside decide, or give the id of the controlling component.
Phone
This form also works with Ajax. The element gets a markup id and a placeholder of its own, and when you add the controlling component to an AjaxRequestTarget, Wicket repaints the whole element instead, so the row appears or disappears together with the value. With the tag, only the component itself is repainted.

title: Wrap the markup in wicket:enclosure
text: Put the caption and the component inside <wicket:enclosure>. When the component is invisible, Wicket leaves out everything inside the tag. CustomerPanel.html <d
body: Put the caption and the component inside <wicket:enclosure>. When the component is invisible, Wicket leaves out everything inside the tag. CustomerPanel.html <dl> <dt>Name</dt> <dd wicket:id="name"></dd> <wicket:enclosure> <dt>Phone</dt> <dd wicket:id="phone"></dd> </wicket:enclosure> </dl> CustomerPanel.java add(new Label("name", () -> customer.getName())); add(new Label("phone", () -> customer.getPhone()) { @Override protected void onConfigure() { super.onConfigure(); setVisible(customer.getPhone() != null); } }); The components stay children of the panel in Java. Only the markup has the extra level.

title: Swap markup with fragments
text: Keep small alternative pieces of markup inside a page or panel and choose in Java which one to show, without a panel class for each.
keywords: wicket:fragment inline panel alternative markup switch markup replace content conditional markup variant
body: Use a fragment when a spot on a page shows one of a few small blocks of markup, and a separate panel class with its own HTML file for each block would be overkill. A fragment is a component whose markup sits in the file of the page or panel that uses it, inside a <wicket:fragment> tag.

title: Choose between a fragment and a panel
text: A fragment belongs to the page or panel that defines it: other classes cannot use its markup. When the same block is needed in more than one place, make it a pa
body: A fragment belongs to the page or panel that defines it: other classes cannot use its markup. When the same block is needed in more than one place, make it a panel. See Build a reusable panel.

title: Create the fragment in Java
text: The Fragment constructor takes three things: the id of the tag where it goes, the wicket:id of the <wicket:fragment>, and the container whose markup file holds
apis: Fragment RegistrationPage WebPage String Form Void Override EmailTextField LambdaModel Check
body:
The Fragment constructor takes three things: the id of the tag where it goes, the wicket:id of the , and the container whose markup file holds the fragment. Components inside the fragment are added to the Fragment. RegistrationPage.java public class RegistrationPage extends WebPage { private String email; public RegistrationPage() { Fragment formFragment = new Fragment("content", "formFragment", this); add(formFragment); Form form = new Form("form") { @Override protected void onSubmit() { register(email); formFragment.replaceWith(new Fragment("content", "doneFragment", RegistrationPage.this)); } }; form.add(new EmailTextField("email", LambdaModel.of(() -> email, value -> email = value))); formFragment.add(form); } } After a successful submit, the
holds the content of the second fragment (shown as in deployment mode, without Wicket attributes):

Check your mail to activate your account.

title: Define the fragments and the place they go
text: Put each alternative in a <wicket:fragment> with its own wicket:id. Wicket does not render fragment markup where it is defined. Add a normal tag where the chose
body:
Put each alternative in a with its own wicket:id. Wicket does not render fragment markup where it is defined. Add a normal tag where the chosen fragment should appear. RegistrationPage.html

Register

Check your mail to activate your account.

title: Swap one fragment for another
text: Fragments are components, so you swap them like any component: replaceWith on the old one, or replace on the parent with a new component that has the same id. T
body: Fragments are components, so you swap them like any component: replaceWith on the old one, or replace on the parent with a new component that has the same id. To swap with Ajax, give the fragment’s tag a markup id with setOutputMarkupId(true) on both fragments, swap, and add the new fragment to the AjaxRequestTarget.

title: Use fragments in a list
text: Fragments work well when the items of a list need different markup. The markup provider is the page or panel whose file holds the fragments, not the list item:
apis: ListView Message Override ListItem String Fragment InboxPage
body: Fragments work well when the items of a list need different markup. The markup provider is the page or panel whose file holds the fragments, not the list item: add(new ListView<Message>("messages", messagesModel) { @Override protected void populateItem(ListItem<Message> item) { String fragmentId = item.getModelObject().isUrgent() ? "urgent" : "normal"; item.add(new Fragment("message", fragmentId, InboxPage.this, item.getModel())); } }); The fourth argument is the fragment’s model; components inside the fragment get it from the fragment with getDefaultModel(), as they would from a panel.

title: Keep data in the session
text: Store per-user data in a typed Wicket session, in session attributes or as metadata, control when the session is created, and end it on logout.
keywords: HttpSession session attribute user data shopping cart current user newSession temporary session bind invalidate logout session fixation metadata scoped variable
body: Keep data in the session when it belongs to the user rather than to one page: the logged-in user, a shopping cart, preferences. Wicket wraps the HTTP session in a Session object, which you reach from anywhere in a request with Session.get(). Everything in the session is serialized when the container stores or replicates it, so keep it small and serializable. Store ids, not entities, and never pages or components.

title: End the session on logout
text: invalidate() ends the session at the end of the current request. The page rendered in this request still works: add(new Link<Void>("logout") { @Override public
body: invalidate() ends the session at the end of the current request. The page rendered in this request still works: add(new Link<Void>("logout") { @Override public void onClick() { getSession().invalidate(); setResponsePage(getApplication().getHomePage()); } }); invalidateNow() ends it immediately and removes all pages of the session, so the rest of the request cannot use them. After a successful login, give the session a new id with changeSessionId(), to protect against session fixation. Log users in shows this in context.

title: Reach the HTTP session directly
text: Some tools need an attribute with an exact name in the HttpSession, without Wicket’s prefix. Get the servlet session from the request: HttpSession httpSession =
body: Some tools need an attribute with an exact name in the HttpSession, without Wicket’s prefix. Get the servlet session from the request: HttpSession httpSession = ((ServletWebRequest) RequestCycle.get().getRequest()) .getContainerRequest().getSession(); httpSession.setAttribute("userName", user.getName()); Prefer the Wicket session for everything else: it works the same in tests with WicketTester and does not tie your code to the servlet API.

title: React to new sessions
text: Register an ISessionListener to run code when a session is created or unbound: getSessionListeners().add(new ISessionListener() { @Override public void onCreate
body: Register an ISessionListener to run code when a session is created or unbound: getSessionListeners().add(new ISessionListener() { @Override public void onCreated(Session session) { log.info("Session created, locale {}", session.getLocale()); } @Override public void onUnbound(String sessionId) { log.info("Session {} ended", sessionId); } });

title: Store loose values as session attributes
text: For a value that does not deserve a field, use attributes. The value must be Serializable: Session.get().setAttribute("lastSearch", query); String last = (Strin
body: For a value that does not deserve a field, use attributes. The value must be Serializable: Session.get().setAttribute("lastSearch", query); String last = (String) Session.get().getAttribute("lastSearch"); Session.get().removeAttribute("lastSearch"); Wicket stores the attributes in the HTTP session, with a prefix in front of the name so that they do not clash with attributes of other applications or filters in the same session.

title: Store typed data in your own session class
text: Subclass WebSession, give it fields with getters and setters, and add a static get() that casts: AppSession.java public class AppSession extends WebSession { pr
apis: WebSession AppSession Long Request Session Override Response
body: Subclass WebSession, give it fields with getters and setters, and add a static get() that casts: AppSession.java public class AppSession extends WebSession { private Long userId; public AppSession(Request request) { super(request); } public static AppSession get() { return (AppSession) Session.get(); } public Long getUserId() { return userId; } public void setUserId(Long userId) { this.userId = userId; dirty(); } } Tell the application to create it: WicketApplication.java @Override public Session newSession(Request request, Response response) { return new AppSession(request); } Read and write it anywhere in a request: AppSession.get().getUserId(). Call dirty() after a change, as the setter does. It tells Wicket to store the session again at the end of the request, which session replication in a cluster needs, and it makes a temporary session permanent.

title: Store values under a typed key
text: Metadata stores a value under a MetaDataKey, which gives you type safety without a session subclass. Define the key once, as a constant: public static final Met
apis: MetaDataKey Cart Session Serializable Application RequestCycle Component
body: Metadata stores a value under a MetaDataKey, which gives you type safety without a session subclass. Define the key once, as a constant: public static final MetaDataKey<Cart> CART = new MetaDataKey<>() {}; Session.get().setMetaData(CART, cart); Cart cart = Session.get().getMetaData(CART); The value must be Serializable. The same API exists on Application, RequestCycle and Component, for values that live as long as the application, the request or the component. Values stored on Application and RequestCycle do not have to be serializable.

title: Temporary and permanent sessions
text: As long as a user only sees stateless pages, Wicket does not create an HTTP session. Session.get() still works, but returns a temporary session that is thrown a
body: As long as a user only sees stateless pages, Wicket does not create an HTTP session. Session.get() still works, but returns a temporary session that is thrown away at the end of the request. isTemporary() returns true and getId() returns null. Wicket makes the session permanent when a stateful page has to be stored. To keep data from a stateless page, make it permanent yourself with bind(): public class LandingPage extends WebPage { public LandingPage(PageParameters parameters) { Session.get().setAttribute("campaign", parameters.get("utm_campaign").toString()); Session.get().bind(); setResponsePage(HomePage.class); } } Without bind(), the attribute would be gone in the next request.

title: Push updates over a WebSocket
text: Set up wicket-native-websocket, handle messages from the browser and push component updates to a page from a background thread.
keywords: server push real-time live update broadcast notification background job progress wicket-native-websocket-javax Spring Boot websocket
apis: WebSocketBehavior WebSocketRequestHandler WebSocketPushBroadcaster IWebSocketPushMessage WebSocketPushPayload JavaxWebSocketFilter WebSocketSettings ConnectedMessage WebSocketResource
body: Use this when the server has to update a page without the user doing anything: a job that reports progress, a chat, a dashboard that follows live data. How native WebSockets work explains what happens underneath.

title: Add the dependency and the filter
text: Add the module to your build: pom.xml <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-native-websocket-javax</artifactId> <version>${wicket
apis: WicketFilter JavaxWebSocketFilter WicketApplication Bean FilterRegistrationBean DispatcherType SpringWebApplicationFactory ServerEndpointExporter WicketServerEndpointConfig
body: Add the module to your build: pom.xml <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.wicket</groupId> <artifactId>wicket-native-websocket-javax</artifactId> <version>${wicket.version}</version> </dependency> Replace WicketFilter with JavaxWebSocketFilter. In web.xml, only the filter class changes: web.xml <filter> <filter-name>wicket</filter-name> <filter-class>org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.javax.JavaxWebSocketFilter</filter-class> <init-param> <param-name>applicationClassName</param-name> <param-value>com.example.WicketApplication</param-value> </init-param> </filter> The servlet container has to support Jakarta WebSocket, as Tomcat, Jetty and WildFly do. With Spring Boot Add spring-boot-starter-websocket, register the filter, and export Wicket’s endpoint: @Bean public FilterRegistrationBean<JavaxWebSocketFilter> wicketFilter() { var registration = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(new JavaxWebSocketFilter()); registration.setDispatcherTypes(DispatcherType.REQUEST, DispatcherType.ERROR, DispatcherType.FORWARD, DispatcherType.ASYNC); registration.setAsyncSupported(true); registration.addInitParameter(WicketFilter.APP_FACT_PARAM, SpringWebApplicationFactory.class.getName()); registration.addInitParameter(WicketFilter.FILTER_MAPPING_PARAM, "/*"); registration.addUrlPatterns("/*"); return registration; } @Bean public ServerEndpointExporter serverEndpointExporter() { return new ServerEndpointExporter(); } @Bean public WicketServerEndpointConfig wicketServerEndpointConfig() { return new WicketServerEndpointConfig(); }

title: Answer messages from the browser
text: Add a WebSocketBehavior to the page, or to a component on it. The browser opens the connection when the page loads. Override the callbacks you need: add(new Web
apis: WebSocketBehavior Override WebSocketRequestHandler TextMessage AjaxRequestTarget String
body: Add a WebSocketBehavior to the page, or to a component on it. The browser opens the connection when the page loads. Override the callbacks you need: add(new WebSocketBehavior() { @Override protected void onMessage(WebSocketRequestHandler handler, TextMessage message) { chat.add(message.getText()); handler.add(messages); } }); handler.add(...) re-renders components in the browser, exactly as with an AjaxRequestTarget; the components need a markup id. handler.push(String) sends a plain text message instead, which your JavaScript receives; see WebSocket JavaScript API. appendJavaScript and prependJavaScript work as well.

title: Push an update from a background thread
text: Code outside a request cannot touch components. It sends a message object, and the page’s components turn it into an update. Define the message as a class imple
apis: IWebSocketPushMessage JobProgress WebSocketBehavior Override ConnectedMessage ProgressReporter String IKey Serializable Application WebSocketSettings Holder WebSocketPushBroadcaster IEvent WebSocketPushPayload
body: Code outside a request cannot touch components. It sends a message object, and the page’s components turn it into an update. Define the message as a class implementing IWebSocketPushMessage: public record JobProgress(int percent) implements IWebSocketPushMessage { } Remember where to send it. The connection is identified by the application name, the session id and a key for the page. onConnect gives you all three: add(new WebSocketBehavior() { @Override protected void onConnect(ConnectedMessage message) { jobs.start(new ProgressReporter(message.getApplication().getName(), message.getSessionId(), message.getKey())); } }); In the background thread, broadcast the message to that connection: public record ProgressReporter(String applicationName, String sessionId, IKey key) implements Serializable { public void report(int percent) { Application application = Application.get(applicationName); var registry = WebSocketSettings.Holder.get(application).getConnectionRegistry(); new WebSocketPushBroadcaster(registry).broadcast( new ConnectedMessage(application, sessionId, key), new JobProgress(percent)); } } Receive it in the page or a component and update the components: @Override public void onEvent(IEvent<?> event) { super.onEvent(event); if (event.getPayload() instanceof WebSocketPushPayload payload && payload.getMessage() instanceof JobProgress progress) { percent = progress.percent(); payload.getHandler().add(progressBar); } } WebSocketBehavior.onPush(handler, message) receives the same messages, if you prefer to handle them in the behavior. A connection that has closed in the meantime is skipped without an error.

body: WebSocketPushBroadcaster also has broadcastAll(application, message) for every connection of the application, broadcastAllInSession(application, sessionId, message) for one user’s pages, and broadcastAllMatchingFilter(application, filter, message) with a lambda that selects connections by session id and key: broadcaster.broadcastAllMatchingFilter(application, (sessionId, key) -> key instanceof PageIdKey, new PriceChanged(product)); By default the broadcast runs in the calling thread, one page after the other. WebSocketSettings.setWebSocketPushMessageExecutor moves it to other threads.

body: When the browser renders the data itself, for example a chart that receives a stream of numbers, send text straight to the connection and skip the page: IWebSocketConnection connection = registry.getConnection(application, sessionId, key); if (connection != null && connection.isOpen()) { connection.sendMessageAsync(json); } For many messages from the browser, a WebSocketResource handles them without taking the page lock. Register it with getSharedResources().add("prices", new PriceResource()) in init() and add new BaseWebSocketBehavior("prices") to the page. It has the same callbacks as WebSocketBehavior, but cannot re-render components.

body: A page with a WebSocketBehavior or BaseWebSocketBehavior loads wicket-websocket-jquery.js and opens one connection when the DOM is ready. The script is a thin layer over the browser’s WebSocket: it builds the connection URL, applies <ajax-response> messages from the server and publishes everything else as events.

title: Connection URL
text: The connection goes to /wicket/websocket under the context path and the filter prefix, with ws: or wss: matching the page’s protocol. The query string carries t
body: The connection goes to /wicket/websocket under the context path and the filter prefix, with ws: or wss: matching the page’s protocol. The query string carries the page id or the resource name of a WebSocketResource, the page class as context, the application name and the base URL. The session id is added to the path when the session is tracked in the URL or no session cookie is available. The parts can be changed in WebSocketSettings: Setting Default setPort(int) The port of the page. setSecurePort(int) The port of the page, for wss:. setContextPath(CharSequence) The servlet context path. setFilterPrefix(CharSequence) Empty. Set it to the filter path when the filter is not mapped to /*, for example /app. setBaseUrl(CharSequence) The base URL of the page. WebSocketSettings.Holder.get(this).setPort(8000); Behind a proxy that serves WebSockets on another port, set the ports. Subclasses of BaseWebSocketBehavior can override getPort, getSecurePort, getContextPath, getFilterPrefix and getBaseUrl to compute them per page.

body: Subscribe with Wicket.Event.subscribe(topic, function (event, ...) { }). The first argument is Wicket’s event object; the other arguments are listed below. Topic Arguments after the event Published when /websocket/open the browser’s open event The connection is open. /websocket/message the message data A message arrives that is not an <ajax-response>, such as text sent with WebSocketRequestHandler.push(String) or IWebSocketConnection.sendMessage(String). /websocket/closed the browser’s close event The connection is closed. /websocket/error the browser’s error event A communication error occurred. The connection is closed. /websocket/notsupported an error message The browser has no WebSocket support. Wicket.Event.subscribe('/websocket/message', function (event, message) { var data = JSON.parse(message); updateChart(data); }); The topic names are also available as Wicket.Event.Topic.WebSocket.Opened, Message, Closed, Error and NotSupported.

title: Why component-oriented
text: What a component-oriented framework does differently from request-based MVC frameworks, what Wicket gains from it, and what it costs.
keywords: component tree component-based MVC action-based request-based server-side state compare frameworks JSF Vaadin Spring MVC Thymeleaf single-page application plain HTML templates Swing
body: Wicket is a component-oriented web framework: you build a web page the way you build a desktop window in Swing, as a tree of Java objects, and the framework turns that tree into HTML. Most Java web frameworks work the other way around. To understand the trade-off, it helps to look at what each approach makes you do yourself.

title: A tree of components on the server
text: A component-oriented framework keeps a model of the page on the server. In Wicket, a page is an instance of a WebPage subclass. It contains components, such as
body: A component-oriented framework keeps a model of the page on the server. In Wicket, a page is an instance of a WebPage subclass. It contains components, such as labels, links, forms and text fields, and containers that hold other components. Together they form a tree. When a request comes in, Wicket finds or creates the page, lets the components handle the request, and then asks each component to render its part of the HTML. You can think of this tree as a DOM that lives on the server: it exists before any HTML does, and the HTML is generated from it, not the other way around. A link is not a URL you construct, but a component with an onClick() method. A text field is not a request parameter, but an object that converts and validates its input and writes it to your Java object. Wicket shares this idea with other component frameworks. Jakarta Faces builds a component tree from its view definitions, and Vaadin builds the whole user interface in Java and renders it with its own client-side widgets. Wicket’s version keeps the HTML in plain HTML files and the behavior in plain Java classes.

title: Request-based frameworks
text: Frameworks such as Spring MVC, Jakarta MVC and Struts are request-based. A controller method handles one HTTP request: it reads request parameters, calls the bu
body: Frameworks such as Spring MVC, Jakarta MVC and Struts are request-based. A controller method handles one HTTP request: it reads request parameters, calls the business code, puts some values in a model map and names a template. The template, in Thymeleaf, JSP or FreeMarker, pulls the values out of that map with an expression language and produces HTML. This maps directly onto HTTP, and that is its strength. Every request stands on its own, the server keeps nothing between requests unless you put it in the session, and URLs and parameters are under your control. It also means the web is never hidden from you. A form that a user edits over three requests is three separate controller calls, and keeping the values in between is your job: in hidden fields, in the session, or in the URL. Converting the request parameters, which are strings, to your types and back is your job too, as is deciding which part of the page changes after an action. The page itself is not an object you can hold on to; it is the output of a template.

title: What it costs
text: Memory and serialization. Keeping pages on the server has a price. Wicket keeps the most recent pages of each session in memory and writes pages to disk, which
body: Memory and serialization. Keeping pages on the server has a price. Wicket keeps the most recent pages of each session in memory and writes pages to disk, which means everything a page refers to must be serializable and should be small. Models that load data per request and let it go at the end, detachable models, exist for this reason. How pages are stored describes the mechanism. Stateless pages take effort. A page with a plain Link or Form is stateful: its URLs point to a stored page instance, and the page expires with the session. For pages that search engines index or that must survive a server restart, you choose stateless components and bookmarkable URLs deliberately. Stateful and stateless pages explains when Wicket keeps a page and when it does not. HTTP is further away. Wicket generates URLs, so readable URLs require mounting pages. A developer who knows request-based frameworks has to learn when a component’s code runs, and that a page instance lives longer than one request. It is not a client-side framework. Wicket renders HTML on the server, also for Ajax updates. It suits applications with many forms and much business logic: administration screens, line-of-business applications, portals. If your interface lives mostly in the browser and talks to the server through a JSON API, a JavaScript framework fits better, and Wicket can still wrap JavaScript widgets as components when you need some of both.

title: What you gain
text: Pages are objects. You write a page as a Java class, so everything you know about classes applies. A base class gives all pages the same layout, and Wicket exte
body: Pages are objects. You write a page as a Java class, so everything you know about classes applies. A base class gives all pages the same layout, and Wicket extends that inheritance to the markup. A panel you write once is a component you use on any page, packaged with its markup, CSS and JavaScript in a jar if you like. State is ordinary Java state. Because Wicket keeps the page between requests, a field on a page keeps its value. A wizard can hold the object it is building in a field, a list can remember its sort order, and a form shows the values the user typed after a validation error, without you storing anything in the session by hand. Wicket stores the pages for you, per user session. HTML stays HTML. A Wicket template is an HTML file with wicket:id attributes on the tags that components fill in. It has no loops, no conditions and no expression language: those live in Java, where the compiler checks them and your IDE can refactor them. A designer can open the template in a browser, and you can put example content in it that Wicket replaces at run time. Data binding is built in. Components read and write their values through models. A text field converts the submitted string to your type, validates it and sets it on your object, and shows the current value when it renders. You do not parse request parameters. You can test without a browser. Since pages and components are objects, WicketTester can render them, click their links and submit their forms in a plain JUnit test, without a servlet container.

title: Why Wicket among component frameworks
text: Wicket has existed since 2004 and has been an Apache Software Foundation project since 2007, developed in the open under the Apache License 2.0. It is not tied
body: Wicket has existed since 2004 and has been an Apache Software Foundation project since 2007, developed in the open under the Apache License 2.0. It is not tied to a company’s product line or license changes. Its user list and issue tracker are open to anyone. It also stays small in what it asks of you. There is no special template language and no XML configuration besides an optional web.xml: an application is a class with getHomePage() and an init() method, and pages are classes with HTML files next to them. Everything else is Java, which is where Wicket wants your application’s logic to be.

title: Which anchors are left alone
text: Inside <wicket:link>, Wicket only rewrites tags that have no wicket:id and whose href or src contains no colon. Links such as https://wicket.apache.org or mailt
body: Inside <wicket:link>, Wicket only rewrites tags that have no wicket:id and whose href or src contains no colon. Links such as https://wicket.apache.org or mailto:dev@wicket.apache.org stay as they are. A href that does not end in .html (or .xml, .wml, .svg) is treated as a package resource instead of a page: <link href="style.css"> inside <wicket:link> becomes a URL to style.css in the package of the page. See Serve files from your Java packages.

apis: HomePage Home ProductListPage Products ProfilePage Your PageParameters
body: Point each href at the markup file of the target page, relative to the package of the current page: HomePage.html, in package com.example Home Products Your profile Wicket strips the .html, resolves the rest as a class name relative to the package, and creates a link to that page. account/ProfilePage.html becomes com.example.account.ProfilePage, and ../HomePage.html in a page from com.example.account points back to com.example.HomePage. The target page must be bookmarkable: it needs a constructor without arguments or one that takes PageParameters. Because the href values are real file paths, the links also work when you open the markup files in a browser from your source tree.

body: Wicket reads a small set of tags and attributes from your HTML. They all live in the wicket XML namespace. Declare it on the <html> tag of every markup file: <!DOCTYPE html> <html xmlns:wicket="http://wicket.apache.org"> The declaration is optional: Wicket assumes the prefix wicket when there is none. It keeps editors and validators quiet, and it lets you choose another prefix. Any namespace URI that starts with http://wicket.apache.org works, so xmlns:w="http://wicket.apache.org" makes Wicket read w:id and <w:panel> instead.

body: Tag or attribute Kind What it does wicket:id attribute Attaches an HTML tag to a Java component wicket:panel tag Marks the part of a panel’s file that is the panel wicket:child tag Marks where a subclass inserts its markup wicket:extend tag Marks the markup a subclass contributes to its parent’s markup wicket:fragment tag Defines inline markup for a Fragment wicket:border tag Marks the part of a border’s file that wraps the body wicket:body tag Marks where a border puts the content it wraps wicket:enclosure tag and attribute Hides surrounding markup together with one component wicket:container tag A component tag that leaves no HTML element in the output wicket:message tag and attribute Inserts a localized text, or localizes attribute values wicket:label tag Writes the label text of a form component wicket:for attribute Connects a <label> to a form component wicket:link tag Turns plain links and resource references into Wicket links wicket:head tag Content a panel, border or page contributes to the page <head> wicket:header-items tag Marks where in <head> Wicket writes header contributions wicket:remove tag Preview markup that never reaches the browser Any other tag in the namespace stops the parser with Unknown tag name with Wicket namespace.

title: Wicket tags in development and deployment mode
text: In development mode Wicket tags and wicket: attributes stay in the HTML sent to the browser, which helps when you inspect the page. In deployment mode Wicket st
body: In development mode Wicket tags and wicket: attributes stay in the HTML sent to the browser, which helps when you inspect the page. In deployment mode Wicket strips them. The MarkupSettings#setStripWicketTags(boolean) setting controls this; the configuration type sets it for you. Browsers ignore unknown tags, but CSS selectors such as div > p see the extra elements, so a selector can match in deployment mode and not in development mode. See Switch between development and deployment mode.

body: Marks the place in a page’s or panel’s markup where a subclass inserts its markup. A markup file contains at most one <wicket:child>. Write it as an empty tag; Wicket does not allow Wicket tags or components between an opening and a closing wicket:child. Attributes: none. text: A tag for a component that should not produce an HTML element of its own. Use it where an extra <div> or <span> would be invalid, such as between table rows, or
body:
A tag for a component that should not produce an HTML element of its own. Use it where an extra
or would be invalid, such as between table rows, or where it would get in the way of your CSS. Attribute Required Meaning wicket:id yes The component id Do not put other attributes on it: in deployment mode the whole tag is stripped, attributes included. Wicket logs a warning in development mode when it finds any.

title: wicket:enclosure
text: Shows or hides a block of markup together with one component inside it. When that component is invisible, the whole block is left out. It exists as a tag and as
body:
Shows or hides a block of markup together with one component inside it. When that component is invisible, the whole block is left out. It exists as a tag and as an attribute. As a tag Attribute Required Meaning child only with more than one component inside Id of the component that controls visibility. A path such as address:street reaches a nested component. The tag cannot be empty ( is an error). Enclosures can be nested.
Phone
 As an attribute Put wicket:enclosure on any HTML element that can contain other elements. Leave the value empty to let the first component inside control the visibility, or give the controlling component’s id. This form keeps its HTML element, gets a markup id, and is updated along with its controlling component in Ajax requests. Phone If the element has both an id and a wicket:id, the two must be equal. See Hide surrounding markup with wicket:enclosure.

title: wicket:extend
text: Wraps the markup a subclass contributes to its parent’s markup. Wicket merges it into the parent’s markup at <wicket:child>. Everything outside <wicket:extend>
body:
Wraps the markup a subclass contributes to its parent’s markup. Wicket merges it into the parent’s markup at . Everything outside is ignored, except . Without , a subclass’s markup file replaces the parent’s markup instead of extending it. Attributes: none. ProductPage.html

If the parent’s markup has no , loading fails with Expected to find in base markup.

title: wicket:for
text: Connects a <label> tag to a form component without a component of its own. Wicket renders the for attribute with the form component’s markup id and turns on set
body: Connects a <label> tag to a form component without a component of its own. Wicket renders the for attribute with the form component’s markup id and turns on setOutputMarkupId(true) for it. It also adds CSS classes to the label: required when the component is required, error when it failed validation, and disabled when it is not enabled. Override the class names with the resource keys AutoLabel.CSS.required, AutoLabel.CSS.error and AutoLabel.CSS.disabled. Rule Detail Value Id of the form component, or a path relative to the label’s container. .. steps up to the parent container. When the path does not resolve, Wicket searches for the id in every container from the label up to the page. Allowed on <label> only, and not together with wicket:id wicket:auto true re-renders the label whenever the form component is updated with Ajax. MarkupSettings#setUpdateAutoLabelsTogetherWithFormComponent(true) does this for every label. <label wicket:for="name">Name</label> <input type="text" wicket:id="name">
